concepts.def: An ad hoc addition to the discount rate for risks unique to one firm, common in private company valuation. Theory says diversifiable risk should be handled in cash flows instead, so it is easily abused.
concepts.aliases: alpha premium,cs rp,specific risk premium,unsystematic risk premium

concepts.name: Build-up method
concepts.def: Estimating cost of equity by stacking premia on the risk-free rate: equity risk premium, size, industry and company-specific premia. Used for private firms without a traded beta.
concepts.formula: Ke = Rf + ERP + size premium + specific premium

concepts.name: Levered beta
concepts.def: Equity beta reflecting both business risk and financial leverage. Hamada's equation relevers an asset beta for a target debt to equity ratio.
concepts.formula: beta_L = beta_U x (1 + (1 - t) x D/E)

concepts.name: Unlevered beta
concepts.def: Beta of a firm's assets as if it had no debt, isolating business risk. Computed from peers' equity betas and leverage, then relevered for the target's capital structure.
concepts.formula: beta_U = beta_L / (1 + (1 - t) x D/E)

concepts.name: Bottom-up beta
concepts.def: A beta built from the average unlevered beta of comparable firms in the same businesses, weighted by the target's mix and relevered. More stable than one firm's regression beta, which has large standard error.

concepts.name: Blume-adjusted beta
concepts.def: A regression beta shrunk toward one, reflecting Blume's (1971) finding that betas mean-revert over time. Used by common data terminals as the default adjusted beta.
concepts.formula: adjusted beta = 0.67 x raw beta + 0.33

concepts.name: Cost of preferred stock
concepts.def: The required return on preferred shares, approximated for perpetual preferred as the dividend divided by price. Enters WACC as a separate weight; preferred dividends are not tax-deductible.
concepts.formula: Kp = preferred dividend / preferred price

concepts.name: Synthetic credit rating
concepts.def: A rating estimated from a firm's interest coverage or leverage by mapping it to typical ratios of rated companies. Provides a default spread and pre-tax cost of debt when no rating exists.
concepts.formula: pre-tax Kd = risk-free rate + spread for synthetic rating

concepts.name: Effective tax rate
concepts.def: Income tax expense divided by pretax income. It differs from the statutory rate because of foreign rates, credits, deferred items and permanent differences; reconciliation appears in the tax note.
concepts.formula: ETR = tax expense / pretax income

concepts.name: Marginal tax rate
concepts.def: The tax rate on the next unit of income. It determines the value of interest deductions and is the right rate for interest tax shields, while the effective rate may suit near-term operating taxes.

concepts.name: Target capital structure
concepts.def: The mix of debt and equity a firm aims to maintain over time. WACC weights should reflect it rather than a temporary current mix.

concepts.name: Market value weights
concepts.def: Weighting debt and equity in WACC by market values rather than book values, because investors' required returns apply to what their claims are worth now.
concepts.formula: w_E = E / (D + E)

concepts.name: Implied cost of capital
concepts.def: The discount rate that equates current price to the present value of forecast cash flows or earnings. A forward-looking expected-return estimate, sensitive to analyst forecast bias.
concepts.formula: solve P0 = sum CF_t / (1 + r)^t for r

concepts.name: Interest tax shield
concepts.def: Tax saved because interest expense is deductible. Its present value is the main gain from debt in Modigliani-Miller with taxes and is captured in WACC through the after-tax cost of debt.
concepts.formula: shield = interest x tax rate

concepts.name: Divisional cost of capital
concepts.def: Using a discount rate matched to each business line's risk instead of one corporate WACC. A single rate over-funds risky units and under-funds safe ones.
concepts.aliases: project discount rate,divisional wacc,risk adjusted hurdle

concepts.name: Capital budgeting
concepts.def: Deciding which long-term investments to make by estimating incremental cash flows and comparing their value with cost using NPV, IRR or payback.

concepts.name: Payback period
concepts.def: Time for a project's cumulative cash flows to recover its initial cost. Easy to explain but ignores the time value of money and cash flows after payback.

concepts.name: Profitability index
concepts.def: Present value of future cash flows divided by initial investment. Above one means positive NPV; useful for ranking projects when capital is limited.
concepts.formula: PI = PV(future cash flows) / investment

concepts.name: Capital rationing
concepts.def: A limit on investment funds that forces a firm to choose among positive-NPV projects. Projects are then ranked by value per unit of scarce capital.

concepts.name: Capital allocation
concepts.def: Management's choice of how to deploy cash among reinvestment, acquisitions, debt reduction, dividends and buybacks. Over long periods it shapes per-share value as much as operations do.

concepts.name: Modigliani-Miller theorem
concepts.def: Modigliani and Miller (1958) showed that, without taxes, distress costs or frictions, firm value does not depend on capital structure. Its value lies in pointing to which frictions do make financing matter.
concepts.formula: V_L = V_U
concepts.aliases: m&m,mm theorem,capital structure irrelevance,mm proposition i

concepts.name: MM proposition II and taxes
concepts.def: Cost of equity rises linearly with leverage because shareholders bear more risk. With corporate taxes, firm value rises by the present value of the interest tax shield.
concepts.formula: Ke = Ku + (Ku - Kd) x (1 - t) x D/E; V_L = V_U + t x D

concepts.name: Trade-off theory
concepts.def: Firms choose leverage by balancing the tax benefit of debt against expected financial distress and agency costs. Predicts that stable, tangible-asset firms carry more debt.

concepts.name: Pecking order theory
concepts.def: Myers and Majluf (1984): because managers know more than investors, firms fund first with internal cash, then debt, and issue equity last. Explains why profitable firms often carry little debt.

concepts.name: Market timing theory
concepts.def: Baker and Wurgler (2002): firms issue equity when their shares are richly valued and repurchase when cheap, so capital structure reflects the history of past timing attempts.

concepts.name: Financial distress costs
concepts.def: Costs of being near default: legal fees, lost customers and suppliers, fire sales and forgone investment. They offset the tax benefit of debt and are higher for firms with intangible assets.
concepts.aliases: bankruptcy costs,distress costs,costs of financial distress

concepts.name: Debt overhang
concepts.def: Myers (1977): when debt is heavy, much of the payoff from new investment goes to creditors, so shareholders pass up positive-NPV projects. A reason distressed firms underinvest.

concepts.name: Asset substitution
concepts.def: Shareholders of a levered firm gain from shifting into riskier projects, since they keep the upside while creditors bear more of the downside. A core agency cost of debt that covenants try to limit.

concepts.name: Free cash flow hypothesis
concepts.def: Jensen (1986): managers with cash beyond profitable investment tend to waste it. Debt, dividends and buybacks discipline them by forcing payouts.
concepts.aliases: jensen free cash flow,agency cost of free cash flow

concepts.name: Agency problem
concepts.def: Conflict that arises when managers act for owners but have their own interests, or when shareholders and creditors want different things. Monitoring, incentives and contracts reduce but never remove it.

concepts.name: Optimal capital structure
concepts.def: The debt to equity mix that minimizes WACC and maximizes firm value given taxes, distress costs and agency effects. In practice it is a range, not a point.

concepts.name: Debt capacity
concepts.def: How much a firm can borrow while keeping acceptable credit metrics and covenant headroom through a downturn. Driven by cash flow stability, asset collateral value and rating targets.

concepts.name: Dividend policy
concepts.def: A firm's approach to how much and how regularly it pays out cash to shareholders. Most firms smooth dividends and treat cuts as a last resort.

concepts.name: Dividend irrelevance
concepts.def: Miller and Modigliani (1961): with no taxes or frictions, payout policy does not change firm value, since investors can create homemade dividends by selling shares.

concepts.name: Dividend signaling
concepts.def: Dividend changes convey management's view of future earnings because cutting is costly. Increases tend to lift prices and cuts to drop them sharply.

concepts.name: Clientele effect
concepts.def: Different investors prefer different payout policies due to taxes, income needs or mandates, so firms attract a clientele matching their policy and changing it can trigger turnover.

concepts.name: Lintner dividend model
concepts.def: Lintner (1956) found firms set a target payout and adjust dividends only partially toward it each year, producing smooth dividends that lag earnings.
concepts.formula: change in D = speed x (target payout x E - D_prior)

concepts.name: Special dividend
concepts.def: A one-off cash distribution outside the regular dividend, often after an asset sale or a cash buildup. Signals excess cash without committing to a higher recurring payout.

concepts.name: Stock split
concepts.def: Issuing more shares per existing share, such as two for one, reducing the price per share without changing total value. Sometimes followed by positive returns, attributed to signaling or retail access.

concepts.name: Reverse split
concepts.def: Combining shares, such as one for ten, to raise the share price, often to meet exchange listing minimums. Usually associated with weak firms and followed by poor returns.

concepts.name: Stock dividend
concepts.def: A distribution of additional shares instead of cash. It moves amounts within equity accounts but does not change firm value or any holder's proportional stake.

concepts.name: Ex-dividend date
concepts.def: The first trading day a share trades without the right to the next dividend. The price typically drops by roughly the dividend amount at the open, adjusted for taxes.

concepts.name: Record date
concepts.def: The date on which a holder must be on the company's books to receive a dividend or vote. With T+1 settlement the ex-date generally falls on the record date.
concepts.aliases: date of record,holder of record date

concepts.name: Dividend cut
concepts.def: A reduction or suspension of a regular dividend, typically after earnings or cash flow fall or leverage rises. Because firms resist cuts, they carry strong negative signaling.

concepts.name: Dividend coverage
concepts.def: How many times earnings or free cash flow cover the dividend. Coverage near or below one warns that the payout depends on borrowing or asset sales.
concepts.formula: coverage = EPS / DPS or FCF / dividends

concepts.name: Dividend aristocrats
concepts.def: Index constituents that have raised dividends every year for a long run, twenty-five years for the S&P 500 version. A screen for durable payers, not a guarantee of future returns.

concepts.name: Dilution
concepts.def: A reduction in existing holders' ownership share or per-share value from new share issuance through equity raises, stock pay, convertibles or stock-funded deals. Value-neutral only if new shares are sold at fair value.

concepts.name: Accelerated share repurchase
concepts.def: A buyback in which a bank delivers most shares to the company upfront, borrows them, and covers by buying in the market over months, with a final price adjustment to the average price.

concepts.name: Dutch auction tender offer
concepts.def: A buyback in which shareholders tender at prices within a stated range and the company pays the lowest single price that fills its target. Quick and large, usually at a premium.
concepts.aliases: dutch auction buyback,modified dutch auction,self tender

concepts.name: Open market repurchase
concepts.def: Buying back shares gradually on the exchange under an authorization, within volume and timing safe harbors. The most common and flexible buyback form; authorizations need not be completed.

concepts.name: Rule 10b5-1 plan
concepts.def: A prearranged trading plan, adopted when the insider lacks material nonpublic information, that lets insiders or companies buy or sell on a schedule while defending against insider trading claims.

concepts.name: Buyback EPS illusion
concepts.def: Buybacks lift EPS mechanically by shrinking share count, but create value only if shares are bought below intrinsic value. Debt-funded buybacks also raise risk, which a higher P/E should not ignore.

concepts.name: Equity issuance signal
concepts.def: Seasoned equity offerings tend to be followed by a price drop at announcement and weak long-run returns, consistent with managers issuing when they think shares are overvalued.

concepts.name: Follow-on offering
concepts.def: A sale of shares by a company that is already public, either newly issued primary shares that dilute holders or secondary shares sold by existing holders.

concepts.name: Rights offering
concepts.def: New shares offered first to existing holders in proportion to their stakes, usually at a discount, with tradable rights. Lets holders avoid dilution if they take up or sell their rights.
concepts.formula: theoretical ex-rights price = (N x P + n x S) / (N + n)

concepts.name: At-the-market offering
concepts.def: A program that lets a listed company sell new shares gradually into the market through a broker at prevailing prices. Common for REITs, utilities and cash-hungry growth firms.

concepts.name: PIPE
concepts.def: Private investment in public equity: a listed company sells shares or convertibles directly to selected investors, often at a discount. Fast, but can signal weak access to ordinary markets.
concepts.aliases: pipe,private placement,private investment in public equity

concepts.name: Underwriting spread
concepts.def: The difference between the price paid by the public and the proceeds to the issuer, kept by underwriting banks. Larger for IPOs and smaller deals.
concepts.formula: gross spread = offer price - price paid to issuer

concepts.name: Greenshoe option
concepts.def: An overallotment option allowing underwriters to sell up to an extra share of the offering, usually fifteen percent, then cover by buying in the market if the price falls or exercising if it rises. Supports post-offering trading.

concepts.name: IPO underpricing
concepts.def: New issues on average close their first day above the offer price, leaving money on the table for issuers. Explanations include information asymmetry, winner's curse among investors and banker incentives.
concepts.formula: first day return = first close / offer price - 1

concepts.name: Lockup expiry
concepts.def: The end of a contractual period, often 180 days after an IPO, during which insiders cannot sell. Expected supply around expiry has been associated with price weakness.

concepts.name: Direct listing
concepts.def: Going public by listing existing shares on an exchange without underwriters selling a new issue. Avoids underwriting fees and lockups but historically raised no new capital.

concepts.name: Debt covenants
concepts.def: Contract terms in loans and bonds that restrict borrower actions or require financial ratios to stay within limits. Breaches give lenders rights to renegotiate, raise pricing or accelerate.

concepts.name: Senior secured debt
concepts.def: Debt with first claim on specified collateral and top payment priority. Lower yields and higher recoveries in default than unsecured or subordinated debt.

concepts.name: Mezzanine financing
concepts.def: Subordinated debt or preferred equity between senior debt and common equity, often with PIK interest and warrants. Fills a financing gap in buyouts at a high cost.

concepts.name: Unitranche loan
concepts.def: A single loan combining senior and junior debt at one blended rate, provided mainly by direct lenders. Faster and simpler than a syndicated capital structure.

concepts.name: Change of control clause
concepts.def: A provision giving bondholders or lenders the right to be repaid, often at 101 percent of par, if the company is acquired. Protects creditors against leveraged takeovers.

concepts.name: Refinancing risk
concepts.def: The risk that maturing debt cannot be rolled over, or only at much higher cost. Highest for weak credits with near-term maturities and for floating-rate borrowers.

concepts.name: Debt-for-equity swap
concepts.def: Creditors cancel debt in exchange for equity in the restructured company. Cuts leverage and usually wipes out or heavily dilutes existing shareholders.

concepts.name: Chapter 7
concepts.def: US bankruptcy liquidation: a trustee sells the debtor's assets and distributes proceeds to creditors by priority. Operations normally cease.

concepts.name: Leveraged recapitalization
concepts.def: Borrowing heavily to pay a large dividend or buy back shares, sharply raising leverage without a change of control. Historically used as a takeover defense or to return cash.

concepts.name: Dividend recapitalization
concepts.def: A sponsor-owned company raises new debt to pay a dividend to its private equity owner. Returns capital early and boosts IRR, at the cost of higher leverage.

concepts.name: Capital structure arbitrage
concepts.def: Trading mispricing between different securities of the same issuer, such as long bonds and short equity, or CDS against stock, on the view that their prices imply inconsistent default risk.

concepts.name: Preferred stock
concepts.def: Equity with priority over common for dividends and liquidation, usually without voting rights and with fixed dividends that may be cumulative. Treated like debt in the equity bridge.

concepts.name: Rating agency credit metrics
concepts.def: Ratios agencies weigh for corporate ratings, chiefly debt to EBITDA, funds from operations to debt and interest coverage, adjusted for leases and pensions. Ratings also reflect business risk and scale.

concepts.name: Merger and acquisition
concepts.def: The combination of two companies, either by one buying the other or both forming a new entity. Value is created for the buyer only if synergies exceed the premium paid plus integration costs.
concepts.formula: buyer value created = PV(synergies) - premium - integration costs

concepts.name: Synergies
concepts.def: Extra value from combining two firms beyond their standalone values, from cost savings, revenue gains, tax or financing benefits. Usually overestimated and slower to arrive than planned.
concepts.formula: synergy = V(A+B) - V(A) - V(B)

concepts.name: Cost synergies
concepts.def: Savings from eliminating overlapping functions, facilities and procurement after a merger. More reliably achieved than revenue synergies, though they carry one-time costs to realize.

concepts.name: Revenue synergies
concepts.def: Extra sales from cross-selling, wider distribution or pricing power after a merger. Hard to realize and often offset by customer losses, so investors heavily discount them.

concepts.name: Merger arbitrage
concepts.def: Buying a takeover target after announcement, and shorting the acquirer in stock deals, to earn the spread to the deal price. Returns resemble selling insurance against deal failure.

concepts.name: Deal spread
concepts.def: The gap between the offer value and the target's market price after announcement. It reflects time to close, financing and regulatory risk, and the downside if the deal breaks.
concepts.formula: implied p(close) = (price - fallback) / (offer - fallback)

concepts.name: Stock-for-stock merger
concepts.def: An acquisition paid in acquirer shares. Target holders share in the combined firm's risk and synergies; announcement returns for acquirers tend to be worse than in cash deals.

concepts.name: Exchange ratio
concepts.def: The number of acquirer shares given per target share in a stock deal. A fixed ratio shifts price risk to target holders; a fixed value with a floating ratio shifts it to the acquirer.
concepts.formula: exchange ratio = offer price per target share / acquirer share price
concepts.aliases: swap ratio,fixed exchange ratio,floating exchange ratio

concepts.name: Cash versus stock consideration
concepts.def: The choice of paying for an acquisition in cash or shares. Cash signals confidence and gives target holders certainty; stock shares risk and can signal the acquirer views its shares as rich.

concepts.name: Earnout
concepts.def: Part of an acquisition price paid later only if the target meets agreed milestones. Bridges valuation gaps between buyer and seller but often leads to disputes.

concepts.name: Breakup fee
concepts.def: A fee the target pays the buyer if the target walks away, typically for a superior offer. Compensates the first bidder and deters interlopers.

concepts.name: Reverse termination fee
concepts.def: A fee the buyer pays the target if the deal fails due to the buyer, such as a financing failure or regulatory block. Signals how much regulatory risk the buyer accepts.

concepts.name: Go-shop provision
concepts.def: A period after signing in which the target may solicit competing bids, with a reduced breakup fee. Common in private equity take-privates to support the board's fiduciary duty.

concepts.name: No-shop clause
concepts.def: A merger term barring the target from soliciting other offers after signing, usually with a fiduciary out allowing it to accept a clearly superior unsolicited bid.

concepts.name: MAC clause
concepts.def: A material adverse change condition letting a buyer abandon a deal if the target suffers a severe, durable deterioration. Courts set a high bar, and broad industry events are usually carved out.

concepts.name: Hostile takeover
concepts.def: An acquisition pursued against the target board's wishes, by a tender offer directly to holders or a proxy fight to replace the board.

concepts.name: Tender offer
concepts.def: A public offer to buy shares directly from holders at a stated price, usually a premium, within a set period and subject to a minimum acceptance condition.

concepts.name: Poison pill
concepts.def: A shareholder rights plan that lets all holders except a hostile bidder buy discounted shares once the bidder crosses an ownership threshold, making an unapproved acquisition prohibitively dilutive.

concepts.name: Staggered board
concepts.def: A board divided into classes with only one elected each year, so a challenger needs two annual meetings to win control. A strong takeover defense often opposed by governance advocates.

concepts.name: White knight
concepts.def: A friendlier acquirer invited by a target's board to outbid a hostile bidder.

concepts.name: Proxy fight
concepts.def: A contest in which a shareholder solicits votes to elect its own director nominees or pass proposals against management's recommendations.

concepts.name: Fairness opinion
concepts.def: A bank's letter to a board stating that a deal price is fair from a financial point of view, backed by comps, precedents and DCF. Fees contingent on closing create conflicts.

concepts.name: Due diligence
concepts.def: Investigation of a target's financials, operations, legal exposure and commercial position before committing capital. Confirms the thesis and surfaces issues to price or protect against.

concepts.name: Antitrust review
concepts.def: Government review of whether a merger would substantially lessen competition, such as under the US Hart-Scott-Rodino process or by the European Commission. Can delay, condition or block deals.

concepts.name: Appraisal rights
concepts.def: The right of dissenting shareholders in certain mergers to ask a court to determine fair value and pay that instead of the deal price.

concepts.name: Reverse merger
concepts.def: A private company becomes public by merging into an existing listed shell, skipping a traditional IPO. Faster, but historically associated with weaker disclosure and fraud risk.

concepts.name: Bolt-on acquisition
concepts.def: A smaller acquisition added to an existing platform company, usually at a lower multiple. Lets a sponsor blend down its entry multiple and add synergies.

concepts.name: Roll-up
concepts.def: Consolidating a fragmented industry by acquiring many small firms into one platform. Value can come from scale and multiple arbitrage, but rapid acquisition can hide weak organic growth.

concepts.name: Platform company
concepts.def: The initial acquisition in a sponsor's buy-and-build strategy, with the management and systems to absorb further add-on acquisitions.

concepts.name: Serial acquirer
concepts.def: A company whose strategy is a steady stream of acquisitions, often of small private firms at modest multiples, with capital redeployed under decentralized management. Success depends on price discipline and returns on capital.

concepts.name: Empire building
concepts.def: Managers growing the firm through acquisitions or investment for size, status or pay rather than returns. A central agency cost that buybacks, debt and activists try to curb.
concepts.aliases: empire building,growth for its own sake

concepts.name: Hubris hypothesis
concepts.def: Roll (1986): acquirers overpay because overconfident managers believe their valuations beat the market's. Helps explain why target holders gain while acquirer holders often lose.

concepts.name: Acquirer returns
concepts.def: Studies find target shareholders capture most M&A gains while acquirer returns around announcement average near zero, worse for large public stock deals and better for small private cash deals.

concepts.name: Accretion and dilution analysis
concepts.def: Testing whether a deal raises or lowers the acquirer's EPS. Paying with cash or cheap debt is easily accretive, so EPS accretion says little about whether value is created.
concepts.formula: accretive if acquirer P/E > target P/E paid, for all-stock deals

concepts.name: Pro forma financials
concepts.def: Financial statements restated as if a transaction such as an acquisition, disposal or refinancing had occurred earlier. Required in some filings; also a common vehicle for flattering adjustments.

concepts.name: Purchase price allocation
concepts.def: Assigning an acquisition's price to the fair value of identifiable assets and liabilities, with any excess recorded as goodwill. Creates amortizable intangibles and a step-up in asset bases.
concepts.formula: goodwill = price - fair value of net identifiable assets

concepts.name: Equity carve-out
concepts.def: A parent sells a minority stake in a subsidiary through an IPO, keeping control. Raises cash and sets a market value for the unit, often ahead of a full spin-off.

concepts.name: Spin-off
concepts.def: A parent distributes shares of a subsidiary to its own holders, creating a separate listed company. Often tax-free; aims to close a conglomerate discount and sharpen management focus.

concepts.name: Spin-off effect
concepts.def: Spun-off companies have historically outperformed after separation, partly because index and mandate holders sell shares they did not choose. Popularized by Greenblatt; the effect varies by period.

concepts.name: Split-off
concepts.def: A parent offers its holders subsidiary shares in exchange for their parent shares, which shrinks the parent's share count. Usually done at a small premium to entice tendering.

concepts.name: Reverse Morris Trust
concepts.def: A US structure in which a parent spins off a unit that then merges with a third party, with the parent's holders owning the majority of the combined company, allowing a tax-free disposal.

concepts.name: Tracking stock
concepts.def: A class of a company's shares meant to follow the performance of one division, without separate legal ownership of its assets. Usually trades at a discount to the economics it tracks.

concepts.name: Divestiture
concepts.def: Selling a business unit or assets for cash or securities. Proceeds and the price received reveal what the market will pay for a part of the company.

concepts.name: Conglomerate
concepts.def: A company running many unrelated businesses under one owner. Can allocate capital internally well, but often trades at a discount for opacity and cross-subsidy.

concepts.name: Sources and uses
concepts.def: A table showing where transaction money comes from, such as debt tranches, sponsor equity and rollover, and where it goes, such as purchase equity, refinanced debt and fees. Both sides must balance.
concepts.formula: total sources = total uses

concepts.name: Equity contribution
concepts.def: The share of an LBO's price funded by the sponsor's equity rather than debt. A larger contribution lowers risk and returns; lenders often require a minimum.
concepts.formula: equity % = sponsor equity / total sources

concepts.name: LBO returns attribution
concepts.def: Breaking a buyout's equity return into EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt paydown from free cash flow. Shows how much came from operations versus leverage and market timing.
concepts.formula: equity gain = EBITDA growth x entry multiple + multiple change x exit EBITDA + net debt reduction

concepts.name: Multiple arbitrage
concepts.def: Gaining value by buying businesses at a low multiple and selling or valuing the combination at a higher one, typically because size and quality command higher multiples.

concepts.name: Management rollover
concepts.def: Existing managers or founders reinvesting part of their sale proceeds in the new company's equity. Aligns incentives and reduces the cash a sponsor must pay.

concepts.name: Management incentive plan
concepts.def: An equity pool granted to managers in a sponsor-backed company, often a set percentage of shares vesting on time and return hurdles. Pays out heavily when the sponsor hits its target return.

concepts.name: Cash sweep
concepts.def: A loan provision requiring a share of excess free cash flow to repay debt early. Speeds deleveraging and is modeled in LBOs to show debt falling over the hold.
concepts.aliases: excess cash flow sweep,ecf sweep,mandatory prepayment

concepts.name: Minimum cash balance
concepts.def: The cash a company must keep for operations, which cannot be swept to lenders or counted as excess in valuation.

concepts.name: Senior and total leverage
concepts.def: Senior leverage is secured or senior debt divided by EBITDA; total leverage includes all debt. Lenders set limits on each by tranche at entry and in covenants.
concepts.formula: senior leverage = senior debt / EBITDA
concepts.aliases: senior leverage,total leverage,first lien leverage,net leverage

concepts.name: Covenant headroom
concepts.def: How far a covenant ratio sits from its limit, often expressed as the percentage EBITDA decline before a breach. Thin headroom signals renegotiation or equity cures ahead.
concepts.formula: EBITDA cushion = 1 - (debt / max leverage multiple) / current EBITDA

concepts.name: Take-private
concepts.def: A buyer, usually a sponsor or controlling holder, acquires all public shares and delists the company. Requires a premium and board process protecting minority holders.

concepts.name: Management buyout
concepts.def: A buyout led by a company's own managers, usually with sponsor and debt funding. Raises conflicts because managers are both sellers' agents and buyers.

concepts.name: Paper LBO
concepts.def: A simplified buyout model done by hand: entry price, debt, cash generation and exit multiple to estimate IRR and MOIC. A common interview test and quick screening tool.
concepts.formula: IRR = MOIC^(1/years) - 1, with no interim cash flows

concepts.name: Entry multiple
concepts.def: The EV/EBITDA multiple paid to acquire a company. The main driver of buyout risk, because a high entry leaves returns dependent on growth and a high exit multiple.

concepts.name: Shareholder activism
concepts.def: Investors buying stakes to push for changes in strategy, capital allocation, governance or a sale. Tactics range from private letters to public campaigns and proxy fights.

concepts.name: Schedule 13D
concepts.def: An SEC filing required within a short period after an investor acquires more than five percent of a voting class with intent to influence control. Discloses the holder's purpose and plans; passive holders file 13G instead.

concepts.name: Universal proxy
concepts.def: A ballot listing both management and dissident nominees so holders can mix candidates from each side. Mandatory in US contested elections, it makes partial board wins for activists easier.

concepts.name: Say on pay
concepts.def: A shareholder advisory vote on executive compensation. Not binding, but low support pressures boards to redesign pay.

concepts.name: Dual-class shares
concepts.def: Share structures where one class carries more votes per share, letting founders keep control with a minority economic stake. Shields long-term plans but weakens accountability.
concepts.aliases: dual class,super voting shares,multiple class shares

concepts.name: Corporate governance
concepts.def: The rules and practices by which boards oversee managers and protect shareholder interests: board independence, voting rights, pay design and disclosure.

concepts.name: Proxy advisors
concepts.def: Firms such as ISS and Glass Lewis that recommend how institutions should vote at shareholder meetings. Their support often decides close votes and contests.

concepts.name: Wolf pack
concepts.def: Several investors building positions in the same target around an activist campaign, adding voting power without forming a formal group that triggers joint disclosure.

concepts.name: Proxy statement
concepts.def: The filing sent before a shareholder meeting describing matters to be voted on, director nominees, executive pay and related party dealings. In the US it is form DEF 14A.

concepts.name: Executive compensation
concepts.def: Salary, bonus and equity awards for top managers. The metrics it rewards, such as EPS, revenue, TSR or ROIC, shape decisions and are worth reading before a thesis.

concepts.name: Insider ownership
concepts.def: The share of a company owned by its officers and directors. Meaningful personal stakes align interests, though very high control can entrench management.

concepts.name: Owner-operator
concepts.def: A company run by a founder or large holder whose wealth is concentrated in its shares. Often associated with long-term capital allocation and lower agency costs.

concepts.name: Network effects
concepts.def: When a product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join, directly or through a second side of a market. Can produce winner-take-most outcomes and a strong moat.
concepts.aliases: network effect,metcalfe,demand side economies of scale

concepts.name: Switching costs
concepts.def: The money, time, risk and retraining a customer bears to move to a competitor. High switching costs let incumbents raise prices and retain customers; enterprise software is a classic case.

concepts.name: Intangible asset moat
concepts.def: Protection from brands, patents, licenses or regulatory approvals that competitors cannot easily copy. Brands matter as a moat only if they raise willingness to pay or lower acquisition costs.

concepts.name: Cost advantage
concepts.def: Producing at durably lower cost than rivals through process, location, scale or unique resources. Most valuable in commodity-like industries where price is set by the marginal producer.

concepts.name: Industry cost curve
concepts.def: Producers ranked from lowest to highest unit cost against cumulative capacity. Price tends toward the cost of the marginal producer needed to meet demand, so low-cost producers earn rents.

concepts.name: Efficient scale
concepts.def: A market only large enough to support one or a few profitable firms, such as a regional airport or pipeline, so new entry would make returns inadequate for everyone.

concepts.name: Economies of scale
concepts.def: Unit costs falling as volume rises because fixed costs are spread over more units. A moat when the scale needed is large relative to the market.

concepts.name: 7 Powers
concepts.def: Hamilton Helmer's framework for durable advantage: scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource and process power. Each needs both a benefit and a barrier.

concepts.name: Counter-positioning
concepts.def: A newcomer adopts a business model the incumbent could copy but will not, because doing so would damage its existing business. Index funds versus active managers are a standard example.

concepts.name: Cornered resource
concepts.def: Preferential access to a valuable asset on attractive terms, such as a patent, unique talent, licence or low-cost deposit. One of Helmer's seven powers.

concepts.name: Process power
concepts.def: Embedded organizational know-how that lowers cost or improves quality and takes rivals years to replicate, such as a lean manufacturing system. The rarest of Helmer's powers.

concepts.name: Brand power
concepts.def: The ability of a brand to command a price premium or lower customer acquisition cost through trust and reputation built over time.

concepts.name: Porter's five forces
concepts.def: Porter's (1979) framework for industry profitability: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Explains why some industries earn high returns on capital and others do not.

concepts.name: Buyer power
concepts.def: Customers' ability to push down prices or demand more, highest when buyers are concentrated, purchase in volume, face low switching costs or can integrate backward.

concepts.name: Supplier power
concepts.def: Suppliers' ability to raise prices or cut quality, strongest when they are concentrated, their input is critical and unique, or switching costs are high.

concepts.name: Threat of substitutes
concepts.def: Products from other industries that meet the same need cap what an industry can charge. Substitutes are often missed because they do not look like competitors.

concepts.name: Barriers to entry
concepts.def: Obstacles that make it hard for new firms to enter profitably: scale, capital needs, regulation, brands, switching costs or network effects. Without them, excess returns attract entry.

concepts.name: Value chain
concepts.def: The sequence of activities from raw inputs to end customer. Analyzing where profit pools sit along it shows which links have power and which are commoditized.

concepts.name: Pricing power
concepts.def: The ability to raise prices without losing much volume. Buffett called it the single most important factor in evaluating a business; visible in stable or rising gross margins through inflation.

concepts.name: Total addressable market
concepts.def: The total revenue available if a product won every possible customer. Useful for bounding growth, but routinely overstated; serviceable and obtainable market are narrower estimates.

concepts.name: Market share
concepts.def: A firm's sales as a percentage of total industry sales. Gains in share signal competitive advantage only if they come without sacrificing margins or returns.
concepts.formula: share = firm sales / industry sales

concepts.name: Industry life cycle
concepts.def: The progression from introduction through growth, shakeout and maturity to decline. Appropriate valuation methods, margins and capital needs differ at each stage.

concepts.name: Commoditization
concepts.def: A product becoming undifferentiated so buyers choose mainly on price, compressing margins toward cost of capital. Driven by standardization, new entrants and transparent pricing.

concepts.name: Disruptive innovation
concepts.def: Christensen's term for a cheaper, simpler product that starts in overlooked low-end or new markets and improves until it displaces incumbents, who rationally focus on their best customers.

concepts.name: Winner-take-most market
concepts.def: A market where network effects, scale or data advantages let the leader capture most profits. Valuation then depends heavily on the probability of becoming the leader.

concepts.name: Scale economies shared
concepts.def: A model, associated with Costco and described by Nick Sleep, in which a firm passes scale savings to customers through lower prices, driving more volume and further savings.

concepts.name: Capital cycle
concepts.def: Marathon's framework: high returns attract capital and new supply, which drives returns down, and vice versa. Investors watch industry capex and consolidation rather than demand forecasts.

concepts.name: Management quality
concepts.def: How well executives allocate capital, execute, communicate and treat shareholders. Judged from track record, incentives, candor about mistakes and per-share results over full cycles.

concepts.name: Scuttlebutt
concepts.def: Philip Fisher's method of learning about a company by talking to customers, suppliers, competitors and former employees. The forerunner of modern channel checks.

concepts.name: Circle of competence
concepts.def: Buffett's idea that an investor should stay within businesses they understand well enough to judge. Knowing the boundary matters more than its size.

concepts.name: Quality compounder
concepts.def: A business able to reinvest large amounts at high returns on capital for many years, compounding intrinsic value. Its value depends on the length and size of the reinvestment runway.

concepts.name: Turnaround situation
concepts.def: A troubled company with a plan to restore profitability through new management, restructuring or refinancing. Outcomes are binary and base rates of success are modest.

concepts.name: Special situations
concepts.def: Investments driven by corporate events such as spin-offs, mergers, restructurings, rights issues or index changes, where value depends more on the event than on the market.

concepts.name: Deep value
concepts.def: Buying stocks at very low prices relative to assets or normalized earnings, often troubled or unloved. Returns come from mean reversion, with high exposure to value traps.

concepts.name: Growth at a reasonable price
concepts.def: A style combining growth and value screens, seeking above-average earnings growth at moderate multiples, often using the PEG ratio.

concepts.name: Razor and blades model
concepts.def: Selling a base product cheaply to lock in high-margin recurring sales of consumables or services. Value rests on the installed base and its attachment rate.

concepts.name: Near-zero marginal cost
concepts.def: Digital goods such as software and content cost little to serve an extra user once built, so incremental margins can be very high. Competition can push prices toward that low cost.

concepts.name: Matching principle
concepts.def: Expenses are recognized in the same period as the revenues they help produce, which is why assets are depreciated and costs are accrued rather than booked when cash moves.

concepts.name: Conservatism principle
concepts.def: Accounting's asymmetric tendency to recognize losses when probable but gains only when realized. Leaves book values below economic values for firms with internally built intangibles.

concepts.name: Materiality
concepts.def: An item is material if omitting or misstating it could change a reasonable investor's decision. Auditors and preparers use it to decide what to disclose and correct; small items can still be material qualitatively.

concepts.name: IFRS
concepts.def: International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the IASB and used for listed companies in the EU and many other countries. More principles-based than US GAAP.

concepts.name: GAAP and IFRS differences
concepts.def: Key differences that affect comparisons: IFRS bans LIFO, allows capitalizing development costs, lets impairments reverse, treats nearly all leases as finance leases, and allows interest paid in financing cash flow.
concepts.aliases: us gaap vs ifrs,ifrs vs gaap

concepts.name: Five-step revenue model
concepts.def: The ASC 606 and IFRS 15 framework: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it to obligations, and recognize revenue as each is satisfied.

concepts.name: Performance obligation
concepts.def: A distinct promise in a customer contract to transfer a good or service. Revenue is recognized as each obligation is satisfied, at a point in time or over time.

concepts.name: Standalone selling price
concepts.def: The price at which an entity would sell a good or service separately, used to allocate a bundled contract's price among its performance obligations. Estimates shift revenue between periods.

concepts.name: Variable consideration
concepts.def: Parts of a contract price that depend on future events, such as rebates, returns, bonuses or usage fees. Included in revenue only to the extent a significant reversal is unlikely.

concepts.name: Principal versus agent
concepts.def: Whether a company controls a good before transfer and reports gross revenue as principal, or arranges it for others and reports only its net fee as agent. Changes revenue and margins without changing profit.
concepts.aliases: gross vs net revenue,gross versus net,principal agent revenue

concepts.name: Bill-and-hold
concepts.def: Billing a customer and recognizing revenue while the seller keeps physical goods. Allowed only under strict conditions; a recurring red flag in revenue manipulation cases.

concepts.name: Channel stuffing
concepts.def: Pushing excess inventory onto distributors near period end, often with discounts or return rights, to pull revenue forward. Tends to show up as rising receivables and weaker sales later.

concepts.name: Over-time revenue recognition
concepts.def: Recognizing revenue progressively as work is performed, measured by inputs such as costs incurred or outputs delivered. Used in construction, defense and services; estimates of total cost drive reported profit.
concepts.formula: revenue to date = contract price x costs incurred / total estimated costs
concepts.aliases: percentage of completion,poc,cost to cost method

concepts.name: Contract asset
concepts.def: A right to payment for work already performed that is conditional on something other than time, such as further delivery. Rising contract assets relative to revenue warrant scrutiny.
concepts.aliases: unbilled receivables,contract assets,costs in excess of billings

concepts.name: Remaining performance obligations
concepts.def: Contracted revenue not yet recognized, including both deferred revenue and unbilled amounts. Current RPO, due within twelve months, is a leading indicator for subscription firms.

concepts.name: Billings
concepts.def: Revenue plus the change in deferred revenue, a proxy for amounts invoiced in a period. Popular in software, though shifts in billing terms can distort it.
concepts.formula: billings = revenue + change in deferred revenue

concepts.name: Backlog
concepts.def: The value of orders received but not yet delivered or recognized. Common for industrials and defense; definitions vary and cancellable orders can inflate it.

concepts.name: Book-to-bill ratio
concepts.def: Orders received divided by revenue billed in a period. Above one means backlog is growing; watched closely in semiconductors, equipment and defense.
concepts.formula: book-to-bill = orders / billings

concepts.name: Capitalized contract costs
concepts.def: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract, mainly sales commissions, capitalized and amortized over the expected customer life under ASC 340-40. Inflates near-term margins for fast-growing subscription firms.

concepts.name: ASC 842
concepts.def: The US lease standard putting most leases on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and lease liability. Operating leases still show a single straight-line rent expense in the income statement.

concepts.name: IFRS 16
concepts.def: The IFRS lease standard treating nearly all leases like financing: depreciation of the asset plus interest on the liability. Raises EBITDA versus US GAAP operating leases and moves the principal part of lease payments into financing cash flow.

concepts.name: Right-of-use asset
concepts.def: The balance sheet asset representing a lessee's right to use a leased item over the lease term, initially equal to the lease liability plus direct costs and prepayments.

concepts.name: Lease liability
concepts.def: The present value of remaining lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or the lessee's incremental borrowing rate. Treated as debt by rating agencies and in lease-adjusted leverage.

concepts.name: Sale-leaseback
concepts.def: Selling an owned asset, usually real estate, and leasing it back. Raises cash and can book a gain, but replaces ownership with a long-term rent obligation that behaves like debt.

concepts.name: Lease-adjusted leverage
concepts.def: Debt plus lease liabilities divided by EBITDAR. Lets analysts compare firms that lease assets with firms that own and borrow to fund them.
concepts.formula: (debt + lease liabilities) / EBITDAR

concepts.name: Restricted stock unit
concepts.def: A promise to deliver shares once vesting conditions, usually continued service, are met. Expensed at grant-date fair value over the vesting period; always has value unlike an option.

concepts.name: Stock option expense
concepts.def: The grant-date fair value of employee options, estimated with Black-Scholes or a lattice model, recognized over the vesting period. Required under ASC 718 and IFRS 2.

concepts.name: Performance share unit
concepts.def: An equity award whose payout depends on hitting targets such as TSR, EPS or revenue over several years. The chosen metrics reveal what management is paid to optimize.

concepts.name: Net share settlement
concepts.def: Withholding some vesting shares to pay employees' taxes, with the company paying cash to tax authorities. That cash is a real cost of stock pay often reported in financing cash flow.
concepts.aliases: tax withholding on vesting,net settlement,shares withheld for taxes

concepts.name: Option overhang
concepts.def: Outstanding options and unvested awards plus shares available for future grants, as a share of shares outstanding. Measures potential dilution from equity plans.
concepts.formula: overhang = (awards outstanding + available for grant) / shares outstanding

concepts.name: Equity burn rate
concepts.def: Shares granted under equity plans in a year as a percentage of weighted shares outstanding. Shows how fast stock pay dilutes holders absent buybacks.
concepts.formula: burn rate = shares granted / weighted average shares

concepts.name: Stock comp add-back
concepts.def: Adding stock-based compensation back to non-GAAP earnings or free cash flow because it is non-cash. It is still a real cost paid in dilution or buyback cash, so add-backs can greatly overstate owner economics.

concepts.name: Segment reporting
concepts.def: Disclosure of revenue, profit and assets by operating segment, as defined by how the chief operating decision maker reviews results (ASC 280, IFRS 8). The raw material for sum-of-the-parts work.

concepts.name: EBITDA add-backs
concepts.def: Adjustments added to EBITDA for items deemed non-recurring or non-cash, such as restructuring, synergies not yet achieved and stock pay. Aggressive add-backs inflate deal leverage capacity and valuation.

concepts.name: Adjusted EPS
concepts.def: Earnings per share excluding items management labels non-recurring or non-cash, often amortization of acquired intangibles, restructuring and stock pay. Consensus forecasts are usually on this basis.
concepts.aliases: non-gaap eps,core eps,cash eps,pro forma eps

concepts.name: Constant currency growth
concepts.def: Growth recomputed at prior-period exchange rates to remove currency translation effects. Helps isolate underlying demand but hides real economic currency exposure.

concepts.name: Organic growth
concepts.def: Revenue growth excluding acquisitions, divestitures and currency effects. Shows whether the existing business is gaining, especially for serial acquirers and roll-ups.
concepts.aliases: organic revenue growth,like for like growth,underlying growth

concepts.name: Same-store sales
concepts.def: Sales growth from stores open at least a year, excluding new and closed units. Separates demand at existing locations from footprint expansion in retail and restaurants.

concepts.name: Days sales outstanding
concepts.def: Average receivables divided by revenue, times days in the period: how long customers take to pay. Rising DSO can mean looser credit terms or aggressive revenue recognition.
concepts.formula: DSO = receivables / revenue x 365

concepts.name: Days inventory outstanding
concepts.def: Inventory divided by cost of goods sold, times days: how long stock sits before being sold. A rising figure can warn of slowing demand or obsolete goods.
concepts.formula: DIO = inventory / COGS x 365

concepts.name: Days payable outstanding
concepts.def: Payables divided by cost of goods sold, times days: how long the firm takes to pay suppliers. Stretching payables boosts operating cash flow temporarily.
concepts.formula: DPO = payables / COGS x 365

concepts.name: Cash conversion cycle
concepts.def: Days from paying suppliers to collecting from customers. A shorter or negative cycle means the business funds growth with suppliers' and customers' money.
concepts.formula: CCC = DSO + DIO - DPO

concepts.name: Negative working capital model
concepts.def: A business that collects from customers before paying suppliers, such as many retailers, subscription firms and marketplaces. Growth then releases cash, but a slowdown reverses the effect.

concepts.name: Working capital peg
concepts.def: A target level of net working capital agreed in an acquisition; the price is adjusted up or down at closing by the difference from the actual level. Stops sellers draining working capital before closing.
concepts.formula: price adjustment = closing NWC - peg

concepts.name: Accounts receivable
concepts.def: Money owed by customers for goods or services delivered on credit, reported net of an allowance for expected non-payment.

concepts.name: Allowance for doubtful accounts
concepts.def: A reserve against receivables that will not be collected. Cutting it relative to receivables lifts earnings and is a classic quiet lever.
concepts.aliases: bad debt reserve,allowance for credit losses on receivables,provision for doubtful debts

concepts.name: Factoring
concepts.def: Selling receivables to a third party at a discount for immediate cash. Lowers DSO and lifts operating cash flow, so disclosure of its use matters for cash-flow quality.

concepts.name: Supply chain finance
concepts.def: A bank pays a firm's suppliers early and the firm repays the bank later, letting the firm extend payables. Can make bank debt look like trade payables and flatter operating cash flow.

concepts.name: Inventory write-down
concepts.def: Reducing inventory's carrying value when it falls below net realizable value due to obsolescence or price declines. Hits gross margin and often follows a demand slowdown.

concepts.name: FIFO
concepts.def: First-in, first-out: the oldest inventory costs flow to cost of goods sold first. In rising prices it shows higher profits and a balance sheet nearer current cost.

concepts.name: LIFO
concepts.def: Last-in, first-out: the newest inventory costs flow to cost of goods sold first. Allowed under US GAAP but not IFRS; in rising prices it lowers reported profit and taxes.

concepts.name: LIFO reserve
concepts.def: The difference between inventory at FIFO and at LIFO cost, disclosed by LIFO users. Adding it back puts LIFO and FIFO firms on a comparable basis; a shrinking reserve can boost margins.
concepts.formula: FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS - change in LIFO reserve

concepts.name: Inventory turnover
concepts.def: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory: how many times stock is sold and replaced a year. Low or falling turnover can warn of obsolete inventory.
concepts.formula: turnover = COGS / average inventory

concepts.name: GMROI
concepts.def: Gross margin return on inventory investment: gross profit divided by average inventory at cost. Tells a retailer how much margin each unit of inventory earns.
concepts.formula: GMROI = gross profit / average inventory cost

concepts.name: Asset turnover
concepts.def: Revenue divided by average total assets: how efficiently a firm uses assets to generate sales. A DuPont component that varies widely by industry.
concepts.formula: asset turnover = revenue / average total assets

concepts.name: Property, plant and equipment
concepts.def: Long-lived tangible assets used in operations, carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment. Gross PP&E versus net PP&E shows how old the asset base is.

concepts.name: Intangible assets
concepts.def: Non-physical assets such as patents, customer relationships, software and brands. Mostly recognized only when acquired; internally built ones are expensed and missing from the balance sheet.

concepts.name: Amortization
concepts.def: Allocating the cost of a finite-lived intangible asset over its useful life, the intangible counterpart of depreciation. Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized under US GAAP for public firms or IFRS.

concepts.name: Acquired intangibles amortization
concepts.def: Amortization of intangibles recognized in acquisitions. Usually excluded from adjusted EPS, defensibly when no reinvestment is needed to maintain them, less so when acquisitions are recurring.
concepts.aliases: purchase accounting amortization,ppa amortization,amortization of acquired intangibles

concepts.name: Capitalized software
concepts.def: Development costs for internal-use or sale software recorded as an asset once technical feasibility or the application stage is reached, then amortized. Rising capitalization rates flatter operating margins.

concepts.name: Capitalized interest
concepts.def: Interest on borrowing used to build long-lived assets, added to the asset's cost rather than expensed. It lowers reported interest expense, so coverage ratios should add it back.

concepts.name: R&D capitalization
concepts.def: An analyst adjustment treating research spending as an investment: capitalizing past R&D as an asset and amortizing it. Raises invested capital and often changes ROIC for intangible-heavy firms.
concepts.formula: research asset = sum of unamortized past R&D

concepts.name: Bargain purchase
concepts.def: An acquisition where the fair value of net identifiable assets exceeds the price paid, producing an immediate gain instead of goodwill. Rare and worth checking for optimistic fair values.

concepts.name: Deferred tax asset
concepts.def: Future tax savings from deductible temporary differences and loss carryforwards. Recognized only to the extent future taxable profit is probable.

concepts.name: Deferred tax liability
concepts.def: Taxes owed in the future because book income currently exceeds taxable income, often from accelerated tax depreciation. A growing firm can defer it for a long time, so it partly behaves like equity.

concepts.name: Valuation allowance
concepts.def: A reserve reducing deferred tax assets that are unlikely to be used. Releasing it boosts earnings in one period, which analysts usually exclude from run-rate profit.

concepts.name: Net operating loss carryforward
concepts.def: Past tax losses that can offset future taxable income, lowering cash taxes. Worth valuing separately; ownership changes can limit their use under US Section 382.

concepts.name: Cash taxes
concepts.def: Income taxes actually paid in a period, disclosed in the cash flow statement or notes. Differs from book tax expense because of deferrals, credits and timing.

concepts.name: Tax receivable agreement
concepts.def: A contract, common in Up-C IPOs, requiring the company to pay pre-IPO owners most of the tax savings it realizes from a basis step-up. A real liability that belongs in the equity bridge.

concepts.name: Contingent liabilities
concepts.def: Possible obligations from lawsuits, guarantees or environmental claims that depend on future events. Accrued if probable and estimable, otherwise disclosed in notes.

concepts.name: Asset retirement obligation
concepts.def: The present value of legally required costs to dismantle and restore sites at the end of an asset's life, such as wells, mines and nuclear plants. A debt-like item for energy and utility valuation.

concepts.name: Restructuring charges
concepts.def: Costs of layoffs, closures and reorganizations, typically excluded from adjusted results. When they recur every year they are part of the normal cost of running the business.

concepts.name: Big bath
concepts.def: Taking unusually large write-offs and reserves in one period, often after a CEO change or in a bad year, so that later periods look better as charges reverse or costs disappear.

concepts.name: Cookie jar reserves
concepts.def: Over-reserving in good times, then releasing reserves to smooth earnings in weak periods. Hard to see except through reserve trends relative to the underlying exposure.

concepts.name: Pension accounting
concepts.def: Reporting defined benefit plans: the funded status sits on the balance sheet, while service cost, interest cost and expected asset returns run through income. Assumption changes can move earnings and equity materially.
concepts.formula: funded status = plan assets - DBO
concepts.aliases: defined benefit pension,pension plan accounting,funded status

concepts.name: Defined benefit obligation
concepts.def: The present value of pension benefits employees have earned, discounted at high-grade corporate bond yields. Rising rates shrink it, so funded status depends heavily on rates.

concepts.name: Other comprehensive income
concepts.def: Gains and losses that bypass net income and go straight to equity, such as currency translation, some securities, hedge results and pension remeasurements. Accumulated OCI can hide large unrealized losses.

concepts.name: Retained earnings
concepts.def: Cumulative net income kept in the business after dividends since inception. Large deficits signal a history of losses, while large balances show the capacity to pay.
concepts.formula: RE_end = RE_begin + net income - dividends

concepts.name: Treasury stock
concepts.def: Shares a company has repurchased and holds rather than retiring, shown as a reduction of equity at cost. Large buybacks can push book equity negative.

concepts.name: Noncontrolling interest
concepts.def: The share of a consolidated subsidiary owned by outsiders. Because 100 percent of the subsidiary's EBITDA is consolidated, its value must be subtracted when bridging from EV to the parent's equity.

concepts.name: Equity method
concepts.def: Accounting for a stake typically of 20 to 50 percent: the investment is carried at cost plus the share of profits, with no revenue or EBITDA consolidated. Such stakes are added separately in the equity bridge.

concepts.name: Consolidated financial statements
concepts.def: Statements combining a parent and all entities it controls as one economic unit, line by line, with intercompany items eliminated and outside owners shown as noncontrolling interest.

concepts.name: Variable interest entity
concepts.def: An entity controlled through contracts rather than voting equity, which must be consolidated by its primary beneficiary. Used in structured finance and in offshore structures for some Chinese listings.

concepts.name: Fair value hierarchy
concepts.def: The three-level ranking of fair value inputs: Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 model-based unobservable inputs. Level 3 marks deserve the most skepticism.

concepts.name: Held-to-maturity securities
concepts.def: Debt securities a bank intends to hold to maturity, carried at amortized cost so price changes do not hit earnings or equity. Large unrealized losses can be invisible until assets must be sold.

concepts.name: Available-for-sale securities
concepts.def: Debt securities carried at fair value with unrealized gains and losses in other comprehensive income rather than net income. Hits book equity but not reported earnings.

concepts.name: Currency translation
concepts.def: Converting foreign subsidiaries' results into the reporting currency, which changes reported figures without changing local performance. Translation gains and losses on net assets go to OCI.

concepts.name: Hedge accounting
concepts.def: Rules that let a company match the timing of gains and losses on a hedge with the item hedged, so derivative swings do not create artificial earnings volatility. Requires documentation and effectiveness.
concepts.aliases: cash flow hedge,fair value hedge,asc 815,ifrs 9 hedging

concepts.name: Discontinued operations
concepts.def: A component disposed of or held for sale that represents a strategic shift, reported separately below continuing operations. Results of continuing operations are the run-rate base.

concepts.name: Held for sale
concepts.def: Assets expected to be sold within a year, carried at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and no longer depreciated.

concepts.name: Going concern
concepts.def: The assumption that a company will keep operating for the foreseeable future. An auditor's going concern warning signals substantial doubt about survival over the next year.
concepts.aliases: going concern opinion,going concern doubt,going concern qualification

concepts.name: Audit opinion
concepts.def: The auditor's conclusion on whether statements are fairly presented: unqualified, qualified, adverse or disclaimer. Critical audit matters in the report flag the areas of most judgment.
concepts.aliases: auditor report,clean opinion,qualified opinion,critical audit matters

concepts.name: Material weakness
concepts.def: A deficiency in internal control over financial reporting with a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement. Disclosed under Sarbanes-Oxley and often precedes restatements.

concepts.name: Restatement
concepts.def: Revising previously issued financial statements to correct a material error. Usually damages credibility and is followed by weak returns, regulatory scrutiny and management turnover.

concepts.name: Auditor change
concepts.def: Replacing the external auditor, especially abruptly, with a smaller firm, or after disagreements. A red flag requiring an 8-K disclosure in the US.

concepts.name: Related party transactions
concepts.def: Dealings between a company and its insiders, their families or affiliated entities. Must be disclosed; large or recurring ones can transfer value away from outside shareholders.

concepts.name: Restricted cash
concepts.def: Cash held for a specific purpose, such as collateral, escrow or regulatory reserves, that cannot fund operations or be distributed. Excluded from net debt calculations by careful analysts.

concepts.name: Accounting red flags
concepts.def: Warning signs that reported earnings overstate economics: receivables or inventory outgrowing sales, profits without cash, rising capitalization, frequent one-offs, auditor changes, late filings and complex related-party dealings. Each warrants questions, not conclusions.

concepts.name: Earnings management
concepts.def: Using accounting judgment or timing of real decisions to steer reported results toward targets, from reserve timing to cutting R&D at quarter end. Within GAAP it is legal but reduces earnings quality.
concepts.aliases: earnings smoothing,income smoothing,managed earnings,real earnings management

concepts.name: Receivables outgrowing revenue
concepts.def: Receivables rising much faster than sales, lifting DSO. Can mean extended terms, weaker customers or revenue booked before it is earned; inventory outgrowing sales is the parallel warning.
concepts.formula: gap = receivables growth - revenue growth

concepts.name: Capitalizing operating costs
concepts.def: Recording ordinary expenses as assets so they hit earnings slowly through amortization and leave operating cash flow for investing cash flow. A rising capitalized share of spending lifts both margins and reported operating cash flow.

concepts.name: Cash flow classification
concepts.def: How items are split among operating, investing and financing cash flows. Choices such as factoring, supply chain finance, capitalized costs and IFRS interest placement can flatter operating cash flow without changing total cash.
concepts.aliases: cash flow presentation,cfo manipulation,operating cash flow quality

concepts.name: Accrual ratio
concepts.def: The gap between earnings and operating cash flow scaled by average net operating assets. High accruals suggest earnings that are less likely to persist.
concepts.formula: accrual ratio = (net income - CFO - CFI) / average net operating assets
concepts.aliases: balance sheet accruals,cash flow accrual ratio,accruals ratio

concepts.name: Accrual anomaly
concepts.def: Sloan (1996) found that firms with high accruals subsequently underperform those with low accruals, because investors fail to see that accrual-driven earnings persist less than cash earnings.

concepts.name: Non-GAAP gap
concepts.def: The difference between adjusted and GAAP earnings. A wide or widening gap, especially from recurring items like stock pay, restructuring or acquired amortization, points to lower earnings quality.
concepts.formula: gap = adjusted earnings / GAAP earnings - 1
concepts.aliases: adjusted vs gaap gap,non gaap spread,adjustment ratio

concepts.name: Round-tripping
concepts.def: Booking revenue from transactions where cash flows back to the customer through offsetting purchases, investments or loans, so no real economic sale occurs. Inflates revenue and growth.

concepts.name: Ohlson O-score
concepts.def: Ohlson's (1980) logit model of bankruptcy probability using size, leverage, working capital, liquidity, profitability, funds from operations and recent losses. A complement to the Altman Z-score.

concepts.name: Short seller report
concepts.def: A public research report by an investor short a stock, alleging fraud, accounting problems or overvaluation. Can move prices sharply; claims need independent checking since authors profit from declines.

concepts.name: Current ratio
concepts.def: Current assets divided by current liabilities, a basic liquidity test. The stricter quick ratio drops inventory and prepaid items; very high values can also mean idle capital.
concepts.formula: current ratio = current assets / current liabilities; quick ratio = (cash + securities + receivables) / current liabilities

concepts.name: Debt to equity
concepts.def: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity, in book or market value terms. Book values become meaningless when buybacks or losses push equity near zero, so market values or debt to EBITDA often work better.
concepts.formula: D/E = total debt / equity

concepts.name: Fixed charge coverage
concepts.def: Earnings before fixed charges divided by interest plus lease payments and sometimes required principal. Stricter than interest coverage for lease-heavy firms; also a common loan covenant.
concepts.formula: FCCR = (EBITDA - capex - cash taxes) / (interest + scheduled principal)

concepts.name: FFO to debt
concepts.def: Funds from operations, roughly operating cash flow before working capital, divided by adjusted debt. A core rating agency leverage metric; higher is stronger.
concepts.formula: FFO / debt

concepts.name: Cash runway
concepts.def: How many months a loss-making company can operate before cash runs out, given its current burn. A short runway forces a raise, often on poor terms.
concepts.formula: runway = cash / monthly net burn

concepts.name: Return on assets
concepts.def: Net income divided by average total assets. The core profitability measure for banks, where small differences in ROA translate into large differences in ROE because of leverage.
concepts.formula: ROA = net income / average total assets

concepts.name: Return on capital employed
concepts.def: EBIT divided by capital employed, usually total assets less current liabilities. A pre-tax cousin of ROIC widely used in Europe and in capital-intensive industries.
concepts.formula: ROCE = EBIT / (total assets - current liabilities)

concepts.name: CROCI
concepts.def: Cash return on capital invested: cash flow divided by gross capital invested, a Deutsche Bank method that treats intangibles and leases consistently across firms.

concepts.name: Gross profitability
concepts.def: Gross profit divided by total assets. Novy-Marx (2013) showed it predicts returns about as well as book to market does, and is cleaner than net income because it sits high in the income statement.
concepts.formula: GP/A = (revenue - COGS) / total assets

concepts.name: Gross profit
concepts.def: Revenue minus cost of goods sold. Shows what remains to cover operating expenses and reflects pricing power and production costs.
concepts.formula: gross profit = revenue - COGS

concepts.name: EBIT
concepts.def: Earnings before interest and taxes, usually operating income adjusted for non-operating items. Captures operating performance after depreciation and amortization, independent of financing.
concepts.formula: EBIT = revenue - COGS - opex - D&A

concepts.name: Incremental margin
concepts.def: Change in operating profit divided by change in revenue. Shows operating leverage as sales grow, and decremental margins when sales fall; high fixed-cost firms have large swings.
concepts.formula: incremental margin = change in EBIT / change in revenue

concepts.name: Contribution margin
concepts.def: Revenue less variable costs, per unit or in total, showing what each sale contributes to fixed costs and profit. The basis of unit economics and breakeven analysis.
concepts.formula: contribution margin = (revenue - variable costs) / revenue

concepts.name: Capex intensity
concepts.def: Capital expenditure as a share of revenue. Distinguishes asset-light from asset-heavy models and, compared with depreciation, shows whether a firm is growing or shrinking its asset base.
concepts.formula: capex / revenue; capex / depreciation
concepts.aliases: capital intensity,capex to sales,capex to depreciation

concepts.name: Free cash flow margin
concepts.def: Free cash flow divided by revenue. Combines profitability, capital intensity and working capital needs into one figure.
concepts.formula: FCF margin = FCF / revenue

concepts.name: Tangible book value
concepts.def: Shareholders' equity less goodwill and other intangible assets, often also less preferred stock. The capital base banks and regulators focus on.
concepts.formula: TBV = equity - goodwill - intangibles

concepts.name: Form 10-K
concepts.def: The audited annual report US public companies file with the SEC, covering the business, risk factors, MD&A, statements and notes. The quarterly 10-Q is unaudited and shorter.

concepts.name: Form 8-K
concepts.def: An SEC filing reporting material events between periodic reports, such as earnings, acquisitions, executive departures, auditor changes or non-reliance on past statements, usually within four business days.

concepts.name: MD&A
concepts.def: Management's discussion and analysis: the narrative section of annual and quarterly reports explaining results, liquidity, trends and critical accounting estimates. Changes in wording between periods can be informative.

concepts.name: Notes to the financial statements
concepts.def: Disclosures following the primary statements covering accounting policies, segments, debt, leases, taxes, pensions, stock pay and contingencies. Most adjustments analysts make come from here.

concepts.name: Management guidance
concepts.def: A company's own forecast of upcoming revenue, margins or EPS. Firms often guide conservatively to beat later; changes in guidance move stocks more than results relative to consensus.

concepts.name: Earnings surprise
concepts.def: Reported earnings minus consensus forecast, often scaled by the forecast's dispersion or price. Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) scales by the volatility of past surprises.
concepts.formula: SUE = (actual EPS - expected EPS) / std dev of surprises

concepts.name: Post-earnings announcement drift
concepts.def: The tendency of stock prices to keep moving in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks after the announcement, first documented by Ball and Brown (1968). Evidence of investor underreaction.

concepts.name: Three-statement model
concepts.def: A financial model linking forecast income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, so that net income flows to retained earnings and cash balances the sheet. The base for DCF, LBO and credit work.

concepts.name: Price, volume and mix
concepts.def: Decomposing revenue or margin change into price changes, units sold and shifts in product or customer mix. Separates pricing power from demand.
concepts.formula: revenue change = price effect + volume effect + mix effect

concepts.name: Channel checks
concepts.def: Gathering evidence on a company's sales by surveying distributors, retailers, suppliers and customers before results are reported. Useful but prone to small samples and selective sources.

concepts.name: Sell-side research
concepts.def: Research published by brokers and banks, with ratings, target prices and estimates. Valuable for models and industry facts; ratings skew positive because of business conflicts.

concepts.name: Investment thesis
concepts.def: A short, testable statement of why an asset is mispriced, what the market misses, how value will be realized and what would prove the view wrong.

concepts.name: Unit economics
concepts.def: Revenue and costs per unit of business, such as a customer, order or store, showing whether each unit is profitable once scaled. The test of whether growth adds value.

concepts.name: Customer acquisition cost
concepts.def: Sales and marketing spending divided by new customers acquired in a period. Blended CAC including organic customers looks better than paid CAC.
concepts.formula: CAC = sales and marketing spend / new customers

concepts.name: Customer lifetime value
concepts.def: The present value of gross profit a customer generates over the relationship. Highly sensitive to the churn assumption and often computed on revenue rather than margin, which overstates it.
concepts.formula: LTV = ARPU x gross margin / churn rate (simple form)

concepts.name: LTV to CAC
concepts.def: Customer lifetime value divided by acquisition cost. A ratio comfortably above one, often cited as three, suggests acquisition spending creates value; inputs are easily flattered.
concepts.formula: LTV / CAC

concepts.name: CAC payback
concepts.def: Months of gross profit from a new customer needed to recover its acquisition cost. Shorter payback means less capital tied up in growth.
concepts.formula: payback months = CAC / (monthly ARPU x gross margin)

concepts.name: Cohort analysis
concepts.def: Tracking groups of customers who joined in the same period through time for retention, spend and margin. Reveals whether newer cohorts behave better or worse than older ones.

concepts.name: Churn rate
concepts.def: The share of customers lost in a period. Small monthly churn compounds into large annual losses, and the rate drives lifetime value.
