concepts.def: Post-2008 rules requiring two-way initial and variation margin on OTC derivatives that are not centrally cleared, phased in by firm size.

concepts.name: Trade compression
concepts.def: Tearing up offsetting derivative trades among dealers to cut gross notional and counterparty exposures while keeping net risk unchanged.

concepts.name: Counterparty credit risk
concepts.def: Risk that the other side of a derivative defaults while the contract is worth money to you. Exposure moves with market prices, unlike a loan.

concepts.name: Potential future exposure
concepts.def: High percentile of the positive mark-to-market a counterparty could owe over the life of a portfolio. Used to set credit limits and capital.

concepts.name: Debit valuation adjustment
concepts.def: Value adjustment for a firm's own default risk on derivatives where it owes money. Gains when the firm's credit worsens, which makes it controversial.

concepts.name: XVA
concepts.def: Family of valuation adjustments to derivative prices for credit, funding, capital and margin costs: CVA, DVA, FVA, KVA and MVA. Run by dedicated desks at large dealers.

concepts.name: Funding valuation adjustment
concepts.def: Adjustment for the cost of funding uncollateralized derivative exposures at the bank's own borrowing rate rather than the risk-free rate.

concepts.name: CDS index
concepts.def: Standardized basket of single-name credit default swaps, such as CDX in North America and iTraxx in Europe, rolled every six months. The most liquid way to trade or hedge broad credit.

concepts.name: CDS basis
concepts.def: CDS spread minus the bond's spread over the swap curve. A negative basis suggests buying the bond and protection; funding and liquidity can keep it negative for long periods.
concepts.formula: Basis = CDS spread - bond asset swap spread

concepts.name: Base correlation
concepts.def: Market convention quoting tranche prices as the single Gaussian copula correlation that prices each equity tranche from zero to a detachment point. The credit equivalent of implied vol skew.

concepts.name: Swap hedging
concepts.def: Using interest rate swaps to change the duration of assets or liabilities, such as a corporation converting fixed rate debt to floating. Hedge accounting rules govern P&L treatment.

concepts.name: Treasury rate lock
concepts.def: Forward contract that fixes a Treasury yield for a planned bond issue, paying the issuer if yields rise before pricing.

concepts.name: Stop-limit order
concepts.def: Order that becomes a limit order once a stop price trades. It controls the fill price but may not execute at all if the market gaps through the limit.

concepts.name: Trailing stop
concepts.def: Stop order whose trigger follows the price at a set distance or percentage as it moves favorably, locking in gains while staying in the trend.

concepts.name: Market-on-close order
concepts.def: Order to trade at the official closing price in the closing auction. Used by index funds and benchmark-driven traders to match closing marks.

concepts.name: Limit-on-close order
concepts.def: Order that participates in the closing auction only if the closing price is at or better than its limit.

concepts.name: Market-on-open order
concepts.def: Order executed in the opening auction at the official opening price.

concepts.name: Iceberg order
concepts.def: Limit order that shows only a small displayed quantity, refilling from a hidden reserve as the visible part trades. Reduces signaling at the cost of queue priority on the hidden part.

concepts.name: Hidden order
concepts.def: Non-displayed limit order resting on an exchange book. It can be executed against but is invisible in market data and usually ranks behind displayed orders at the same price.

concepts.name: Pegged order
concepts.def: Order whose price automatically tracks a reference such as the bid, offer or midpoint. Midpoint pegs are a common way to rest in dark pools.

concepts.name: Time in force
concepts.def: Instruction for how long an order stays active: day, good till cancelled, immediate or cancel, fill or kill, or until a session such as the opening or closing auction.
concepts.aliases: tif,day order,gtc,good till cancelled,good til canceled

concepts.name: Immediate-or-cancel order
concepts.def: Order that executes whatever quantity is available immediately and cancels the rest. Used by liquidity takers to probe without leaving a resting signal.

concepts.name: Fill-or-kill order
concepts.def: Order that must execute in full immediately or be cancelled entirely, with no partial fills.

concepts.name: All-or-none order
concepts.def: Order that fills only for its entire quantity, though not necessarily immediately. Can wait behind other orders because it cannot take partial liquidity.

concepts.name: Minimum quantity order
concepts.def: Order condition requiring each fill to exceed a set size, common in dark pools to avoid small probing trades from predatory traders.

concepts.name: Post-only order
concepts.def: Limit order that is cancelled or repriced rather than executing on arrival if it would take liquidity. Ensures the trader earns maker rebates.

concepts.name: Intermarket sweep order
concepts.def: US equity order flagged to execute at one venue while simultaneous orders take better-priced quotes elsewhere, exempting it from trade-through checks. Lets fast traders sweep multiple venues at once.

concepts.name: One-cancels-other order
concepts.def: Pair of linked orders where execution of one cancels the other, such as a profit target and a stop loss. Bracket orders attach both to an entry.

concepts.name: Odd lot
concepts.def: Order or trade smaller than a round lot, usually under 100 shares in US equities. Odd lots are common in high priced stocks and traditionally excluded from the NBBO.

concepts.name: Round lot
concepts.def: Standard trading unit, traditionally 100 shares in US equities. Round lot definitions determine which quotes count toward the national best bid and offer.

concepts.name: Short sale uptick rule
concepts.def: Restriction allowing short sales only above the current best bid once a stock falls 10 percent in a day, under SEC Rule 201. The original tick test was repealed in 2007.

concepts.name: Regulation SHO
concepts.def: SEC rules for US short selling: brokers must locate borrowable shares before a short sale, close out persistent fails to deliver, and observe Rule 201 price tests.

concepts.name: Locate
concepts.def: Broker's confirmation that shares can reasonably be borrowed before a short sale, required under Reg SHO. A locate is not a borrow and does not guarantee delivery.

concepts.name: Naked short selling
concepts.def: Selling shares short without borrowing or arranging to borrow them, which can create fails to deliver. Abusive naked shorting is prohibited in the US.

concepts.name: Fails to deliver
concepts.def: Trades where the seller does not deliver securities by settlement date. Persistent fails put a stock on threshold lists and trigger close-out requirements.

concepts.name: Price-time priority
concepts.def: Matching rule where the best priced order executes first and, at equal prices, the earliest order goes first. Rewards speed and queue position.

concepts.name: Pro-rata matching
concepts.def: Matching rule that allocates incoming orders among resting orders at the best price in proportion to their size, used in some futures and options markets. Encourages oversized quoting.

concepts.name: Queue position
concepts.def: Place of a resting limit order in the line at its price level. Front of queue orders fill first and face less adverse selection, so queue position has economic value.

concepts.name: Top of book
concepts.def: Best bid and best offer with their sizes for an instrument on a venue. Level 1 market data.

concepts.name: Depth of book
concepts.def: Resting orders beyond the best prices at each price level, shown in Level 2 data and full order-by-order Level 3 feeds.

concepts.name: Market depth
concepts.def: Volume available to trade at or near the best prices without moving the market much. Thin depth means large orders have large impact.

concepts.name: Market resiliency
concepts.def: Speed at which prices and depth recover after a large trade or shock. One of the three dimensions of liquidity with tightness (spread) and depth.

concepts.name: NBBO
concepts.def: National best bid and offer: the highest bid and lowest offer across all US exchanges for a stock, computed by the securities information processors. The benchmark for best execution and price improvement.

concepts.name: Securities information processor
concepts.def: Consolidated feed that gathers quotes and trades from all US exchanges and publishes the NBBO and last sale. Slower than exchanges' direct feeds.

concepts.name: Direct market data feeds
concepts.def: Proprietary data feeds sold by exchanges, delivering full depth and updates faster than the consolidated tape. Speed gaps between direct feeds and SIP enable latency arbitrage.

concepts.name: Consolidated tape
concepts.def: Unified record of trades and quotes across venues for a market. In the US it is run by the SIPs; Europe has been building one for equities and bonds.

concepts.name: Mid price
concepts.def: Average of the best bid and best offer. Common benchmark for fair value and for dark pool executions.
concepts.formula: Mid = (bid + ask) / 2

concepts.name: Microprice
concepts.def: Fair price estimate that weights bid and ask by opposite-side sizes, leaning toward the side more likely to trade next. Better short-term predictor than the mid.
concepts.formula: Microprice = (bid x ask size + ask x bid size) / (bid size + ask size)

concepts.name: Order book imbalance
concepts.def: Difference between resting bid and ask volume near the top of the book, scaled by their total. Predicts the next mid-price move over very short horizons.
concepts.formula: OBI = (bid size - ask size) / (bid size + ask size)

concepts.name: Order flow imbalance
concepts.def: Net pressure from changes in best bid and ask sizes from new orders, cancels and trades over an interval. Price changes are roughly linear in it at short horizons.

concepts.name: Quoted spread
concepts.def: Difference between the best ask and best bid, often in basis points of the mid. The cost a small market order pays to cross.
concepts.formula: Quoted spread (bps) = (ask - bid) / mid x 10000

concepts.name: Effective spread
concepts.def: Twice the distance between a trade's execution price and the mid at order arrival. Captures price improvement and hidden liquidity, so it is a truer cost than the quoted spread.
concepts.formula: Effective spread = 2 x side x (price - mid)

concepts.name: Realized spread
concepts.def: Twice the difference between trade price and the mid a few seconds or minutes later, signed by trade direction. The liquidity provider's gain after adverse selection.
concepts.formula: Realized spread = 2 x side x (price - mid at t + delta)

concepts.name: Spread decomposition
concepts.def: Splitting the bid-ask spread into order processing costs, inventory holding costs and adverse selection, or the effective spread into realized spread plus price impact.
concepts.formula: Effective spread = realized spread + price impact

concepts.name: Price improvement
concepts.def: Execution at a better price than the prevailing NBBO, such as filling a buy below the offer. Wholesalers and midpoint venues advertise it; its size matters more than its frequency.

concepts.name: Locked and crossed markets
concepts.def: A locked market has the bid equal to the offer across venues; a crossed market has the bid above the offer. Reg NMS bars displaying quotes that lock or cross.

concepts.name: Trade-through
concepts.def: Execution at a price worse than a protected quote displayed on another venue. The Reg NMS order protection rule requires venues to prevent them.

concepts.name: Regulation NMS
concepts.def: SEC framework adopted in 2005 for US equity markets covering order protection, access fees, sub-penny quoting and market data. It fostered competition among venues and fragmentation.

concepts.name: Maker-taker fees
concepts.def: Exchange pricing that pays a rebate to orders adding liquidity and charges a fee to orders removing it. Inverted venues do the opposite. Creates routing conflicts for brokers.

concepts.name: Market fragmentation
concepts.def: Trading in one security split across many exchanges, dark pools and internalizers. Increases competition but complicates finding liquidity and best execution.

concepts.name: Alternative trading system
concepts.def: SEC-registered trading venue that is not an exchange, such as a dark pool or electronic crossing network. Lighter regulation but must file operational disclosures.

concepts.name: Lit market
concepts.def: Venue that displays orders in a public order book before trading, such as an exchange. Opposite of dark venues.

concepts.name: Crossing network
concepts.def: Venue that matches buy and sell orders at a price derived from elsewhere, often the midpoint, without displaying them. Common for block size institutional trades.

concepts.name: Midpoint execution
concepts.def: Trade executed at the mid between the best bid and offer, splitting the spread. Typical of dark pools and midpoint peg orders.

concepts.name: Internalization
concepts.def: Broker or wholesaler filling customer orders from its own inventory instead of routing to an exchange. In US retail equities, wholesalers internalize most marketable flow.

concepts.name: Smart order router
concepts.def: Software that splits and sends orders across venues based on price, size, fees, latency and fill probability.

concepts.name: Last look
concepts.def: Practice in FX where a liquidity provider gets a brief window to accept or reject a trade at its quoted price. Protects against latency arbitrage but can harm clients if abused.

concepts.name: Request for quote
concepts.def: Trading protocol where a client asks one or more dealers for a price on a specific size. Dominant in bonds and OTC derivatives.

concepts.name: All-to-all trading
concepts.def: Market structure where any participant, including buy-side firms, can provide liquidity to any other, rather than only dealers. Growing in corporate bonds.

concepts.name: Risk bid
concepts.def: Principal trade where a dealer buys or sells a whole block or portfolio at a set price and takes the market risk. Faster and more certain than agency execution but costlier.

concepts.name: Agency trading
concepts.def: Broker executes on the client's behalf for a commission without taking the other side, so the client bears market risk.

concepts.name: High-touch trading
concepts.def: Order handling by human sales traders who work orders, find natural blocks and use judgment. Low-touch means electronic algos and direct market access.

concepts.name: Direct market access
concepts.def: Service letting clients send orders directly to exchanges through a broker's infrastructure and identifiers, controlling routing themselves.

concepts.name: Sponsored access
concepts.def: Arrangement where a client trades directly on an exchange under a broker's membership without passing through the broker's systems. SEC rules require pre-trade risk controls.

concepts.name: Order management system
concepts.def: Software that records portfolio orders, checks compliance and routes them to traders, tracking positions and allocations.

concepts.name: Execution management system
concepts.def: Trader software for working orders across brokers, algos and venues with real-time market data and analytics.

concepts.name: FIX protocol
concepts.def: Financial Information eXchange messaging standard for orders, executions and allocations between buy-side, brokers and venues.

concepts.name: Parent and child orders
concepts.def: A large parent order is split by an algorithm into many smaller child orders sent over time and venues to reduce impact and signaling.

concepts.name: Execution algorithm
concepts.def: Automated strategy that executes a parent order according to a benchmark and urgency, such as VWAP, TWAP, POV, implementation shortfall or liquidity seeking.

concepts.name: VWAP algorithm
concepts.def: Execution algorithm that slices an order along the expected intraday volume profile to match the day's volume weighted average price. Low tracking risk but predictable.

concepts.name: Percent of volume algorithm
concepts.def: Execution algorithm that trades a fixed fraction of market volume as it prints, adapting to activity. Completion time is uncertain.

concepts.name: Participation rate
concepts.def: Share of market volume a trader's executions represent over an interval. Higher participation means faster execution but more market impact.
concepts.formula: Participation = own volume / market volume

concepts.name: Liquidity-seeking algorithm
concepts.def: Execution algorithm that pings dark pools and resting liquidity opportunistically to find blocks, trading aggressively when size appears.

concepts.name: Algo wheel
concepts.def: Buy-side process that allocates orders across broker algorithms by rule or randomly, then compares performance with TCA to reduce selection bias.

concepts.name: Intraday volume profile
concepts.def: Typical distribution of trading volume through the day, U-shaped in most equity markets with heavy open and close and a midday lull. The close's share has grown with passive investing.

concepts.name: Arrival price
concepts.def: Market price, usually the mid, when the order reaches the trader or broker. Standard benchmark for implementation shortfall.

concepts.name: Delay cost
concepts.def: Price drift between the portfolio manager's decision and the order reaching the market. A part of implementation shortfall often larger than commissions.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost of unfilled orders
concepts.def: Lost return on the part of an order that was never executed, measured from decision price to a later price. Passive strategies minimize impact but raise this cost.

concepts.name: Timing risk
concepts.def: Uncertainty in execution cost from price moves while an order is worked. Trading slowly lowers impact but raises timing risk, the core tradeoff in optimal execution.

concepts.name: Temporary impact
concepts.def: Part of an order's price impact that reverts after trading stops, caused by consuming liquidity. Depends on trading rate.

concepts.name: Permanent impact
concepts.def: Part of an order's price impact that persists after trading, reflecting information the market infers from the order flow. Depends on total size traded.

concepts.name: Impact decay
concepts.def: Gradual reversion of prices after a metaorder finishes, typically settling well below peak impact. Propagator models describe it as a decay kernel.

concepts.name: Propagator model
concepts.def: Model of price impact as the sum of past signed trades weighted by a decaying kernel, from Bouchaud and coauthors (2004). Reconciles long-memory order flow with efficient prices.

concepts.name: Pre-trade TCA
concepts.def: Estimating expected cost and risk of an order before trading from size, volatility, spread and volume, to choose strategy, algorithm and urgency.

concepts.name: Post-trade TCA
concepts.def: Measuring realized execution costs against benchmarks such as arrival price, VWAP and close, and attributing them to delay, impact and timing.

concepts.name: Transaction cost analysis
concepts.def: Measuring and modeling the explicit and implicit costs of trading, including commissions, spreads, impact and opportunity cost, to improve execution and meet best execution duties.

concepts.name: Best execution
concepts.def: Duty of brokers and managers to seek the most favorable terms reasonably available for client orders, weighing price, cost, speed, likelihood of execution and size.

concepts.name: Rule 605 and 606 reports
concepts.def: SEC disclosures: Rule 605 reports execution quality statistics by venue, Rule 606 reports brokers' order routing and payment for order flow.

concepts.name: MiFID II
concepts.def: EU markets regulation in force since 2018 that tightened best execution and transaction reporting, unbundled research payments and capped some dark trading.

concepts.name: Information leakage in trading
concepts.def: Revealing a large order's intent through visible child orders, quotes or broker contacts, letting others trade ahead and raising impact.

concepts.name: Opening auction
concepts.def: Call auction that aggregates orders before the open and sets a single opening price that maximizes executed volume. Concentrates overnight information.

concepts.name: Closing auction
concepts.def: Call auction at the end of the session that sets the official close used for index valuation, fund NAVs and derivatives. A large and growing share of daily equity volume.

concepts.name: Auction imbalance
concepts.def: Excess of buy over sell interest, or the reverse, published before an auction along with an indicative price, inviting liquidity providers to offset it.

concepts.name: Periodic auction
concepts.def: Frequent short call auctions during the day, used in Europe as an alternative to dark pools. Frequent batch auctions were proposed to blunt speed advantages.

concepts.name: Limit up-limit down
concepts.def: US equity mechanism that bands each stock's price around a recent average and pauses trading for five minutes if the band is breached, adopted after the 2010 flash crash.

concepts.name: Trading halt
concepts.def: Suspension of trading in a security by an exchange or regulator for news pending, order imbalance, volatility or regulatory concerns, usually reopened via an auction.

concepts.name: Kill switch
concepts.def: Control that instantly cancels a firm's resting orders and blocks new ones when risk limits are breached. Mandated pre-trade controls followed the Knight Capital failure.

concepts.name: Fat-finger error
concepts.def: Erroneous order caused by a manual input mistake in size or price. Exchanges use price collars, size limits and clearly erroneous rules to contain them.

concepts.name: Clearly erroneous trade
concepts.def: Exchange rule permitting cancellation or adjustment of trades executed at prices far from the prevailing market, under set thresholds.

concepts.name: Designated market maker
concepts.def: Exchange-appointed firm obliged to maintain fair and orderly markets in assigned securities, quote continuously within set spreads and run auctions, in return for benefits.

concepts.name: Avellaneda-Stoikov model
concepts.def: Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008) market-making model where the dealer skews quotes around a reservation price that shifts against its inventory and sets spreads from risk aversion and order arrival rates.
concepts.formula: Reservation price = s - q x gamma x sigma^2 x (T - t)

concepts.name: Glosten-Milgrom model
concepts.def: Glosten and Milgrom (1985) model in which a competitive dealer sets bid and ask to break even against a mix of informed and uninformed traders, so spreads widen with adverse selection.

concepts.name: Roll spread estimator
concepts.def: Roll (1984) estimate of the effective spread from negative autocovariance of price changes caused by bid-ask bounce.
concepts.formula: Spread = 2 x sqrt(-cov(dP_t, dP_t-1))

concepts.name: Bid-ask bounce
concepts.def: Trade prices alternating between bid and ask without a change in value, creating negative autocorrelation and inflating measured high-frequency volatility.

concepts.name: Microstructure noise
concepts.def: Deviations of observed high-frequency prices from efficient value due to spreads, discreteness and order flow. Biases realized volatility estimated at very fine sampling.
concepts.aliases: market microstructure noise,noise in tick data

concepts.name: Amihud illiquidity
concepts.def: Amihud (2002) measure of price impact: average absolute daily return per dollar of volume. Higher values mean less liquid stocks.
concepts.formula: ILLIQ = mean(|r_t| / dollar volume_t)

concepts.name: Probability of informed trading
concepts.def: Easley, Kiefer, O'Hara and Paperman (1996) estimate of the fraction of order flow from informed traders, from buy and sell imbalances.

concepts.name: VPIN
concepts.def: Volume-synchronized probability of informed trading, from Easley, Lopez de Prado and O'Hara (2012). Measures order flow imbalance in volume buckets as a flow toxicity gauge; its predictive power is debated.

concepts.name: Toxic order flow
concepts.def: Order flow from informed or faster traders that systematically moves prices against the liquidity provider. Market makers widen spreads or avoid venues where it concentrates.

concepts.name: Trade classification
concepts.def: Inferring whether a trade was buyer or seller initiated, using the Lee-Ready algorithm (quote then tick test), the tick rule or bulk volume classification.
concepts.aliases: lee ready,tick rule,trade signing,bulk volume classification

concepts.name: TAQ data
concepts.def: Trade and quote data recording every trade and quote update on US exchanges with timestamps. Standard raw input for microstructure research and TCA.

concepts.name: Price discovery
concepts.def: Process by which trading incorporates information into prices. Measured across venues with Hasbrouck information shares; futures often lead cash markets.

concepts.name: Latency arbitrage
concepts.def: Profiting from a speed advantage by trading against stale quotes before they update, such as picking off resting orders when prices move on another venue.

concepts.name: Co-location
concepts.def: Placing trading servers in or next to an exchange's data center to cut network latency to microseconds. Exchanges sell it as a service with equalized cable lengths.

concepts.name: Speed bump
concepts.def: Deliberate small delay applied to incoming orders on a venue, as introduced by IEX, to blunt latency arbitrage against resting orders.

concepts.name: Index arbitrage
concepts.def: Trading an index future or ETF against its constituent stocks when prices diverge from fair value. Keeps derivatives and baskets aligned; a large share of HFT activity.

concepts.name: Spoofing
concepts.def: Illegal practice of placing orders with intent to cancel before execution to create a false impression of supply or demand and move prices toward one's real orders.

concepts.name: Layering
concepts.def: Form of spoofing that places multiple non-bona fide orders at several price levels on one side of the book to push prices, then trades on the other side.

concepts.name: Quote stuffing
concepts.def: Flooding a venue with rapid order entries and cancellations to slow competitors' data processing. Considered manipulative.

concepts.name: Momentum ignition
concepts.def: Manipulative strategy of initiating a burst of trades to trigger others' momentum algorithms or stops, then trading against the resulting move.

concepts.name: Front-running
concepts.def: Trading ahead of a known pending client order to profit from its price impact. Illegal for brokers with client order knowledge; similar behavior on public signals is legal anticipation.

concepts.name: Pre-hedging
concepts.def: Dealer trading in anticipation of a likely client trade before it is agreed, to manage the risk of taking it on. Allowed under strict conditions but contentious because it can move the client's price.

concepts.name: Wash trading
concepts.def: Simultaneously buying and selling the same asset to create artificial volume or prices without changing ownership. Illegal in regulated markets.

concepts.name: Market manipulation
concepts.def: Intentional conduct that creates false or misleading prices, volume or appearances, including spoofing, wash trading, marking the close and corners. Prohibited under securities and commodities laws.

concepts.name: Marking the close
concepts.def: Trading near the close to influence the closing price, for example to lift portfolio marks or option payoffs. A recognized form of manipulation.

concepts.name: Prime brokerage
concepts.def: Bundle of services large banks provide to hedge funds: custody, clearing, margin financing, securities borrowing for shorts, synthetic exposure and reporting. Revenue comes mainly from financing spreads and stock loan.

concepts.name: Margin lending
concepts.def: Broker loans to clients secured by securities in their account, used to buy more securities or fund shorts. Rates are a spread over a benchmark and loan size depends on haircuts.

concepts.name: Synthetic prime brokerage
concepts.def: Providing hedge fund exposure through total return or portfolio swaps rather than cash securities and margin loans. Saves the fund balance sheet and borrow logistics but hides positions from public filings.

concepts.name: Delta one
concepts.def: Products and desks with linear, one-for-one exposure to an underlying, such as futures, forwards, swaps, ETFs and stock loan. Profit comes from financing, dividends and basis rather than optionality.

concepts.name: Customer protection rule
concepts.def: SEC Rule 15c3-3 requiring US broker-dealers to keep possession or control of fully paid customer securities and reserve cash owed to customers.

concepts.name: House margin
concepts.def: Margin a prime broker sets above regulatory minimums based on its own risk view of a client portfolio, including concentration, liquidity and correlation add-ons.

concepts.name: Margin lockup
concepts.def: Agreement by a prime broker not to raise margin terms on a client for a set notice period, such as 30 to 90 days, giving the fund financing stability.

concepts.name: Funding liquidity
concepts.def: Ease with which a trader can obtain financing for positions. Falls when lenders raise haircuts, which can force sales and drain market liquidity in a spiral.

concepts.name: Cross-margining
concepts.def: Setting margin on related positions held across products or clearing houses together, so offsetting risks reduce total collateral.

concepts.name: Netting
concepts.def: Offsetting amounts owed between parties so only the net is paid or exposed. Payment netting, settlement netting and close-out netting all reduce gross exposures.

concepts.name: Close-out netting
concepts.def: Right under master agreements to terminate all trades with a defaulting party and net their values into a single claim, sharply reducing credit exposure.

concepts.name: Gross exposure
concepts.def: Sum of the absolute values of long and short positions relative to capital. Measures balance sheet use and leverage; prime brokers monitor it closely.
concepts.formula: Gross = (long + |short|) / equity

concepts.name: Net exposure
concepts.def: Long positions minus short positions relative to capital, the directional market exposure of a portfolio. Often beta-adjusted.
concepts.formula: Net = (long - |short|) / equity

concepts.name: Archegos collapse
concepts.def: 2021 failure of family office Archegos Capital, which built concentrated stock exposure through total return swaps at several prime brokers. Margin calls and forced block sales caused large bank losses.

concepts.name: Repurchase agreement
concepts.def: Sale of securities with an agreement to buy them back later at a higher price, effectively a collateralized loan. The core funding market for dealers and leveraged bond positions.

concepts.name: Repo rate
concepts.def: Interest rate implied by a repo's sale and repurchase prices. General collateral rates track policy rates; specific bonds in demand trade at lower special rates.

concepts.name: General collateral
concepts.def: Repo or securities loans where any security from a broad class is acceptable, so the rate reflects pure funding conditions. In stock lending, easy-to-borrow names.

concepts.name: Special repo
concepts.def: Repo on a specific security in high demand, often to cover shorts, that trades at a rate below general collateral. The lender of cash accepts a lower rate to obtain the bond.

concepts.name: Haircut
concepts.def: Discount applied to collateral value when lending against it, so a loan is smaller than the collateral. Haircuts rise with volatility and illiquidity and jump in stress.
concepts.formula: Loan = collateral value x (1 - haircut)

concepts.name: Securities lending
concepts.def: Temporary transfer of securities from a lender, such as a pension fund or ETF, to a borrower, usually a short seller or dealer, against collateral and a fee.

concepts.name: Agent lender
concepts.def: Custodian bank or specialist that lends securities on behalf of beneficial owners, manages collateral and splits fee revenue with the owner.

concepts.name: Cash collateral reinvestment
concepts.def: Investing cash collateral received on securities loans, typically in short-term instruments. The lender bears reinvestment losses, as some did in 2008.

concepts.name: Rebate rate
concepts.def: Interest a stock lender pays back to the borrower on cash collateral. The lending fee equals the cash reinvestment rate minus the rebate; hard-to-borrow names can have negative rebates.
concepts.formula: Fee = reinvestment rate - rebate rate

concepts.name: Short rebate
concepts.def: Interest a prime broker pays a short seller on the cash proceeds of the short sale, net of the borrow fee. Negative for hard-to-borrow stocks.
concepts.aliases: short interest rebate,credit on short proceeds

concepts.name: Easy to borrow
concepts.def: Stocks with ample lendable supply, borrowable at general collateral fees. Brokers publish easy-to-borrow lists that satisfy the locate requirement.

concepts.name: Hard to borrow
concepts.def: Stocks with scarce lendable supply relative to short demand, carrying high fees, recall risk and limited availability. Often crowded shorts with squeeze potential.

concepts.name: Utilization rate
concepts.def: Share of lendable supply of a security currently on loan. High utilization signals crowded shorting and usually higher fees.
concepts.formula: Utilization = shares on loan / lendable shares

concepts.name: Short interest
concepts.def: Number of shares sold short and not yet covered, reported periodically by exchanges, often expressed as a percentage of float.
concepts.aliases: si,short interest percent of float,shares short

concepts.name: Days to cover
concepts.def: Short interest divided by average daily volume: the number of days shorts would need to buy back their position. Higher values mean more squeeze risk.
concepts.formula: Days to cover = short interest / ADV

concepts.name: Recall risk
concepts.def: Risk that a lender recalls lent shares, forcing the short seller to find another borrow or cover, often when the trade is most crowded. Most stock loans are open and recallable.

concepts.name: Buy-in
concepts.def: Forced purchase of securities to close out a short or failed delivery when the borrower cannot return or deliver shares, executed at the borrower's cost.

concepts.name: Open versus term loan
concepts.def: Most securities loans are open, renewing daily and recallable at any time; term loans fix a period and rate, giving borrowers certainty at higher cost.

concepts.name: Manufactured dividend
concepts.def: Payment from a securities borrower to the lender equal to a dividend paid while the shares were on loan, keeping the lender whole. Tax treatment can differ from a real dividend.
concepts.aliases: substitute payment,payment in lieu of dividend

concepts.name: Dividend arbitrage
concepts.def: Trades exploiting differences in dividend tax treatment or mispriced implied dividends, such as lending shares over record date to tax-advantaged holders. Abusive variants like cum-ex were illegal.

concepts.name: Collateral transformation
concepts.def: Swapping lower-quality assets for high-quality collateral, via repo or securities lending, to meet margin requirements. Shifts liquidity risk to the provider.

concepts.name: Synthetic short
concepts.def: Short exposure created without borrowing shares, through a long put plus short call, a short future or a total return swap. Its cost reflects borrow costs embedded by the dealer.

concepts.name: Securities lending signals
concepts.def: Using lending data such as fees, utilization and loan quantities to gauge informed short demand. High fees and rising utilization tend to precede poor returns.
concepts.aliases: stock loan data,short demand signals,borrow data

concepts.name: Custody
concepts.def: Safekeeping of securities and cash on behalf of clients, with settlement, corporate actions and income collection. Custodians and prime brokers hold hedge fund assets.

concepts.name: Prime broker counterparty risk
concepts.def: Risk to a fund that its prime broker fails or abruptly tightens terms, freezing assets or forcing sales. Using several primes reduces it, as funds learned after Lehman.

concepts.name: Historical simulation VaR
concepts.def: VaR estimated by revaluing today's portfolio under actual past return scenarios and reading the loss quantile from that empirical distribution. It needs no distributional assumption but is only as good as the lookback window it samples.
concepts.aliases: historical var, hs var, hvar, historical simulation

concepts.name: Parametric VaR
concepts.def: VaR computed from an assumed distribution, usually normal, using portfolio volatility from a covariance matrix. Fast and easy to decompose, but it understates tail losses when returns are fat-tailed or positions are nonlinear.
concepts.formula: VaR = z_alpha x sigma_p x V, where sigma_p = sqrt(w' Sigma w)
concepts.aliases: variance-covariance var, delta-normal var, analytical var, gaussian var

concepts.name: Monte Carlo VaR
concepts.def: VaR estimated by simulating many joint scenarios of risk factors from a chosen model, revaluing the portfolio in each, and taking the loss quantile. Handles nonlinear positions well; results depend on the simulation model and are computationally heavy.
concepts.aliases: mc var, simulation var, monte carlo value at risk

concepts.name: Delta-gamma VaR
concepts.def: An approximation of VaR for option books that adds the second-order gamma term to the linear delta exposure, capturing curvature that delta-normal VaR misses. Still unreliable for large moves or complex payoffs.
concepts.formula: dV approx delta x dS + 0.5 x gamma x dS^2

concepts.name: Filtered historical simulation
concepts.def: A VaR method that standardizes past returns by their fitted GARCH volatility and then rescales them by today's volatility forecast, so historical scenarios reflect current market conditions instead of the average of the window.
concepts.formula: r_scenario = (r_t / sigma_t) x sigma_today
concepts.aliases: fhs, filtered hs, volatility-scaled historical simulation

concepts.name: Cornish-Fisher VaR
concepts.def: A modified parametric VaR that adjusts the normal quantile for the sample skewness and excess kurtosis of returns, giving a quick correction for asymmetric and fat-tailed distributions.
concepts.formula: z_cf = z + (z^2-1)S/6 + (z^3-3z)K/24 - (2z^3-5z)S^2/36, with K as excess kurtosis
concepts.aliases: modified var, mvar, cornish fisher expansion

concepts.name: Marginal VaR
concepts.def: The rate at which portfolio VaR changes for a small increase in exposure to one position. It shows which holdings add the most tail risk at the margin and is the building block of component VaR.
concepts.formula: MVaR_i = dVaR / dw_i = z x (Sigma w)_i / sigma_p under normality
concepts.aliases: mvar, marginal value at risk, delta var

concepts.name: Component VaR
concepts.def: The share of total portfolio VaR attributed to one position, equal to its weight times its marginal VaR. Under Euler allocation the components sum exactly to total VaR, so they can be used for limits and capital charges.
concepts.formula: CVaR_i = w_i x MVaR_i; sum of CVaR_i = VaR
concepts.aliases: contribution var, cvar component, var contribution

concepts.name: Incremental VaR
concepts.def: The change in portfolio VaR from adding or removing an entire position or trade, computed by revaluing with and without it. Unlike marginal VaR it captures non-small changes.
concepts.formula: IVaR = VaR(portfolio + trade) - VaR(portfolio)
concepts.aliases: ivar, incremental value at risk, pre-trade var

concepts.name: Stressed VaR
concepts.def: VaR calibrated to a historical window of significant market stress rather than recent data, introduced under Basel 2.5 so trading book capital does not fall in calm periods.
concepts.aliases: svar, stressed value at risk, basel 2.5 var

concepts.name: VaR backtesting
concepts.def: Checking a VaR model by comparing its daily forecasts with realized P&L and testing whether the number and clustering of exceptions match the stated confidence level.
concepts.aliases: var backtest, exception testing, coverage test

concepts.name: VaR exception
concepts.def: A day on which the realized loss exceeds the VaR forecast. At 99% confidence about 2.5 exceptions per 250 days are expected; far more suggests the model understates risk.
concepts.aliases: var breach, exceedance, var overshoot, backtesting exception

concepts.name: Kupiec test
concepts.def: A likelihood ratio test of unconditional coverage that asks whether the observed share of VaR exceptions is consistent with the model's stated probability. It ignores whether exceptions cluster.
concepts.formula: LR_pof = -2 ln[(1-p)^(T-x) p^x] + 2 ln[(1-x/T)^(T-x) (x/T)^x], chi-square with 1 df
concepts.aliases: proportion of failures test, pof test, unconditional coverage test

concepts.name: Christoffersen test
concepts.def: A VaR backtest that checks whether exceptions are independent over time and combines this with the coverage test into a conditional coverage test. Clustered exceptions signal a model slow to react to volatility.
concepts.formula: LR_cc = LR_pof + LR_ind, chi-square with 2 df
concepts.aliases: conditional coverage test, independence test, christoffersen 1998

concepts.name: Basel traffic light
concepts.def: The Basel framework for classifying a bank's 99% one-day VaR model by exceptions over 250 days: green for 0 to 4, yellow for 5 to 9, red for 10 or more, with higher capital multipliers outside green.
concepts.aliases: traffic light test, basel zones, var multiplier zones

concepts.name: Coherent risk measure
concepts.def: A risk measure satisfying the four axioms of Artzner, Delbaen, Eber and Heath (1999): monotonicity, subadditivity, positive homogeneity and translation invariance. Expected shortfall is coherent; VaR is not, because it can fail subadditivity.
concepts.aliases: coherence axioms, artzner axioms, coherent measure

concepts.name: Subadditivity
concepts.def: The property that the risk of a combined portfolio is no greater than the sum of the risks of its parts, so diversification never increases measured risk. VaR can violate it for skewed or fat-tailed positions.
concepts.formula: rho(A + B) <= rho(A) + rho(B)

concepts.name: Spectral risk measure
concepts.def: A coherent risk measure defined as a weighted average of loss quantiles where weights do not decrease toward worse outcomes, letting the weighting reflect a user's risk aversion. Expected shortfall is the case with flat weights in the tail.
concepts.formula: M = integral of phi(p) x q(p) dp, with phi nondecreasing and integrating to 1
concepts.aliases: distortion risk measure, acerbi spectral measure

concepts.name: Expected shortfall backtesting
concepts.def: Testing an expected shortfall model by comparing the size of realized tail losses with predicted averages, for example with the Acerbi and Szekely (2014) tests. Harder than VaR backtesting because ES is not elicitable on its own.
concepts.aliases: es backtest, cvar backtest, acerbi szekely test

concepts.name: Elicitability
concepts.def: A property of a statistic that it minimizes the expected value of some scoring function, which allows forecasts of it to be compared directly. Quantiles, and so VaR, are elicitable; expected shortfall alone is not, though the pair is.

concepts.name: Extreme value theory
concepts.def: The branch of statistics that models the tails of distributions directly, using limit results for maxima and for exceedances over high thresholds. Used to estimate far-tail VaR and ES where data are sparse.
concepts.aliases: evt, tail modeling, extreme value statistics

concepts.name: Peaks over threshold
concepts.def: An extreme value method that fits a generalized Pareto distribution to losses above a high threshold. The choice of threshold trades bias against variance and drives the tail estimate.
concepts.aliases: pot, pot method, threshold exceedance model

concepts.name: Generalized Pareto distribution
concepts.def: The limiting distribution of exceedances over a high threshold for a wide class of distributions, with a shape parameter that sets tail heaviness. A positive shape means a power-law tail.
concepts.formula: G(y) = 1 - (1 + xi y / beta)^(-1/xi)

concepts.name: Block maxima
concepts.def: An extreme value approach that splits data into blocks, such as months, takes the worst loss in each, and fits a generalized extreme value distribution. Simple but wasteful of data compared with peaks over threshold.
concepts.aliases: gev, generalized extreme value, block maximum method

concepts.name: Historical stress scenario
concepts.def: A stress test that applies the factor moves of a real past episode, such as 1987, 2008 or 2020, to today's portfolio. Plausible by construction but blind to crises that have not yet happened.

concepts.name: Hypothetical stress scenario
concepts.def: A forward-looking stress test built from a narrative of shocks that may never have occurred together, translated into consistent moves across risk factors. Useful for new risks but depends on the designer's imagination.
concepts.aliases: hypothetical stress test, forward-looking scenario, narrative scenario

concepts.name: Reverse stress test
concepts.def: A stress test that starts from an outcome the firm cannot survive, such as a loss that breaches capital, and works backward to find the scenarios that would cause it. It exposes hidden vulnerabilities.
concepts.aliases: reverse stress testing, breaking point analysis

concepts.name: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.def: Measuring how portfolio value or a model output changes when one input is moved while others are held fixed, such as a 100 basis point rate shift. Simple and transparent but ignores joint moves.
concepts.aliases: what-if analysis, shock analysis, one-factor stress

concepts.name: CCAR
concepts.def: The Federal Reserve's Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, an annual supervisory stress test and capital planning exercise for large US bank holding companies that informs limits on dividends and buybacks.
concepts.aliases: comprehensive capital analysis and review, fed stress test, dfast

concepts.name: Stress capital buffer
concepts.def: A bank capital requirement set from the projected capital decline in the Fed's severely adverse stress scenario plus planned dividends, so capital needs scale with each bank's own stress losses.

concepts.name: Correlation breakdown
concepts.def: The tendency for correlations between risky assets to rise sharply in sell-offs, so diversification measured in calm periods disappears when it is needed most.
concepts.aliases: correlations go to one, correlation spike, diversification failure

concepts.name: Liquidity-adjusted VaR
concepts.def: VaR extended to include the cost of exiting positions, typically by adding half the bid-ask spread, or its stressed level, times position value, or by lengthening the horizon for illiquid holdings.
concepts.formula: LVaR = VaR + 0.5 x spread x V (Bangia et al. 1999)

concepts.name: Funding liquidity risk
concepts.def: The risk that a firm or fund cannot meet cash obligations, margin calls or redemptions when due, or can only do so at punitive cost. It interacts with market liquidity in a crisis.
concepts.aliases: funding risk, cash flow liquidity risk

concepts.name: Liquidity horizon
concepts.def: The time needed to exit or hedge a position without materially moving the price under stressed conditions. FRTB assigns horizons from 10 to 120 days by risk factor when scaling expected shortfall.

concepts.name: Days to liquidate
concepts.def: An estimate of how many trading days it would take to exit a position while trading no more than a set fraction of average daily volume. A core input to fund liquidity reporting.
concepts.formula: days = position size / (participation rate x ADV)
concepts.aliases: dtl, days to exit, liquidation days, days of volume

concepts.name: Liquidity spiral
concepts.def: Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009): falling prices cause losses and higher margins, forcing leveraged traders to sell, which lowers prices and market liquidity further. Funding and market liquidity reinforce each other.
concepts.aliases: loss spiral, margin spiral, brunnermeier pedersen

concepts.name: Fire sale
concepts.def: Forced selling of assets at prices well below fundamental value because the natural buyers are themselves constrained. Fire sales transmit losses to other holders of the same assets.
concepts.aliases: forced selling, distressed selling, fire-sale prices

concepts.name: Redemption risk
concepts.def: The risk that investors withdraw capital from a fund faster than its assets can be sold at fair prices, forcing losses on remaining holders and possibly gating or suspension.
concepts.aliases: run risk, withdrawal risk, outflow risk

concepts.name: Net stable funding ratio
concepts.def: A Basel III requirement that a bank's available stable funding exceed the stable funding its assets require over a one-year horizon, limiting reliance on short-term wholesale funding.
concepts.formula: NSFR = available stable funding / required stable funding >= 100%

concepts.name: Liquidity stress test
concepts.def: A test of whether a fund or firm can meet redemptions, margin calls and other outflows under severe but plausible conditions, combining stressed asset liquidity with stressed liability behavior.

concepts.name: Current exposure
concepts.def: The cost of replacing a counterparty's trades today if it defaulted, equal to the positive mark-to-market of the netting set after collateral, floored at zero.
concepts.formula: CE = max(MtM - collateral, 0)

concepts.name: Expected exposure
concepts.def: The average of positive counterparty exposure at a future date across simulated scenarios. Its time profile feeds CVA, and its time average gives expected positive exposure.
concepts.formula: EE(t) = E[max(V(t), 0)]; EPE = time average of EE

concepts.name: Exposure at default
concepts.def: The amount a lender or counterparty expects to be owed at the moment of default. For loans it includes expected drawdowns of undrawn lines; for derivatives it comes from exposure simulation.

concepts.name: Unexpected loss
concepts.def: Credit loss above the expected level at a chosen confidence, driven by default correlation and concentration. It is what economic and regulatory capital are meant to absorb.

concepts.name: Margin period of risk
concepts.def: The assumed time between the last successful collateral exchange with a defaulting counterparty and the close-out of its positions. Exposure can grow unsecured during this window.

concepts.name: Central clearing
concepts.def: Interposing a central counterparty between buyer and seller so each faces the clearing house rather than each other, with margin and a default fund mutualizing losses. It concentrates risk in the CCP.

concepts.name: Settlement risk
concepts.def: The risk that one side delivers cash or securities while the other fails to deliver, often because of time-zone gaps in currency trades. Named Herstatt risk after a 1974 bank failure.
concepts.aliases: herstatt risk, delivery risk, principal risk

concepts.name: Credit risk
concepts.def: The risk of loss because a borrower, issuer or counterparty fails to pay as promised or its credit quality deteriorates, which lowers the value of its debt.

concepts.name: Market risk
concepts.def: The risk of loss from moves in market prices and rates: equity prices, interest rates, credit spreads, currencies, commodities and volatility. Measured with sensitivities, VaR and stress tests.

concepts.name: Operational risk
concepts.def: The risk of loss from failed processes, people, systems or external events, including fraud, trade errors, outages and legal risk. Examples include rogue trading and algorithm failures.

concepts.name: Systemic risk
concepts.def: The risk that distress at one institution or market spreads through funding, fire sales and confidence to impair the financial system and the real economy.

concepts.name: CoVaR
concepts.def: Adrian and Brunnermeier's measure of the financial system's VaR conditional on one institution being in distress. Delta CoVaR, the change versus that institution's median state, gauges its systemic contribution.
concepts.formula: Delta CoVaR_i = CoVaR(system | i at VaR) - CoVaR(system | i at median)

concepts.name: Marginal expected shortfall
concepts.def: An institution's average return on the days when the overall market is in its worst tail, measuring how much the firm loses when the system does badly. A building block of SRISK.
concepts.formula: MES_i = E[r_i | r_market < VaR_market]

concepts.name: SRISK
concepts.def: Brownlees and Engle's estimate of the capital a financial firm would need to raise if the market fell sharply, combining its leverage, size and long-run marginal expected shortfall.

concepts.name: Absorption ratio
concepts.def: Kritzman and others' measure of market fragility: the share of total asset return variance explained by a small fixed number of principal components. A high ratio means markets are tightly coupled.
concepts.formula: AR = sum of variance of top n eigenvectors / total variance

concepts.name: Turbulence index
concepts.def: The Mahalanobis distance of current multi-asset returns from their historical mean, accounting for covariance. Large values flag unusual market behavior and have tended to coincide with poor returns.
concepts.formula: d_t = (r_t - mu)' Sigma^-1 (r_t - mu)

concepts.name: Leverage cycle
concepts.def: Geanakoplos' account of how collateral requirements loosen in booms, raising leverage and asset prices, then tighten abruptly in busts, forcing deleveraging and crashes that overshoot fundamentals.

concepts.name: Volatility paradox
concepts.def: The observation that low measured volatility encourages higher leverage and risk-taking, building fragility that makes later crises worse. Associated with Brunnermeier and Sannikov (2014).
concepts.aliases: stability breeds instability, low vol paradox

concepts.name: Procyclicality
concepts.def: When risk models, margins or capital rules amplify the cycle: low volatility allows more leverage in booms, and spikes in measured risk force selling in busts.

concepts.name: Gap risk
concepts.def: The risk that a price jumps discontinuously, often overnight or on news, skipping past stop orders and hedge rebalancing levels, so losses exceed what continuous-trading models assume.

concepts.name: Event risk
concepts.def: Exposure to a discrete, often binary event such as an earnings release, regulatory decision, merger vote, election or default, whose outcome can move prices sharply.
concepts.aliases: binary event risk, headline risk, catalyst risk

concepts.name: Three lines of defense
concepts.def: A governance model in which the business owns and manages risk (first line), independent risk and compliance functions set limits and challenge (second line), and internal audit provides assurance (third line).

concepts.name: FRTB
concepts.def: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book, the Basel market risk rule that replaced VaR with expected shortfall at 97.5%, added liquidity horizons, and tightened the boundary between trading and banking books.
concepts.aliases: fundamental review of the trading book, basel market risk

concepts.name: Covariance matrix
concepts.def: The square table of variances and pairwise covariances of asset returns that underlies portfolio volatility, VaR and optimization. With many assets and short histories it is noisy and needs shrinkage or factor structure.
concepts.formula: portfolio variance = w' Sigma w
concepts.aliases: sigma, cov matrix, variance-covariance matrix, correlation matrix

concepts.name: EWMA volatility
concepts.def: A volatility estimate that weights recent squared returns more heavily with exponentially decaying weights. RiskMetrics used a decay factor of 0.94 for daily data. It is an integrated GARCH with no mean reversion.
concepts.formula: sigma_t^2 = lambda x sigma_(t-1)^2 + (1 - lambda) x r_(t-1)^2

concepts.name: Risk factor mapping
concepts.def: Representing each position by its exposures to a manageable set of market risk factors, such as curve points, spreads, indices and vol surfaces, so a large book can be simulated and aggregated.
concepts.aliases: cash flow mapping, factor mapping, risk mapping

concepts.name: Full revaluation
concepts.def: Pricing every position with its complete pricing model in each risk scenario, rather than approximating with sensitivities. Accurate for options and nonlinear products but computationally expensive.

concepts.name: Proxy risk
concepts.def: The model error introduced when a position's risk is represented by a related but different factor because its own history is short or missing, such as a new bond mapped to a sector curve.

concepts.name: Risks not in VaR
concepts.def: Risks that a firm's VaR model does not capture, such as basis, illiquid factors or jump risk, which must be identified and capitalized separately.
concepts.aliases: rniv, risks not in model, non-modellable risk factors, nmrf

concepts.name: P&L attribution
concepts.def: Explaining daily profit and loss by risk factor moves times sensitivities plus new trades, carry and residual. A large unexplained residual points to missing risks or model errors.
concepts.formula: P&L approx sum of sensitivity_i x factor move_i + carry + new trades + residual
concepts.aliases: p&l explain, pnl explain, risk-based p&l, hypothetical p&l

concepts.name: Risk decomposition
concepts.def: Breaking total portfolio risk into contributions from positions, sectors or factors that sum to the total, showing where risk actually comes from as opposed to where capital is allocated.
concepts.aliases: risk attribution, risk breakdown, ex-ante risk decomposition

concepts.name: Euler allocation
concepts.def: Allocating a risk measure that is homogeneous of degree one, such as volatility, VaR or ES, to positions as weight times marginal risk. By Euler's theorem the contributions sum exactly to the total.
concepts.formula: R(w) = sum of w_i x dR/dw_i

concepts.name: Marginal contribution to risk
concepts.def: The increase in portfolio volatility from a small increase in one asset's weight. Multiplying by the weight gives that asset's contribution to total risk.
concepts.formula: MCTR_i = (Sigma w)_i / sigma_p

concepts.name: Risk contribution
concepts.def: The portion of total portfolio volatility attributable to one asset or factor, equal to weight times marginal contribution, often shown as a percent of total. Risk parity sets these equal.
concepts.formula: RC_i = w_i x (Sigma w)_i / sigma_p; %RC_i = RC_i / sigma_p
concepts.aliases: contribution to risk, ctr, percent contribution to risk, pctr

concepts.name: Risk budgeting
concepts.def: Allocating a total risk allowance across assets, strategies, factors or managers, then sizing positions so each uses its assigned share. It shifts focus from capital weights to risk weights.

concepts.name: Active risk budget
concepts.def: The tracking error a manager or plan sponsor is willing to take relative to a benchmark, allocated across managers or bets in proportion to their expected information ratios.
concepts.formula: optimal TE_i proportional to IR_i
concepts.aliases: tracking error budget, te budget, active risk allocation

concepts.name: Ex-ante versus ex-post risk
concepts.def: Ex-ante risk is forecast from current holdings and a risk model; ex-post risk is measured from realized returns. Persistent gaps reveal model error, style drift or nonlinear exposures.
concepts.aliases: predicted risk, realized risk, forecast tracking error, ex ante te

concepts.name: Risk limits
concepts.def: Hard or soft caps on exposures, sensitivities, VaR, stress losses, concentration or drawdown that keep a desk, fund or manager within risk appetite. Breaches trigger escalation or forced reduction.
concepts.aliases: limit framework, position limits, var limit, exposure limits

concepts.name: Risk appetite
concepts.def: The amount and type of risk an institution is willing to accept to meet its objectives, stated in measurable terms such as maximum drawdown, earnings volatility or capital at risk, and cascaded into limits.
concepts.aliases: risk appetite statement, ras, risk tolerance

concepts.name: Risk capacity
concepts.def: The maximum loss an investor or firm can absorb without failing its obligations or goals, set by balance sheet, liabilities and time horizon. Distinct from willingness to take risk.
concepts.aliases: ability to take risk, loss capacity

concepts.name: Economic capital
concepts.def: A firm's own estimate of the capital needed to absorb unexpected losses at a target confidence over a horizon, aggregated across market, credit and operational risk. Used to price and allocate risk.
concepts.aliases: risk capital, capital at risk, car

concepts.name: RAROC
concepts.def: Risk-adjusted return on capital: a business line's return after expected losses divided by the economic capital it consumes. Compared with a hurdle to decide whether activities create value.
concepts.formula: RAROC = (revenue - costs - expected loss) / economic capital
concepts.aliases: risk adjusted return on capital, rorac

concepts.name: Beta-adjusted exposure
concepts.def: Net exposure computed by weighting each position by its beta to the market, which better reflects true market sensitivity than dollar net exposure when longs and shorts differ in beta.
concepts.formula: beta-adjusted net = sum of w_i x beta_i
concepts.aliases: beta-adjusted net, beta net exposure, delta-adjusted exposure

concepts.name: Semivariance
concepts.def: The variance of returns below a threshold, usually zero or the mean, which penalizes only downside moves. Its square root, downside deviation, is the denominator of the Sortino ratio.
concepts.formula: SV = E[min(r - target, 0)^2]
concepts.aliases: downside deviation, downside risk, lower partial moment, lpm

concepts.name: Drawdown limit
concepts.def: A rule that cuts risk or stops a strategy once its loss from peak exceeds a set level, often in stages. It caps the damage from a broken strategy at the cost of sometimes locking in losses before a recovery.
concepts.aliases: drawdown control, drawdown stop, loss limit, de-risking trigger

concepts.name: CPPI
concepts.def: Constant proportion portfolio insurance: keep risky exposure equal to a multiple of the cushion above a protected floor, adding risk as the portfolio rises and cutting it as it falls. Gap risk can breach the floor.
concepts.formula: risky exposure = m x (portfolio value - floor)
concepts.aliases: constant proportion portfolio insurance, black jones perold

concepts.name: TIPP
concepts.def: Time-invariant portfolio protection: a CPPI variant whose floor ratchets up to a fixed fraction of the highest portfolio value reached, locking in gains.
concepts.formula: floor_t = k x max portfolio value to date
concepts.aliases: time invariant portfolio protection, ratchet floor

concepts.name: Conditional drawdown at risk
concepts.def: The average of the worst drawdowns beyond a chosen percentile, a tail measure of path losses analogous to expected shortfall but applied to drawdowns rather than single-period returns.

concepts.name: Calmar ratio
concepts.def: Annualized return divided by maximum drawdown, usually over three years. Popular with managed futures investors; noisy because maximum drawdown is a single worst event.
concepts.formula: Calmar = annualized return / |max drawdown|
concepts.aliases: mar ratio, return over max drawdown

concepts.name: Ulcer index
concepts.def: Peter Martin's measure of drawdown pain: the root mean square of percentage drawdowns from running peaks. It captures both depth and duration of declines.
concepts.formula: UI = sqrt(mean of D_t^2), where D_t is percent below prior peak

concepts.name: Time under water
concepts.def: The length of time a portfolio spends below its previous high before recovering, often more damaging to investor behavior than the depth of the drawdown itself.
concepts.aliases: drawdown duration, recovery time, underwater period

concepts.name: Copula
concepts.def: A function that joins separate marginal distributions into a joint distribution, isolating the dependence structure. Lets risk models pair fat-tailed marginals with tail dependence.
concepts.formula: F(x, y) = C(F_X(x), F_Y(y)) by Sklar's theorem
concepts.aliases: sklar's theorem, t copula, dependence structure

concepts.name: Model validation
concepts.def: Independent review of a model's conceptual soundness, data, implementation and performance, including outcomes analysis and benchmarking against alternatives. Required for bank models under SR 11-7.

concepts.name: SR 11-7
concepts.def: The US Federal Reserve and OCC supervisory guidance on model risk management (2011), which defines models broadly and requires sound development, independent validation, governance and an inventory.

concepts.name: Challenger model
concepts.def: An independently built alternative model run alongside the production model to test whether its outputs are reasonable. Large disagreements prompt investigation.

concepts.name: Model monitoring
concepts.def: Ongoing tracking of a model's inputs, outputs and accuracy after deployment to detect drift, breaks and degrading performance, with thresholds that trigger review or recalibration.
concepts.aliases: ongoing monitoring, model drift monitoring, performance monitoring

concepts.name: Modern portfolio theory
concepts.def: Markowitz's (1952) framework in which investors choose portfolios by expected return and variance, and diversification lowers risk because assets are imperfectly correlated. The foundation of mean-variance optimization and CAPM.

concepts.name: Mean-variance optimization
concepts.def: Choosing portfolio weights to maximize expected return for a given variance, or minimize variance for a given return, using estimated means and a covariance matrix. Highly sensitive to errors in expected returns.
concepts.formula: max w'mu - (lambda/2) w' Sigma w subject to constraints

concepts.name: Efficient frontier
concepts.def: The set of portfolios offering the highest expected return for each level of risk. Portfolios below it are dominated; estimated frontiers are optimistic because they are fit to the same noisy inputs.

concepts.name: Capital market line
concepts.def: The straight line from the risk-free rate tangent to the efficient frontier of risky assets. Combinations of cash and the tangency portfolio on this line dominate all other risky portfolios.
concepts.formula: E(r) = rf + [(E(r_m) - rf) / sigma_m] x sigma

concepts.name: Tangency portfolio
concepts.def: The risky portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio, where the capital market line touches the efficient frontier. In CAPM it equals the market portfolio.
concepts.formula: w proportional to Sigma^-1 (mu - rf)
concepts.aliases: maximum sharpe portfolio, max sharpe, msr portfolio

concepts.name: Minimum variance portfolio
concepts.def: The portfolio with the lowest possible variance, which depends only on the covariance matrix, not expected returns. Because it avoids return estimates, it is often more robust out of sample and tilts toward low-volatility stocks.
concepts.formula: w = Sigma^-1 1 / (1' Sigma^-1 1)
concepts.aliases: gmv, global minimum variance, min vol portfolio, minimum volatility

concepts.name: Two-fund separation
concepts.def: The result that, with a risk-free asset and mean-variance preferences, every investor holds the same risky portfolio and differs only in how much cash or leverage they combine with it.

concepts.name: Estimation error
concepts.def: The gap between estimated and true expected returns, volatilities and correlations. Mean errors matter most: optimizers treat noise as signal and concentrate in assets whose returns were overestimated.
concepts.aliases: parameter uncertainty, estimation risk, input uncertainty

concepts.name: Error maximization
concepts.def: Michaud's (1989) critique that mean-variance optimizers systematically overweight assets with overestimated returns and underestimated risk, producing extreme, unstable portfolios that perform poorly out of sample.

concepts.name: Resampled efficiency
concepts.def: Michaud's method of resampling inputs many times, optimizing each draw and averaging the weights, which yields more diversified and stable allocations than a single optimization.
concepts.aliases: resampled frontier, michaud resampling, portfolio resampling

concepts.name: Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage
concepts.def: Shrinking the sample covariance matrix toward a structured target, such as constant correlation or a single-factor model, with a data-driven intensity that minimizes expected estimation error. Better conditioned and more stable.
concepts.formula: Sigma_shrunk = delta x F + (1 - delta) x S
concepts.aliases: covariance shrinkage, ledoit wolf, shrunk covariance

concepts.name: Shrinkage estimator
concepts.def: An estimator that pulls noisy individual estimates toward a common target, accepting a little bias for a large cut in variance. Applied to expected returns, betas and covariances.
concepts.formula: estimate = c x target + (1 - c) x sample estimate

concepts.name: Random matrix theory
concepts.def: Results on eigenvalues of large random matrices, such as the Marchenko-Pastur law, used to separate covariance eigenvalues explained by noise from those carrying structure, and to denoise correlation matrices.
concepts.formula: noise eigenvalue bounds = sigma^2 x (1 +/- sqrt(N/T))^2
concepts.aliases: rmt, marchenko-pastur, eigenvalue clipping, covariance denoising

concepts.name: Black-Litterman model
concepts.def: Black and Litterman (1990, 1992) combine market-implied equilibrium returns with an investor's views, weighted by confidence, through a Bayesian update. The result is expected returns that produce intuitive, diversified portfolios.
concepts.formula: E(R) = [(tau Sigma)^-1 + P' Omega^-1 P]^-1 [(tau Sigma)^-1 Pi + P' Omega^-1 Q]

concepts.name: Implied equilibrium returns
concepts.def: Expected returns backed out from market-cap weights by reverse optimization: the returns that would make the market portfolio optimal for a given risk aversion. The neutral prior in Black-Litterman.
concepts.formula: Pi = delta x Sigma x w_mkt
concepts.aliases: reverse optimization, equilibrium returns, implied returns, pi

concepts.name: Idzorek method
concepts.def: A way to set the view uncertainty matrix in Black-Litterman from intuitive confidence percentages, so a 100% confident view moves weights fully to the view-implied portfolio and 0% leaves equilibrium weights.

concepts.name: Robust optimization
concepts.def: Optimizing for the worst case within an uncertainty set around estimated inputs instead of point estimates, so the portfolio holds up if parameters are moderately wrong.

concepts.name: Portfolio constraints
concepts.def: Limits imposed on an optimization such as long-only, weight caps, sector bands, turnover and tracking error. Jagannathan and Ma (2003) showed long-only constraints act like covariance shrinkage.
concepts.aliases: optimization constraints, box constraints, weight limits

concepts.name: Long-only constraint
concepts.def: The prohibition on short positions that most mutual funds and pensions face. It prevents managers from fully expressing negative views and lowers the transfer coefficient.

concepts.name: Hierarchical risk parity
concepts.def: Lopez de Prado's (2016) allocation method that clusters assets by correlation, orders them, and splits capital top-down by inverse variance. It avoids inverting the covariance matrix and is more stable than mean-variance.

concepts.name: Nested clustered optimization
concepts.def: Lopez de Prado's method of optimizing within correlation clusters first and then across cluster portfolios, limiting the instability that correlated assets cause in standard optimizers.

concepts.name: Inverse volatility weighting
concepts.def: Weighting assets in proportion to one over their volatility, ignoring correlations. It is risk parity when all correlations are equal and a common naive risk-balanced allocation.
concepts.formula: w_i = (1/sigma_i) / sum of (1/sigma_j)
concepts.aliases: naive risk parity, inverse vol, 1/vol weighting

concepts.name: Equal-weight portfolio
concepts.def: Allocating 1/N to each asset. DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found optimized portfolios rarely beat it out of sample because estimation error swamps the gains from optimization.
concepts.formula: w_i = 1/N

concepts.name: Maximum diversification portfolio
concepts.def: Choueifaty and Coignard's (2008) portfolio that maximizes the diversification ratio, the ratio of weighted average asset volatility to portfolio volatility.

concepts.name: Diversification ratio
concepts.def: The weighted average of individual asset volatilities divided by portfolio volatility. It equals one with no diversification benefit and rises as correlations fall.
concepts.formula: DR = (w' sigma) / sqrt(w' Sigma w)

concepts.name: Effective number of bets
concepts.def: A measure of how many independent risk sources a portfolio really holds, often computed from the entropy of risk contributions on uncorrelated principal components. Many holdings can still be few bets.
concepts.formula: ENB = exp(-sum of p_i ln p_i), p_i = share of variance from component i
concepts.aliases: enb, meucci effective bets, number of independent bets

concepts.name: Fractional Kelly
concepts.def: Betting a fixed fraction, often half, of the Kelly-optimal size. It sacrifices a little growth for much lower volatility and drawdowns and protects against overestimating the edge.
concepts.formula: half Kelly: roughly 75% of the growth rate with 50% of the volatility

concepts.name: All Weather portfolio
concepts.def: Bridgewater's risk-balanced strategic portfolio built to perform across growth and inflation regimes by balancing risk among equities, nominal bonds, inflation-linked bonds and commodities, often with leverage on bonds.
concepts.aliases: all weather, bridgewater all weather, all-season portfolio

concepts.name: Permanent portfolio
concepts.def: Harry Browne's allocation of equal parts stocks, long-term Treasuries, gold and cash, meant to hold up through prosperity, deflation, inflation and recession without forecasting.
concepts.aliases: harry browne portfolio, browne permanent portfolio

concepts.name: Core-satellite
concepts.def: A structure that holds a low-cost passive core for broad market exposure and surrounds it with smaller active or thematic satellites, concentrating fees and tracking error where conviction is highest.

concepts.name: Strategic asset allocation
concepts.def: The long-term target mix of asset classes set from the investor's objectives, constraints and capital market assumptions. It explains most of the variation in a diversified portfolio's returns over time.

concepts.name: Policy portfolio
concepts.def: The benchmark asset mix an institution adopts as its strategic allocation, against which total fund and staff decisions are measured. Brinson, Hood and Beebower (1986) studied its role in return variation.

concepts.name: Tactical asset allocation
concepts.def: Short to medium-term deviations from strategic weights to exploit perceived mispricing or regime shifts, governed by ranges around policy weights. Evidence for consistent skill is mixed.

concepts.name: Capital market assumptions
concepts.def: Long-horizon forecasts of return, volatility and correlation for asset classes, usually built from yields, valuations and growth building blocks, that feed strategic allocation.
concepts.aliases: cmas, cma forecasts, long-term return assumptions

concepts.name: Total portfolio approach
concepts.def: Managing a fund as one portfolio against a simple reference portfolio of liquid assets, judging each investment by its effect on total risk and return rather than filling fixed asset class buckets.

concepts.name: Funded status
concepts.def: The ratio of a pension plan's assets to the present value of its liabilities. Because liabilities are discounted at bond yields, falling rates can worsen funded status even when assets rise.
concepts.formula: funded status = plan assets / PV of liabilities

concepts.name: Glide path
concepts.def: The planned schedule by which a portfolio shifts from growth assets to safer assets as a target date approaches, the core design choice in target-date funds.
concepts.aliases: glidepath, to versus through glide path

concepts.name: Utility function
concepts.def: A mapping from wealth or returns to satisfaction that encodes risk preferences. Concave utility implies risk aversion, and the chosen form determines optimal portfolios.
concepts.formula: mean-variance: U = E(r) - 0.5 x A x sigma^2
concepts.aliases: investor utility, crra, quadratic utility, log utility

concepts.name: Risk aversion coefficient
concepts.def: The parameter that sets how much expected return an investor gives up per unit of variance. It fixes the point on the capital market line the investor chooses.
concepts.formula: optimal risky share = (E(r) - rf) / (A x sigma^2)
concepts.aliases: lambda, a, relative risk aversion, gamma

concepts.name: Certainty equivalent
concepts.def: The guaranteed return an investor would accept instead of a risky prospect. Comparing certainty equivalents ranks portfolios for a given risk aversion and is used to judge out-of-sample performance.
concepts.formula: CE approx E(r) - 0.5 x A x sigma^2

concepts.name: Mean-CVaR optimization
concepts.def: Optimizing expected return against expected shortfall instead of variance, which penalizes tail losses rather than all volatility. Rockafellar and Uryasev (2000) showed it reduces to a linear program on scenarios.
concepts.aliases: cvar optimization, mean-es optimization, rockafellar uryasev

concepts.name: Critical line algorithm
concepts.def: Markowitz's algorithm that traces the entire constrained efficient frontier exactly by solving a sequence of linear segments between corner portfolios.

concepts.name: Factor risk model
concepts.def: A model that explains asset returns by a small set of common factors plus asset-specific noise, giving a stable covariance matrix and decomposing risk into factor and specific parts.
concepts.formula: Sigma = B F B' + D
concepts.aliases: risk model, multi-factor risk model, equity risk model

concepts.name: Fundamental factor model
concepts.def: A factor risk model whose exposures are observable characteristics such as industry, size, value and momentum, with factor returns estimated each period by cross-sectional regression. Barra models are the classic example.
concepts.formula: r_i = sum of b_ik x f_k + e_i, with b known and f estimated
concepts.aliases: characteristic factor model, cross-sectional factor model

concepts.name: Barra model
