concepts.def: Bank sale of the credit risk on a slice of a loan portfolio to investors, typically via a synthetic securitization, to reduce regulatory capital.

concepts.name: Middle market
concepts.def: Companies too large for small business lending but too small for broadly syndicated loans and bonds; the main arena for direct lenders.

concepts.name: Club deal
concepts.def: Buyout or loan undertaken jointly by several sponsors or lenders to share a large check and its risk.

concepts.name: Hung deal
concepts.def: Underwritten loan or bond that banks cannot sell to investors at expected terms, leaving them holding the risk or selling at a loss.

concepts.name: Opco-propco split
concepts.def: Separating a company's real estate into a property company and its operations into an operating company, often to raise cash; rent obligations raise operating risk.

concepts.name: Recycling provision
concepts.def: LPA clause letting a GP reinvest early proceeds or amounts equal to fees, raising total invested capital above commitments.

concepts.name: ILPA principles
concepts.def: Institutional Limited Partners Association guidance on fund terms, governance and standardized fee and performance reporting.

concepts.name: Private company share market
concepts.def: Trading in shares of venture-backed companies via brokers, platforms or tender offers, subject to transfer restrictions and company rights of first refusal.

concepts.name: Qualified small business stock
concepts.def: US Section 1202 exclusion of capital gains on qualifying small company stock held for a minimum period, up to set limits; a major tax benefit for founders and early investors.

concepts.name: Drag-along and tag-along rights
concepts.def: Drag-along rights let majority holders force minorities to join a sale; tag-along rights let minorities join a sale on the same terms as the majority.

concepts.name: Blockchain
concepts.def: Append-only ledger of transaction blocks, each linked to the previous by a cryptographic hash and replicated across many nodes that agree on its state through a consensus mechanism.

concepts.name: Proof of work
concepts.def: Consensus mechanism in which miners compete to find a block hash below a target, making it very costly to rewrite history; Bitcoin uses it.

concepts.name: Proof of stake
concepts.def: Consensus mechanism in which validators lock tokens as collateral to propose and attest blocks, and lose part of that stake if they misbehave.

concepts.name: Hashrate
concepts.def: Total computing power securing a proof-of-work network, measured in hashes per second; a gauge of security and of miner investment.

concepts.name: Difficulty adjustment
concepts.def: Automatic retargeting of mining difficulty so blocks keep arriving near the target interval; Bitcoin adjusts every 2,016 blocks.

concepts.name: Hashprice
concepts.def: Expected miner revenue per unit of hashrate per day, combining coin price, block subsidy, fees and difficulty; the core bitcoin mining profitability metric.

concepts.name: Block subsidy and fees
concepts.def: Revenue for miners or validators from newly issued coins plus transaction fees; in Bitcoin the subsidy halves on schedule, so fees must eventually carry more of security spending.

concepts.name: UTXO model
concepts.def: Bitcoin's accounting model in which balances are sets of unspent transaction outputs that each transaction consumes and creates; it enables coin-age metrics.

concepts.name: Mempool
concepts.def: Pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions waiting to be included in a block; congestion there pushes fees up.

concepts.name: Gas
concepts.def: Unit measuring computational work on Ethereum; users pay gas used times a price made of a base fee plus an optional priority tip.
concepts.formula: fee = gas used x (base fee + priority fee)

concepts.name: EIP-1559
concepts.def: Ethereum fee mechanism adopted in 2021 that sets an algorithmic base fee per block, which is burned, plus an optional tip to the block producer.

concepts.name: The Merge
concepts.def: Ethereum's 2022 switch from proof of work to proof of stake, sharply cutting new ETH issuance and energy use.

concepts.name: Finality
concepts.def: Point after which a transaction cannot be reversed; probabilistic and growing with confirmations under proof of work, explicit after checkpoints in many proof-of-stake systems.

concepts.name: 51 percent attack
concepts.def: Control of a majority of hashrate or stake that lets an attacker reorder, censor or double-spend recent transactions; cheapest against small networks.

concepts.name: Smart contract
concepts.def: Program deployed on a blockchain that executes deterministically when called and can hold and move assets according to its code.

concepts.name: Ethereum Virtual Machine
concepts.def: Execution environment for Ethereum smart contracts, also adopted by many other chains so that contracts and tools carry over.

concepts.name: Layer 1
concepts.def: Base blockchain that provides its own consensus, data and security, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum or Solana.

concepts.name: Layer 2
concepts.def: Network that executes transactions off the main chain and posts data or proofs back to it, inheriting much of its security while cutting costs.

concepts.name: Optimistic rollup
concepts.def: Layer 2 that treats posted batches as valid unless challenged with a fraud proof during a dispute window, which delays native withdrawals.

concepts.name: ZK rollup
concepts.def: Layer 2 that posts a validity proof showing each batch of transactions is correct, allowing faster settlement on the base chain.

concepts.name: Data availability
concepts.def: Guarantee that the transaction data behind a block or rollup batch is published so anyone can verify state; a main cost driver for rollups.

concepts.name: Solana
concepts.def: High-throughput proof-of-stake layer 1 with a single global state, favored for trading and consumer applications; it has suffered several network outages.

concepts.name: Cross-chain bridge
concepts.def: Protocol that moves assets between blockchains by locking them on one chain and minting representations on another; bridges have been among the largest hack targets.

concepts.name: Wrapped token
concepts.def: Token representing another asset on a different chain, backed by custodied collateral, such as wrapped bitcoin on Ethereum; it adds custodian or bridge risk.

concepts.name: Oracle
concepts.def: Service that feeds off-chain data such as asset prices into smart contracts; manipulated or stale oracle prices are a major source of DeFi losses.

concepts.name: Automated market maker
concepts.def: Decentralized exchange design in which a liquidity pool quotes prices from a formula instead of an order book; the constant product rule is the classic form.
concepts.formula: constant product: x x y = k

concepts.name: Impermanent loss
concepts.def: Shortfall of an AMM liquidity provider's position versus simply holding the two assets, caused by price divergence; providers profit only if fees exceed it.
concepts.formula: constant product IL = 2 x sqrt(r) / (1 + r) - 1, where r = new price ratio / old price ratio

concepts.name: Concentrated liquidity
concepts.def: AMM design, introduced by Uniswap v3, in which providers supply liquidity only within chosen price ranges, raising capital efficiency and fee income but also impermanent loss.

concepts.name: Decentralized exchange
concepts.def: Exchange where trades settle on-chain through smart contracts without a custodian, using AMMs or on-chain order books.

concepts.name: DEX aggregator
concepts.def: Router that splits an order across decentralized venues and paths to get the best net execution after fees and price impact.

concepts.name: Maximal extractable value
concepts.def: Profit block producers and searchers capture by ordering, inserting or censoring transactions, such as arbitrage, liquidations and sandwich attacks.

concepts.name: Sandwich attack
concepts.def: MEV tactic that places a buy just before and a sell just after a victim's DEX trade to profit from the price impact the victim causes.

concepts.name: Proposer-builder separation
concepts.def: Ethereum arrangement in which specialized builders assemble blocks and bid for inclusion by validators, mostly through relays such as MEV-Boost.

concepts.name: Flash loan
concepts.def: Uncollateralized loan that is borrowed and repaid within one transaction or the whole transaction reverts; used for arbitrage and in oracle manipulation attacks.

concepts.name: DeFi lending protocol
concepts.def: Pool-based lending in which borrowers post overcollateralized crypto and rates adjust algorithmically with utilization; Aave and Compound are standard examples.

concepts.name: On-chain liquidation
concepts.def: Automatic sale of a borrower's collateral when its value falls below the required ratio, executed by keepers or bots for a liquidation bonus.
concepts.formula: health factor = collateral value x liquidation threshold / debt value

concepts.name: Liquidation cascade
concepts.def: Forced selling from liquidations pushes prices lower and triggers further liquidations; a recurring cause of sharp crypto crashes.

concepts.name: Yield farming
concepts.def: Moving capital across protocols to earn fees and token incentives; headline yields often come from emissions that dilute token holders.

concepts.name: Real yield in DeFi
concepts.def: Protocol yield paid from actual fee revenue rather than newly emitted tokens, which makes it more sustainable than incentive-driven yield.

concepts.name: Token emissions
concepts.def: Scheduled issuance of new tokens to users, stakers or teams; emissions dilute holders and can make reported yields illusory.

concepts.name: Total value locked
concepts.def: Value of assets deposited in a protocol or chain; a rough usage gauge inflated by double counting of reused collateral and by token price moves.

concepts.name: Governance token
concepts.def: Token giving voting rights over protocol parameters and treasury, sometimes with a claim on fees; low turnout and whale concentration often weaken governance.

concepts.name: Decentralized autonomous organization
concepts.def: Entity governed by token holder votes executed through smart contracts, often controlling a protocol treasury.

concepts.name: Protocol revenue
concepts.def: Fees a protocol keeps for itself or its token holders after paying liquidity providers or validators; the base for fundamental crypto valuation.

concepts.name: Token valuation multiples
concepts.def: Crypto analogs of equity multiples, such as market cap or fully diluted value divided by annualized fees or protocol revenue.
concepts.formula: price to fees = market cap / annualized fees

concepts.name: Fully diluted valuation
concepts.def: Token price times the maximum or eventual total supply; a large gap between FDV and circulating market cap signals future dilution from unlocks.
concepts.formula: FDV = price x total eventual supply

concepts.name: Circulating supply
concepts.def: Tokens currently tradable in the market, excluding locked, vested and treasury holdings; market cap uses this supply.

concepts.name: Token unlock
concepts.def: Scheduled release of vested tokens to insiders and early investors, which adds sellable supply and often pressures price.

concepts.name: Tokenomics
concepts.def: Design of a token's supply, issuance, distribution, utility and value accrual, which determines who gets value and when.

concepts.name: Staking yield
concepts.def: Return to stakers from new issuance plus fees and MEV; the issuance part is largely a transfer from non-stakers through dilution rather than new income.

concepts.name: Liquid staking
concepts.def: Staking through a protocol that issues a tradable receipt token representing staked assets plus rewards, such as Lido's stETH.

concepts.name: Restaking
concepts.def: Reusing staked ETH to secure additional services in exchange for extra yield and extra slashing risk; EigenLayer popularized the model.

concepts.name: Slashing
concepts.def: Penalty that destroys part of a validator's stake for provable misbehavior such as double signing; the enforcement tool of proof of stake.

concepts.name: Airdrop
concepts.def: Free distribution of tokens to users or holders, used to reward early activity and spread ownership; recipients often sell quickly.

concepts.name: Initial coin offering
concepts.def: Public sale of newly created tokens to fund a project; the 2017 boom led US regulators to treat many such sales as unregistered securities offerings.

concepts.name: Howey test
concepts.def: US Supreme Court (1946) test for an investment contract: an investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits from others' efforts; central to whether tokens are securities.

concepts.name: Crypto regulation
concepts.def: Rules governing token issuance, trading venues, custody and stablecoins; the split of authority between securities and commodities regulators shapes market structure.

concepts.name: Memecoin
concepts.def: Token without cash flow claims whose value rests on attention and community; marked by extreme volatility and heavy insider concentration at launch.

concepts.name: Altcoin
concepts.def: Any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin; altcoins usually have higher beta to crypto market moves and higher failure rates.

concepts.name: Bitcoin dominance
concepts.def: Bitcoin's share of total crypto market capitalization; it tends to rise in risk-off phases and fall during speculative altcoin rallies.
concepts.formula: dominance = bitcoin market cap / total crypto market cap

concepts.name: Four-year crypto cycle
concepts.def: Pattern of bitcoin bull and bear phases loosely aligned with halvings; it rests on very few cycles and may reflect global liquidity as much as supply.

concepts.name: Fiat-backed stablecoin
concepts.def: Stablecoin backed by cash and short-term government securities held by an issuer and redeemable at par, such as USDT and USDC.

concepts.name: Crypto-collateralized stablecoin
concepts.def: Stablecoin minted against overcollateralized crypto deposits with automatic liquidations, such as DAI.

concepts.name: Algorithmic stablecoin
concepts.def: Stablecoin that relies on minting and burning a companion token rather than full reserves to hold its peg; prone to death spirals once confidence breaks.

concepts.name: Terra-Luna collapse
concepts.def: May 2022 depeg of the algorithmic stablecoin UST and hyperinflation of its sister token LUNA, erasing tens of billions of dollars of value within days.

concepts.name: Depeg
concepts.def: A stablecoin or pegged token trading away from its target value due to reserve doubts, redemption frictions or collateral failure; USDC briefly depegged in March 2023 when SVB failed.

concepts.name: Stablecoin reserve composition
concepts.def: Mix of cash, Treasury bills, repo and other assets backing a stablecoin; reserve quality, custody and attestation determine run risk.

concepts.name: Stablecoin issuer economics
concepts.def: Issuers earn interest on reserves while holders usually receive no yield, so issuer profits depend heavily on short-term rates and outstanding supply.

concepts.name: Stablecoin supply growth
concepts.def: Change in outstanding stablecoins, watched as a gauge of dollar liquidity available to crypto markets.

concepts.name: GENIUS Act
concepts.def: US federal law enacted in 2025 creating a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, including licensing, reserve and redemption requirements.

concepts.name: MiCA
concepts.def: The EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, a comprehensive framework for crypto issuers, service providers and stablecoins across member states.

concepts.name: Tokenized Treasuries
concepts.def: On-chain tokens representing shares in funds holding US Treasury bills, used as yield-bearing cash and collateral in crypto markets.

concepts.name: Real-world assets on-chain
concepts.def: Off-chain assets such as bonds, private credit, funds or real estate represented by tokens on a blockchain, relying on legal wrappers and custodians.

concepts.name: Central bank digital currency
concepts.def: Digital money issued directly by a central bank, for retail or wholesale use, distinct from privately issued stablecoins.

concepts.name: Crypto custody
concepts.def: Safekeeping of private keys on behalf of clients by custodians using cold storage, multi-party computation and asset segregation.

concepts.name: Private key
concepts.def: Secret number that authorizes spending from a crypto address; whoever controls it controls the funds, and lost keys mean lost assets.

concepts.name: Self-custody
concepts.def: Holding one's own private keys in a hardware or software wallet, removing intermediary risk but taking on loss, theft and inheritance risk.

concepts.name: Hot and cold wallets
concepts.def: Hot wallets keep keys online for operational liquidity; cold wallets keep keys offline for most holdings, trading convenience for security.

concepts.name: Multisig and MPC
concepts.def: Key security schemes requiring several parties to approve a transaction, either through multiple on-chain signatures or through split-key cryptography off-chain.

concepts.name: Proof of reserves
concepts.def: Exchange disclosure showing assets held on-chain, ideally paired with a Merkle-tree proof of liabilities; without liabilities it does not prove solvency.

concepts.name: FTX collapse
concepts.def: November 2022 failure of crypto exchange FTX after it emerged that customer funds had been used by affiliated trading firm Alameda Research; a lesson in custody and commingling risk.

concepts.name: Mt. Gox collapse
concepts.def: Early dominant bitcoin exchange that failed in 2014 after losing a very large amount of customer bitcoin; the first major custodial failure in crypto.

concepts.name: Centralized crypto exchange
concepts.def: Venue combining brokerage, matching, custody, clearing and often lending in one entity, unlike traditional markets where these roles are separated.

concepts.name: Perpetual futures
concepts.def: Futures contract with no expiry that stays near spot through periodic funding payments between longs and shorts; the dominant crypto derivative.

concepts.name: Funding rate
concepts.def: Periodic payment between perpetual futures longs and shorts based on the perp's premium or discount to spot; persistently high positive funding signals crowded leveraged longs.

concepts.name: Crypto cash-and-carry
concepts.def: Buying spot crypto and shorting dated futures or perpetuals to earn the basis or funding; a carry trade exposed to exchange, margin and liquidation risk.

concepts.name: Estimated leverage ratio
concepts.def: Exchange futures open interest divided by the exchange's coin reserves; a rough gauge of leverage building in crypto derivatives.
concepts.formula: ELR = open interest / exchange reserves

concepts.name: Auto-deleveraging
concepts.def: Exchange mechanism that forcibly closes profitable opposing positions when liquidation losses exceed the exchange's insurance fund.

concepts.name: CME crypto futures
concepts.def: Cash-settled, regulated bitcoin and ether futures on CME, used by institutions for hedging and as the short leg of ETF basis trades.

concepts.name: Crypto liquidity fragmentation
concepts.def: Crypto liquidity is split across many exchanges and chains with different fees, collateral and access, creating price gaps that arbitrageurs close imperfectly.

concepts.name: Kimchi premium
concepts.def: Premium of crypto prices on South Korean exchanges over global prices, sustained at times by capital controls; a textbook case of limits to arbitrage.

concepts.name: On-chain analytics
concepts.def: Analysis of public blockchain data, such as holder behavior, flows, fees and cost bases, to infer supply, demand and positioning.

concepts.name: Realized capitalization
concepts.def: Sum of every coin valued at the price when it last moved on-chain; approximates the aggregate cost basis of holders.
concepts.formula: realized cap = sum over coins of price at last movement

concepts.name: MVRV ratio
concepts.def: Market value divided by realized value; high readings mean holders sit on large unrealized gains, low readings suggest capitulation.
concepts.formula: MVRV = market cap / realized cap

concepts.name: Spent output profit ratio
concepts.def: Value of coins when spent divided by their value when last moved; readings above 1 mean coins are being sold at a profit on average.
concepts.formula: SOPR = value at spend / value at creation

concepts.name: NVT ratio
concepts.def: Network value divided by daily on-chain transaction volume; a crypto analog of a price-to-sales ratio.
concepts.formula: NVT = market cap / daily transaction volume

concepts.name: Exchange inflows and outflows
concepts.def: Net movement of coins onto exchanges, read as potential selling, or off them, read as holding; noisy because of internal wallet reshuffles.

concepts.name: Long-term and short-term holders
concepts.def: Coin holders split by how long coins have sat unmoved, commonly about 155 days; long-term holders tend to distribute into bull markets.

concepts.name: Active addresses
concepts.def: Unique addresses transacting in a period; a rough usage proxy distorted by address reuse, exchanges and bots.

concepts.name: HODL waves
concepts.def: Distribution of coin supply by age since last movement, showing how holder behavior shifts across cycles.

concepts.name: Coin days destroyed
concepts.def: Coins moved multiplied by days since they last moved; spikes reveal long-dormant coins being spent.
concepts.formula: CDD = sum of coins moved x days since last moved

concepts.name: Crypto-equity correlation
concepts.def: Co-movement of bitcoin with technology stocks and liquidity conditions, which rose as institutions entered; it undercuts the hedge narrative in risk-off periods.

concepts.name: Crypto treasury company
concepts.def: Listed company that raises equity and debt to hold crypto on its balance sheet, with Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) the main example; shares trade at a premium or discount to holdings.
concepts.formula: mNAV = enterprise value / value of crypto held

concepts.name: Security budget
concepts.def: Total miner or validator revenue that pays for network security; the debate over whether fees can replace shrinking bitcoin subsidies.

concepts.name: Lightning Network
concepts.def: Layer 2 network of bitcoin payment channels that enables fast, cheap payments off-chain, settling net balances on-chain.

concepts.name: Non-fungible token
concepts.def: Unique on-chain token representing ownership of a specific digital item; NFT markets are thin, illiquid and highly speculative.

concepts.name: ERC-20
concepts.def: Ethereum standard interface for fungible tokens, which lets any wallet or protocol handle any compliant token.

concepts.name: Hard fork
concepts.def: Protocol change that is not backward compatible, splitting the chain when some nodes refuse to upgrade, as with Bitcoin Cash in 2017.

concepts.name: Travel rule
concepts.def: Anti-money-laundering requirement, extended to crypto by the FATF, that service providers pass originator and beneficiary information with transfers.

concepts.name: Fiat on-ramp
concepts.def: Service converting bank money into crypto and back (the off-ramp); usually the main regulatory and banking chokepoint for the sector.

concepts.name: Smart contract risk
concepts.def: Risk of loss from code bugs, economic exploits or abuse of upgrade keys in a protocol; audits reduce it but do not eliminate it.

concepts.name: Admin keys and upgradeability
concepts.def: Privileged keys letting a team upgrade, pause or change contracts, adding centralization and governance risk to nominally decentralized protocols.

concepts.name: Rug pull
concepts.def: Scam in which developers drain pool liquidity or dump their tokens after attracting investors.

concepts.name: Centralized crypto lenders
concepts.def: Firms that took crypto deposits promising yield and lent them on, often to leveraged traders; Celsius and BlockFi failed in 2022.

concepts.name: 21 million supply cap
concepts.def: Bitcoin's fixed maximum supply of 21 million coins, approached gradually as the block subsidy halves.

concepts.name: Stock-to-flow model
concepts.def: Model valuing bitcoin by the ratio of existing supply to annual new issuance; criticized as spurious because issuance is preset and the fit rests on a short sample.
concepts.formula: S2F = existing stock / annual new supply

concepts.name: Metcalfe's law
concepts.def: Claim that a network's value scales with the square of its users, applied loosely to value crypto networks from active addresses.
concepts.formula: value proportional to n^2

concepts.name: Token burn
concepts.def: Permanent removal of tokens from supply, through fee burns or buy-and-burn programs; the crypto analog of share buybacks.

concepts.name: Perpetual futures DEX
concepts.def: Decentralized exchange for perpetual futures using on-chain or hybrid order books or pooled liquidity, letting traders keep custody of collateral.

concepts.name: Prediction market
concepts.def: Market trading contracts that pay on event outcomes, so prices can be read as crowd probabilities; examples include Polymarket and Kalshi.

concepts.name: Naphtha
concepts.def: Light refinery and condensate stream used as petrochemical cracker feedstock and gasoline blendstock; it competes with ethane and LPG as feed, so its crack tracks chemical demand.

concepts.name: Futures ETF roll decay
concepts.def: Losses suffered by funds that hold near-month futures and roll them in contango, so the fund lags the spot price over time; oil ETFs in 2020 were a stark case.

concepts.name: 2021 Texas freeze
concepts.def: February 2021 winter storm that froze gas wells and knocked out generation across ERCOT, holding power prices at the price cap for days and bankrupting several retailers and a cooperative.

concepts.name: 2022 European gas crisis
concepts.def: Collapse of Russian pipeline gas deliveries to Europe in 2022 that drove TTF to record highs, forced industrial demand destruction and set off a scramble for LNG import capacity.

concepts.name: Critical minerals
concepts.def: Minerals deemed essential to economic and national security with concentrated supply, such as lithium, cobalt, rare earths and graphite; governments respond with stockpiles, subsidies and trade controls.

concepts.name: Soybean-corn price ratio
concepts.def: New-crop soybean futures price divided by new-crop corn price; it guides farmers' planting mix, with high ratios favoring more soybean acres.
concepts.formula: ratio = November soybeans / December corn

concepts.name: LME cash-to-three-months spread
concepts.def: Price difference between LME cash metal and the three-month contract; backwardation in this spread signals scarce nearby metal.

concepts.name: Jones Act
concepts.def: US law requiring cargo moved between US ports to travel on US-built, US-owned and US-crewed ships, which raises domestic shipping costs and shapes regional fuel prices.

concepts.name: LNG carrier charter rates
concepts.def: Daily hire rates for LNG tankers, which spike when long-haul arbitrage or floating storage ties up the fleet and fall when new ships flood the market.

concepts.name: Contract for difference (power)
concepts.def: Two-way contract paying a generator the difference between a strike price and the market price, and collecting it back when prices exceed the strike; used in renewable auctions such as the UK's.
concepts.formula: payment = (strike - reference price) x MWh generated

concepts.name: Strip sale
concepts.def: Secondary sale of an equal percentage slice of every asset in a fund portfolio, so buyers cannot cherry-pick and the seller keeps proportional exposure.

concepts.name: Venture markup
concepts.def: Increase in a portfolio company's carrying value after a higher-priced financing round; markups from insider-led or structured rounds are weaker evidence of value.

concepts.name: Pay-to-play provision
concepts.def: Financing term requiring existing investors to buy their pro rata share of a new round or lose preferred rights, often by conversion to common stock.

concepts.name: Gross lease
concepts.def: Lease in which the tenant pays a single rent and the landlord covers property taxes, insurance and operating costs, leaving the landlord exposed to expense inflation.

concepts.name: Adaptive reuse
concepts.def: Converting obsolete buildings, most often offices, to other uses such as housing; feasibility depends on floorplate depth, plumbing, windows and the purchase basis.

concepts.name: Below-replacement-cost buying
concepts.def: Buying property for less than it would cost to build today, which offers a margin of safety because new competing supply is uneconomic until rents rise.

concepts.name: Construction loan
concepts.def: Short-term floating-rate loan funding development in draws against completed work, repaid by permanent financing or sale once the property stabilizes.

concepts.name: Commercial real estate bridge loan
concepts.def: Short-term floating-rate loan on a transitional property being leased up or repositioned, refinanced into permanent debt once cash flow stabilizes.

concepts.name: Data center leasing economics
concepts.def: Data centers lease space by megawatts of critical IT load, often to hyperscalers on long pre-signed leases; access to power and grid connections is the binding constraint on supply.

concepts.name: Miner capitulation
concepts.def: Bitcoin miners selling reserves and switching off rigs when hashprice falls below operating costs, often after a halving; hashrate dips and difficulty then adjusts down.

concepts.name: ETH net issuance
concepts.def: Change in ether supply equal to new staking issuance minus base fees burned; it turns negative when network usage is heavy enough.
concepts.formula: net issuance = issuance to validators - fees burned

concepts.name: Crypto options
concepts.def: Options on bitcoin and ether traded mainly on Deribit, with CME and spot ETF options growing; implied volatility indices such as DVOL track their pricing.

concepts.name: Strategic bitcoin reserve
concepts.def: Government holding of bitcoin as a reserve asset; the US established one in 2025 from forfeited coins, and the idea fuels debate about official sector demand.

concepts.name: Tokenized deposits
concepts.def: Commercial bank deposits represented on a blockchain; unlike stablecoins they remain bank liabilities within deposit regulation.

concepts.name: Behavioral finance
concepts.def: Field explaining asset prices and investor choices through psychology and market frictions. Its two pillars are systematic cognitive biases and limits to arbitrage that let mispricing persist. Key figures include Kahneman, Tversky, Thaler, Shiller and Shleifer.

concepts.name: Heuristics and biases
concepts.def: Kahneman and Tversky's research program showing that judgment under uncertainty relies on mental shortcuts such as representativeness, availability and anchoring, which are often useful but produce predictable, systematic errors.

concepts.name: Dual process theory
concepts.def: Model of two modes of thought: System 1 is fast, intuitive and automatic; System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful. Most biases arise when System 1 answers and System 2 fails to check. Popularized by Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
concepts.aliases: system 1 system 2,thinking fast and slow,fast and slow thinking

concepts.name: Availability heuristic
concepts.def: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, recent or heavily reported events such as crashes, frauds and big winners are overweighted relative to their true frequency. Tversky and Kahneman (1973).

concepts.name: Representativeness heuristic
concepts.def: Judging likelihood by resemblance to a stereotype instead of by base rates, for example assuming a company with a great story or fast recent growth must be a great investment. Drives base-rate neglect and the law of small numbers.

concepts.name: Affect heuristic
concepts.def: Letting feelings about an asset drive judgments of both its risk and its return, so liked assets are seen as safer and higher returning at once, contrary to the usual risk-return tradeoff. Studied by Slovic and coauthors.

concepts.name: Attribute substitution
concepts.def: Unknowingly answering an easier question in place of a hard one, such as replacing 'is this stock undervalued' with 'do I like this company'. Kahneman and Frederick's account of how heuristics work.

concepts.name: Status quo bias
concepts.def: Preference for the current state of affairs, so investors keep existing holdings, allocations and default options even when switching would be better. Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988).

concepts.name: Endowment effect
concepts.def: Valuing something more once you own it: owners demand more to sell than they would pay to buy the same item. Thaler (1980); linked to loss aversion. Makes investors reluctant to sell inherited or long-held positions.

concepts.name: Regret aversion
concepts.def: Avoiding choices that could later cause regret, for example holding losers to avoid confirming a mistake or following the crowd so a loss is shared. Regret from action usually stings more than regret from inaction.

concepts.name: Ambiguity aversion
concepts.def: Preferring known risks over unknown probabilities, as shown in the Ellsberg paradox. Investors pay up for familiar assets and avoid ones whose odds feel unknowable, even at similar expected outcomes.

concepts.name: Competence hypothesis
concepts.def: Heath and Tversky (1991): people prefer to bet on uncertain events in areas where they feel knowledgeable, even over equally likely known chances. Feeling competent, not actual odds, drives willingness to take the bet.

concepts.name: Familiarity bias
concepts.def: Favoring investments one knows, such as employer stock, local firms or famous brands, and mistaking familiarity for lower risk. A main driver of home bias and concentrated employee holdings.

concepts.name: Narrow framing
concepts.def: Evaluating each risk in isolation instead of as part of total wealth, so a small positive expected value bet is rejected because its standalone loss looks painful. Kahneman and Lovallo; Barberis, Huang and Thaler.

concepts.name: Myopic loss aversion
concepts.def: Loss aversion combined with frequent evaluation: checking a portfolio often makes losses more visible and pushes investors toward overly safe allocations. Benartzi and Thaler (1995) used it to explain the equity premium puzzle.

concepts.name: House money effect
concepts.def: Taking more risk after gains because profits feel like someone else's money. Thaler and Johnson (1990). Can feed escalating speculation late in rallies.

concepts.name: Break-even effect
concepts.def: After losses, taking extra risk for a chance to get back to even. Thaler and Johnson (1990). Behind doubling down, revenge trading and loss chasing.

concepts.name: Reference point
concepts.def: The benchmark against which outcomes are coded as gains or losses, often purchase price, a recent high or expectations. Moving the reference point changes risk taking even when wealth is unchanged.

concepts.name: Prospect theory value function
concepts.def: Value function over gains and losses relative to a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses. Tversky and Kahneman (1992) estimated curvature about 0.88 and a loss aversion coefficient about 2.25.
concepts.formula: v(x) = x^0.88 for gains; v(x) = -2.25 * (-x)^0.88 for losses
concepts.aliases: value function,s-shaped value function,loss aversion lambda

concepts.name: Cumulative prospect theory
concepts.def: Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 version of prospect theory that applies probability weights to cumulative distributions of outcomes, respecting stochastic dominance and handling many outcomes.

concepts.name: Probability weighting
concepts.def: In prospect theory people overweight small probabilities and underweight moderate to large ones, which explains demand for both lottery tickets and insurance.

concepts.name: Certainty effect
concepts.def: Overweighting outcomes that are certain relative to ones that are merely probable, so a sure gain is valued well above a slightly risky larger gain. Central to the Allais paradox.

concepts.name: Reflection effect
concepts.def: Risk attitudes flip with the sign of outcomes: people are risk averse over gains and risk seeking over losses. A core prospect theory finding behind the disposition effect.

concepts.name: Isolation effect
concepts.def: Ignoring components shared by all options and focusing on differences, so the same choice presented in stages can produce a different decision. Kahneman and Tversky (1979).

concepts.name: Realization utility
concepts.def: Investors get utility from realizing gains and losses on individual positions, not only from total wealth, which helps explain the disposition effect and heavy trading. Barberis and Xiong.

concepts.name: Regret theory
concepts.def: Loomes and Sugden (1982) and Bell (1982): choices account for anticipated regret from comparing the outcome received with what the rejected option would have paid.

concepts.name: Overreaction
concepts.def: Prices moving too far on news or past performance, then reversing. De Bondt and Thaler (1985) found long-term past losers outperformed past winners over the following years.

concepts.name: Underreaction
concepts.def: Prices adjusting too slowly to news, producing drift in the direction of the surprise. A leading explanation for medium-term momentum and post-earnings drift.

concepts.name: Conservatism bias
concepts.def: Updating beliefs too little when new evidence arrives, staying anchored on prior views. Edwards (1968). Contributes to underreaction to earnings news.

concepts.name: Self-attribution bias
concepts.def: Crediting successes to skill and blaming failures on bad luck, which inflates confidence after wins and blocks learning after losses.

concepts.name: Better-than-average effect
concepts.def: Most people rate their own skill above average, in driving, investing and much else, which cannot be true for most of them.

concepts.name: Overprecision
concepts.def: Excessive certainty in one's estimates, shown by confidence intervals far too narrow to contain the truth as often as claimed. The most robust form of overconfidence in forecasting.

concepts.name: Overplacement
concepts.def: Believing you rank higher relative to others than you do, for example that you will beat the market after costs when most participants cannot.

concepts.name: Dunning-Kruger effect
concepts.def: Kruger and Dunning (1999): low-skill people tend to overestimate their competence because they lack the skill to see their own errors. The size of the effect is debated.

concepts.name: Illusion of validity
concepts.def: Confidence that comes from a coherent story rather than from evidence of predictive accuracy. Kahneman found stock pickers and interviewers stayed confident despite records no better than chance.

concepts.name: What you see is all there is
concepts.def: Kahneman's term for building a confident judgment from only the information at hand, without asking what is missing. Leads to neglect of unknowns and of the other side's case.

concepts.name: Optimism bias
concepts.def: Overestimating the chance of good outcomes for oneself or one's project. Shows up in analyst forecasts, management guidance and startup projections.

concepts.name: Hot hand fallacy
concepts.def: Believing a streak of success makes the next success more likely, such as chasing a fund after a few great years. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky (1985); later work found a modest real hot hand in sports, but investors still overweight streaks.

concepts.name: Law of small numbers
concepts.def: Expecting small samples to mirror the population, so a few years of returns or a handful of trades are taken as proof of skill. Tversky and Kahneman (1971).

concepts.name: Clustering illusion
concepts.def: Seeing meaningful streaks or clusters in random data, such as runs of up days, that are expected by chance alone.

concepts.name: Apophenia
concepts.def: General tendency to perceive meaningful patterns and connections in unrelated data; in markets, finding chart shapes or causal stories in noise.

concepts.name: Illusory correlation
concepts.def: Perceiving a relationship between variables that does not exist or is weaker than believed, often because a few memorable co-occurrences stand out.

concepts.name: Salience bias
concepts.def: Overweighting information that is prominent or striking, such as a headline price move, over information that matters more but is dull, such as a footnote change.

concepts.name: Rational inattention
concepts.def: Sims's framework in which agents with finite processing capacity optimally choose what to attend to, explaining sluggish and selective reactions to information.

concepts.name: Attention-driven buying
concepts.def: Retail investors are net buyers of attention-grabbing stocks after news, extreme moves or high volume, because buying means searching thousands of names while selling only covers what they own. Barber and Odean (2008).

concepts.name: Friday announcement effect
concepts.def: Earnings released on Fridays get a weaker immediate price response and more later drift than other days, consistent with investor inattention. DellaVigna and Pollet (2009).

concepts.name: Stale news effect
concepts.def: Prices reacting to information already public, as when a years-old United Airlines bankruptcy story resurfaced online in September 2008 and the stock briefly collapsed. Tetlock (2011) found stale news predicts reversals.

concepts.name: Ticker confusion
concepts.def: Investors trading the wrong security because of similar names or tickers, such as buying an obscure firm instead of a famous one in the news. Rashes (2001) documented comovement from such confusion.

concepts.name: Information overload
concepts.def: More information beyond a point raises confidence without raising accuracy, and pushes analysts to fixate on noise.

concepts.name: Choice overload
concepts.def: Larger menus can reduce decision quality and participation; retirement plans offering many funds see lower enrollment and more naive allocation rules. Iyengar and coauthors.

concepts.name: Default effect
concepts.def: People disproportionately stay with preset options; automatic enrollment raises retirement plan participation sharply. Madrian and Shea (2001).

concepts.name: Nudge
concepts.def: Changing how choices are presented to steer behavior without restricting options or changing incentives much, such as automatic savings escalation. Thaler and Sunstein (2008).

concepts.name: Save More Tomorrow
concepts.def: Thaler and Benartzi's program in which employees commit in advance to raise their savings rate out of future pay raises, turning inertia and present bias into allies.

concepts.name: Cognitive dissonance
concepts.def: Discomfort from holding beliefs that conflict with evidence or actions, often resolved by dismissing the evidence instead of updating. Festinger (1957).

concepts.name: Belief perseverance
concepts.def: Holding a belief after the evidence behind it has been discredited. Keeps investors in broken theses long after the original reason is gone.

concepts.name: Motivated reasoning
concepts.def: Reasoning toward the conclusion one wants, applying harsh scrutiny to unwelcome evidence and little to welcome evidence. Talking one's own book is a market version.

concepts.name: Escalation of commitment
concepts.def: Continuing to invest in a failing course of action because of what has already been invested, often adding capital to defend an earlier decision. Staw (1976).
concepts.aliases: commitment escalation,throwing good money after bad

concepts.name: Ostrich effect
concepts.def: Avoiding information that may be bad; investors log in to check portfolios less often when markets fall. Karlsson, Loewenstein and Seppi (2009).

concepts.name: Naive diversification
concepts.def: Splitting money equally across whatever options are offered, so allocations depend on the menu rather than on risk. Benartzi and Thaler (2001). DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found 1/N hard to beat out of sample.
concepts.formula: w_i = 1/N

concepts.name: Money illusion
concepts.def: Thinking in nominal instead of real terms, such as comparing earnings yields with nominal bond yields or feeling richer from inflationary gains. Modigliani and Cohn (1979) argued it misprices stocks under inflation.

concepts.name: Nominal price illusion
concepts.def: Treating low-priced shares as cheaper or having more upside than high-priced ones, although price per share is arbitrary and changes with splits.
concepts.aliases: unit bias,low price bias,cheap stock illusion

concepts.name: 52-week high anchoring
concepts.def: Investors anchor on a stock's 52-week high and are reluctant to bid above it, so stocks near their highs keep drifting up as news is absorbed. George and Hwang (2004).

concepts.name: Dividend puzzle
concepts.def: Why investors prize cash dividends when, without taxes and costs, selling shares produces equivalent cash (Miller and Modigliani). Behavioral answers include self-control and mental accounting rules to spend income but not capital. Black (1976).

concepts.name: Self-control bias
concepts.def: Failing to act on long-term goals because of short-term temptation, leading to undersaving and to rules such as spending only dividends.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic discounting
concepts.def: Discounting the near future much more steeply than the distant future, so preferences reverse as a reward draws closer, producing time-inconsistent choices.
concepts.formula: V = A / (1 + kD)

concepts.name: Present bias
concepts.def: Overweighting immediate payoffs relative to all later ones, as in Laibson's (1997) beta-delta model; causes procrastination on saving, rebalancing and hard decisions.
concepts.formula: U = u0 + beta x sum(delta^t x ut)

concepts.name: Short-termism
concepts.def: Overweighting near-term results such as quarterly earnings or monthly performance at the expense of long-term value, encouraged by career incentives and frequent evaluation.

concepts.name: Negativity bias
concepts.def: Bad news and losses weigh more heavily in attention and memory than equivalent good news, so fear tends to spread faster than optimism.

concepts.name: Action bias
concepts.def: Preferring to do something over doing nothing even when inaction has better expected value, such as trading in response to every headline. Goalkeepers diving on penalties are the classic example.

concepts.name: Omission bias
concepts.def: Judging harmful actions as worse than equally harmful inactions, so losses from holding feel more acceptable than losses from trading.

concepts.name: Probability neglect
concepts.def: When outcomes are emotionally vivid, people react to whether something could happen rather than how likely it is. Sunstein's term; drives overpayment for protection against salient tail events.

concepts.name: Denominator neglect
concepts.def: Focusing on the count of bad outcomes and ignoring the size of the base, so 10 failures out of 1,000 can feel riskier than 1 out of 10.

concepts.name: Zero-risk bias
concepts.def: Preferring to eliminate a small risk completely over a larger reduction of a bigger risk, even when the latter cuts more expected loss.

concepts.name: Experience effects
concepts.def: Personal experience of returns shapes lifelong risk taking: Malmendier and Nagel (2011) found people who lived through poor stock returns hold fewer stocks decades later.

concepts.name: Relative wealth concerns
concepts.def: Caring about wealth compared with peers, not only about absolute wealth, which pushes investors to chase whatever their neighbors and colleagues own. Keeping up with the Joneses.

concepts.name: Mood effects
concepts.def: Market returns that track investor mood rather than news, such as weaker returns after national sports losses and stronger ones on sunny days. Hirshleifer and Shumway (2003); Edmans, Garcia and Norli (2007).

concepts.name: Information cascade
concepts.def: People rationally ignore their own information and copy predecessors, so early choices can lock in a herd even when wrong. Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992). Cascades are fragile and can reverse sharply on small news.

concepts.name: Groupthink
concepts.def: Cohesive groups suppressing dissent to reach consensus, producing overconfident decisions. Janis (1972). Investment committees counter it by collecting written views before discussion.

concepts.name: Authority bias
concepts.def: Overweighting the views of perceived authorities, such as famous investors or officials, regardless of the evidence offered.

concepts.name: Social proof
concepts.def: Using others' behavior as evidence of the correct action; in markets, crowded ownership and rising prices become reasons to buy in themselves. One of Cialdini's influence principles.

concepts.name: Madness of crowds
concepts.def: Idea, from Mackay's Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841), that people go mad in herds and recover slowly one by one; the book recounts tulip mania and the 1720 bubbles.

concepts.name: Wisdom of crowds
concepts.def: Averages of many independent estimates often beat individual experts, provided judgments are diverse, independent and decentralized. Fails when herding destroys independence. Galton's ox weight contest; Surowiecki (2004).

concepts.name: Contrarian investing
concepts.def: Deliberately positioning against prevailing sentiment, buying what is unloved and selling what is popular when the crowd's view looks fully priced. Works only when the contrarian is also right on fundamentals.

concepts.name: Panic selling
concepts.def: Selling driven by fear rather than analysis, usually after sharp declines, which locks in losses at depressed prices and widens the gap between fund and investor returns.

concepts.name: Euphoria
concepts.def: Late bubble stage in which investors believe prices can only rise, risk feels absent and skeptics are mocked as not getting it.

concepts.name: Wall of worry
concepts.def: Market saying that bull markets climb despite persistent doubts; skepticism keeps positioning light, leaving sidelined buyers to push prices higher.

concepts.name: Irrational exuberance
concepts.def: Unjustified enthusiasm that lifts prices above fundamentals. Greenspan used the phrase in a December 1996 speech, and Shiller used it as the title of his 2000 book on stock market valuation.

concepts.name: Animal spirits
concepts.def: Keynes's term in the General Theory (1936) for spontaneous optimism that drives investment more than calculated expected values; swings in animal spirits help explain booms and slumps.

concepts.name: Narrative economics
concepts.def: Shiller's (2019) idea that popular stories spread like epidemics and drive spending, investing and market events, somewhat independently of fundamentals.

concepts.name: Hype cycle
concepts.def: Gartner's model of how expectations for a new technology evolve: trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, plateau of productivity. A frame for story-driven tech stocks.

concepts.name: This time is different
concepts.def: Belief that old valuation and leverage limits no longer apply because of a new era. Reinhart and Rogoff (2009) documented the pattern across centuries of crises; Templeton called it among the most dangerous phrases in investing.

concepts.name: Bubble stages
concepts.def: Minsky-Kindleberger sequence for manias: displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion. Set out in Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes (1978).
concepts.aliases: kindleberger stages,displacement boom euphoria distress revulsion

concepts.name: Financial instability hypothesis
concepts.def: Minsky's theory that stability breeds instability: calm periods encourage a shift from hedge to speculative to Ponzi finance until a shock forces deleveraging.

concepts.name: Ponzi finance
concepts.def: Minsky's term for borrowers whose cash flows cover neither interest nor principal, so they rely on rising asset prices or new borrowing. Hedge finance covers both; speculative finance covers interest only.

concepts.name: Greater fool theory
concepts.def: Buying an asset not for its cash flows but because someone should pay more later. Works until buyers run out.

concepts.name: Rational bubble
concepts.def: A price above fundamental value that rational investors still hold because the bubble component is expected to grow at the required return. Blanchard and Watson (1982). Requires an infinite horizon, ruling it out for finite-lived assets.

concepts.name: Riding the bubble
concepts.def: Knowingly buying overpriced assets expecting to sell before the collapse. Brunnermeier and Nagel (2004) found hedge funds were overweight tech stocks in 1999 and 2000 and cut exposure before the peak.

concepts.name: Synchronization risk
concepts.def: Arbitrageurs may know a bubble exists but not when others will act, so each rides it instead of attacking alone, and the bubble persists. Abreu and Brunnermeier (2003).

concepts.name: Noise trader risk
concepts.def: Risk that irrational traders push a mispricing further before it corrects, which deters arbitrageurs with short horizons or outside capital. De Long, Shleifer, Summers and Waldmann (1990).

concepts.name: Siamese twin stocks
concepts.def: Pairs such as Royal Dutch and Shell with fixed claims on the same cash flows that traded at persistent deviations from parity, a textbook case of limits to arbitrage. Froot and Dabora (1999).

concepts.name: Joint hypothesis problem
concepts.def: Any test of market efficiency is also a test of some asset pricing model, so an anomaly could be mispricing or a missing risk factor; efficiency cannot be tested alone. Fama.

concepts.name: Adaptive markets hypothesis
concepts.def: Lo's (2004) view that efficiency varies over time as participants adapt, compete and exit, so strategies work in some environments and fail in others.

concepts.name: Excess volatility puzzle
concepts.def: Shiller (1981) showed stock prices move far more than later realized dividends can justify, contradicting simple present-value efficient market models.

concepts.name: Equity premium puzzle
concepts.def: Mehra and Prescott (1985): historical US stock returns exceeded safe returns by far more than standard consumption models can explain without implausibly high risk aversion.

concepts.name: Glamour stocks
concepts.def: Popular, high-multiple stocks with strong past growth that investors extrapolate. Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny (1994) argued value beats glamour because investors overextrapolate past growth.

concepts.name: Neglected firm effect
concepts.def: Stocks with little analyst coverage or institutional ownership have historically earned higher returns, partly as pay for information costs and illiquidity.

concepts.name: Skewness preference
concepts.def: Investors pay up for positively skewed, lottery-like payoffs, so such assets earn low average returns. Barberis and Huang (2008) tied it to probability weighting.

concepts.name: Favorite-longshot bias
concepts.def: In betting markets longshots are overpriced and favorites underpriced, so bets on longshots lose far more per dollar. Mirrors overpriced lottery stocks and out-of-the-money options.

concepts.name: Overtrading
concepts.def: Trading more than one's information justifies, so costs erode returns. Barber and Odean (2000) found the most active retail accounts earned the lowest net returns.
concepts.aliases: excessive trading,trading is hazardous to your wealth

concepts.name: Gamification of trading
concepts.def: App features such as confetti, streaks, push alerts and one-tap options that raise retail trading frequency and risk taking.

concepts.name: Career risk
concepts.def: Risk to a professional manager of trailing peers or the benchmark, which encourages index hugging and herding and discourages unconventional bets even with positive expected value. Keynes noted it is better to fail conventionally.

concepts.name: Performance chasing
concepts.def: Moving money into funds or assets after strong returns and out after weak ones, which tends to buy high and sell low and makes investor returns trail fund returns.

concepts.name: Smart money and dumb money
concepts.def: Folklore separating informed professional flows from late retail flows; gauges built on the split are used as contrarian or confirming signals, with mixed evidence.

concepts.name: AAII sentiment survey
concepts.def: Weekly American Association of Individual Investors poll of members' six-month outlook as bullish, neutral or bearish. Used as a contrarian indicator at extremes.

concepts.name: Margin debt
concepts.def: Total borrowing against securities in brokerage accounts. Rapid growth signals leveraged speculation and raises forced selling risk when prices fall.

concepts.name: Baker-Wurgler sentiment index
concepts.def: Composite investor sentiment measure built from proxies such as IPO volume and first-day returns, closed-end fund discounts, equity share of issuance and the dividend premium. High readings predict weak future returns on speculative, hard-to-value stocks.

concepts.name: Dot-com name effect
concepts.def: In 1998 and 1999 firms that added .com to their names earned large abnormal returns regardless of any change in business. Cooper, Dimitrov and Rau (2001). A clean measure of mania mispricing.

concepts.name: Halo effect
concepts.def: Letting one positive trait shape judgment of unrelated ones, such as assuming a great product or celebrated CEO implies a great stock at any price. Rosenzweig showed it distorts business success studies.

concepts.name: Curse of knowledge
concepts.def: Experts struggle to imagine not knowing what they know, so they misjudge how others will read information and how fast it will be priced.

concepts.name: Loss chasing
concepts.def: Raising bet size or risk to recover losses quickly; in trading it leads to revenge trades and blowups.

concepts.name: Averaging down
concepts.def: Buying more of a position after it falls to lower the average cost. Sound when the thesis still holds and sizing allows; dangerous when it is escalation of commitment in disguise.

concepts.name: Affinity fraud
concepts.def: Fraud that targets members of a group, such as a religious, ethnic or professional community, exploiting trust within it. Madoff's scheme spread largely through social and charitable networks.

concepts.name: Decoy effect
concepts.def: Adding an option that is clearly worse than one alternative shifts choice toward that alternative. Used in pricing tiers and in presenting negotiation packages.

concepts.name: Expected utility theory
concepts.def: Von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) showed that choices satisfying a few axioms maximize the probability-weighted average of utility of outcomes rather than of the outcomes themselves; risk aversion is concave utility.
concepts.formula: EU = sum of p_i x u(x_i)

concepts.name: Risk aversion
concepts.def: Preferring a sure outcome to a gamble with the same expected value; in utility terms, a concave utility function. Measured by Arrow-Pratt coefficients.
concepts.formula: ARA = -u''(w)/u'(w); RRA = -w x u''(w)/u'(w)

concepts.name: CRRA utility
concepts.def: Constant relative risk aversion utility, under which an investor keeps the same fraction of wealth in risky assets at any wealth level; log utility is the case gamma equals 1.
concepts.formula: u(w) = w^(1-gamma) / (1-gamma)
concepts.aliases: power utility,isoelastic utility,constant relative risk aversion

concepts.name: Log utility
concepts.def: Utility equal to the natural log of wealth. Maximizing expected log wealth is the Kelly criterion and maximizes the long-run growth rate. Bernoulli (1738) proposed it to resolve the St. Petersburg paradox.
concepts.formula: u(w) = ln(w)

concepts.name: Diminishing marginal utility
concepts.def: Each extra unit of wealth adds less satisfaction than the last, which implies risk aversion and explains why ruinous bets are bad even at positive expected value.

concepts.name: St. Petersburg paradox
concepts.def: A coin-flip game with infinite expected payout that people will pay only a small sum to play. Resolved by diminishing marginal utility (Bernoulli) or by the finite wealth of any counterparty.
concepts.formula: EV = sum over n of (1/2)^n x 2^n = infinity

concepts.name: Allais paradox
concepts.def: Allais (1953) showed people choose in ways that violate the independence axiom of expected utility, typically by overweighting certainty.

concepts.name: Ellsberg paradox
concepts.def: Ellsberg (1961) showed people prefer bets on urns with known odds over unknown odds even when that is inconsistent with any single subjective probability, demonstrating ambiguity aversion.

concepts.name: Stochastic dominance
concepts.def: Option A first-order dominates B if A's chance of exceeding every outcome level is at least as high; any investor preferring more wealth picks A. Second-order dominance adds risk aversion.
concepts.aliases: first order stochastic dominance,second order stochastic dominance

concepts.name: Maximin criterion
concepts.def: Choose the option whose worst outcome is best; a rule for deep uncertainty. Gilboa and Schmeidler's maxmin expected utility applies it over a set of plausible probability models.

concepts.name: Minimax regret
concepts.def: Choose the option that minimizes the largest regret, the gap between its payoff and the best payoff in each state. Savage (1951). Less conservative than maximin.

concepts.name: Bounded rationality
concepts.def: Simon's idea that real decision makers have limited information, time and computing power, so they use rules and satisfice instead of optimizing.

concepts.name: Satisficing
concepts.def: Choosing the first option that meets an acceptability threshold instead of searching for the best. Simon (1956). Sensible when search is costly.

concepts.name: Ecological rationality
concepts.def: Gigerenzer's view that a heuristic is rational when matched to its environment; simple rules can beat complex models in uncertain, data-poor settings.

concepts.name: Fast and frugal heuristics
concepts.def: Simple rules that use little information, such as take-the-best, and often predict as well as regression out of sample because they cannot overfit. Gigerenzer and Goldstein (1996).

concepts.name: Recognition heuristic
concepts.def: If one of two options is recognized and the other is not, infer the recognized one scores higher on the criterion. Tested for stock picking with mixed results. Goldstein and Gigerenzer.

concepts.name: Decision noise
concepts.def: Unwanted variability in judgments that should be identical, such as different underwriters pricing the same risk differently. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein (2021) argue it rivals bias as a source of error.
concepts.formula: MSE = bias^2 + noise^2

concepts.name: Decision hygiene
concepts.def: Procedures that reduce error without knowing its direction: independent judgments before discussion, structured criteria, averaging several estimates and delaying intuition until the facts are in.

concepts.name: Decision quality
concepts.def: Judging a decision by its process: framing, alternatives considered, information, clear values, sound reasoning and commitment to act, separately from how it turned out. Decision analysis school of Howard.

concepts.name: Second-order thinking
concepts.def: Considering the consequences of consequences and how others will respond, not only the first effect of an action.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.def: The value of the best alternative given up. Every holding should be compared with the next best use of capital, not with zero; Buffett and Munger use it as the bar for any new idea.

concepts.name: Asymmetric payoff
concepts.def: A bet where the potential gain greatly exceeds the potential loss, so it can be attractive even with a low chance of success. Central to options, venture capital and Pabrai's heads-I-win approach.

concepts.name: Two-way door decisions
concepts.def: Separating reversible decisions, which should be made quickly, from irreversible ones, which deserve care. Bezos's one-way and two-way doors.

concepts.name: Investment checklist
concepts.def: Structured list of questions and known failure modes reviewed before committing capital, borrowed from aviation and surgery. Pabrai and Munger popularized checklists to catch predictable errors.

concepts.name: Devil's advocate
concepts.def: A person assigned to argue against the prevailing view so dissent is legitimate and assumptions get tested.

concepts.name: Variant view test
concepts.def: Before buying, state the consensus view, your differing view, why you are right and what will make the market see it; if you cannot, there is no edge.

concepts.name: After action review
concepts.def: Structured debrief asking what was planned, what happened, why, and what to sustain or improve. US Army practice adapted to trade and deal postmortems.

concepts.name: Superforecasting
concepts.def: Tetlock and Gardner's (2015) findings from the Good Judgment Project: some forecasters beat others reliably by starting from base rates, breaking problems down, updating often in small steps and tracking accuracy.

concepts.name: Foxes and hedgehogs
concepts.def: Tetlock's (2005) distinction: hedgehogs know one big idea and forecast confidently but poorly; foxes draw on many ideas, hedge and forecast better.

concepts.name: Fermi estimation
concepts.def: Breaking an unknown quantity into factors that can be estimated and multiplying them, to reach an order-of-magnitude answer fast; used for market sizing and sanity checks.

concepts.name: Extremizing
concepts.def: Pushing an average of forecasters' probabilities away from 50% because each forecaster holds only part of the shared information; improves aggregate accuracy in forecasting tournaments.

concepts.name: Forecast aggregation
concepts.def: Combining many judgmental forecasts by mean, median or track-record weights to cut noise. Distinct from statistical combination of model forecasts.

concepts.name: Delphi method
concepts.def: Structured, anonymous, multi-round expert survey in which panelists revise estimates after seeing a summary of others' views, limiting dominance and groupthink. Developed at RAND in the 1950s.

concepts.name: Optimal stopping
concepts.def: Choosing when to stop searching to maximize expected payoff. In the secretary problem the best rule rejects the first n/e (about 37%) of candidates, then takes the next one better than all seen.
concepts.formula: look phase = n / e

concepts.name: Explore-exploit tradeoff
concepts.def: Balancing gathering information on uncertain options against using the best known one, formalized as multi-armed bandit problems. Applies to strategy allocation and research time.

concepts.name: Conjunction fallacy
concepts.def: Judging a specific combination of conditions as more likely than one of its parts, which breaks probability rules. Tversky and Kahneman's Linda problem (1983). Detailed scenarios feel more plausible but are less probable.

concepts.name: Prosecutor's fallacy
concepts.def: Confusing P(evidence given innocence) with P(innocence given evidence). In markets, mistaking how unlikely a backtest is under pure chance for the probability the strategy is real.

concepts.name: Regression fallacy
concepts.def: Crediting an intervention for what was simple regression toward the mean, such as praising a new manager for recovery after an unusually bad year.

concepts.name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
concepts.def: Drawing the target after shooting: finding clusters in data and presenting them as if predicted. The backtest version is postdiction.

concepts.name: Berkson's paradox
concepts.def: A spurious negative correlation created by selecting on an outcome that depends on both variables, such as looking only at funded startups or listed firms.

concepts.name: OODA loop
concepts.def: Boyd's cycle of observe, orient, decide, act; the side that cycles faster and orients better gains the advantage. Applied to trading and competitive strategy.

concepts.name: Precommitment
concepts.def: Binding yourself in advance to a course of action to resist later temptation, such as written sell rules or automatic contributions; a Ulysses contract.

concepts.name: Type I and Type II errors
concepts.def: A Type I error is a false positive, acting on an edge that is not real; a Type II error is a false negative, missing a real edge. Tightening one usually loosens the other.

concepts.name: Inside view
concepts.def: Forecasting from the specifics of the case at hand, its plan and its story, which tends toward optimism; the outside view starts instead from base rates of similar cases.

concepts.name: Time diversification fallacy
concepts.def: The claim that stocks get less risky with a longer horizon because annualized return volatility falls. Samuelson (1963) showed the spread of terminal wealth still widens, so horizon alone does not justify more risk.
concepts.aliases: time diversification,samuelson fallacy of large numbers

concepts.name: Taleb barbell
concepts.def: Holding mostly very safe assets plus a small allocation to highly convex, high-risk bets, while avoiding the middle; Taleb's recipe for robustness under uncertainty.

concepts.name: Antifragility
concepts.def: Taleb's term for systems that gain from volatility and stress rather than merely surviving it; convex exposures are antifragile and concave ones fragile.

concepts.name: Pareto principle
concepts.def: Rule of thumb that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes, as when a few holdings drive most portfolio returns. Reflects skewed, power-law-like distributions.

concepts.name: Compounding
concepts.def: Earning returns on prior returns so wealth grows geometrically; the rule of 72 gives the approximate doubling time. Buffett's snowball: long runway plus time.
concepts.formula: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n; doubling time about 72 / r%

concepts.name: Dominant strategy
concepts.def: A strategy that pays at least as well as any other no matter what opponents do. In the prisoner's dilemma, defecting is dominant for both players.

concepts.name: Iterated dominance
concepts.def: Repeatedly removing dominated strategies to narrow likely play; deeper rounds assume common knowledge of rationality.

concepts.name: Best response
concepts.def: The strategy that maximizes a player's payoff given others' strategies; a Nash equilibrium is a set of mutual best responses.

concepts.name: Pareto efficiency
concepts.def: An outcome where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. Nash equilibria need not be Pareto efficient, as the prisoner's dilemma shows.

concepts.name: Zero-sum game
concepts.def: A game where one side's gains equal the other's losses, such as poker before rake. Active management against the market is zero sum before costs and negative sum after.

concepts.name: Positive-sum game
concepts.def: An interaction where total value can grow, such as trade, long-run business ownership and integrative negotiation.

concepts.name: Minimax theorem
concepts.def: Von Neumann (1928): in finite two-player zero-sum games a mixed strategy guarantees each player the value of the game; maximizing one's worst case equals minimizing the opponent's best case.

concepts.name: Sequential game
concepts.def: A game where players move in turn and later movers see earlier moves; drawn as a game tree in extensive form and solved by backward induction.

concepts.name: Simultaneous game
concepts.def: A game where players choose without seeing each other's choices, shown as a payoff matrix in normal form.

concepts.name: Backward induction
concepts.def: Solving a sequential game from the last move backward, choosing the best action at each point given best play afterward.

concepts.name: Subgame perfect equilibrium
concepts.def: A Nash equilibrium that is also an equilibrium in every subgame, which rules out threats that would not be carried out. Selten (1965).

concepts.name: Bayesian game
concepts.def: A game of incomplete information in which players have private types drawn from known distributions and update beliefs with Bayes' rule. Harsanyi; Bayesian Nash equilibrium extends Nash to it.

concepts.name: Repeated game
concepts.def: The same stage game played many times, where the threat of future retaliation can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game would not.

concepts.name: Folk theorem
concepts.def: In infinitely repeated games with patient players, almost any outcome giving each player more than their minimum guaranteed payoff can be sustained as an equilibrium, including cooperation.

concepts.name: Tit for tat
concepts.def: Cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move. Won Axelrod's iterated prisoner's dilemma tournaments by being nice, retaliatory, forgiving and easy to read.

concepts.name: Grim trigger
concepts.def: Cooperate until the opponent defects once, then defect forever; the harshest punishment, which sustains cooperation if players are patient enough.

concepts.name: Reputation building
concepts.def: In repeated play with uncertainty about types, a player acts tough or reliable early to shape beliefs and gain later. Kreps, Wilson, Milgrom and Roberts (1982).

concepts.name: Chain-store paradox
concepts.def: Selten (1978): backward induction says an incumbent should never fight entrants in a finite sequence of markets, yet fighting early seems sensible; resolved by reputation models with uncertainty about type.

concepts.name: Coordination game
concepts.def: A game where players gain by choosing the same action and there are several equilibria, so outcomes depend on expectations, as in bank runs and currency pegs.

concepts.name: Stag hunt
concepts.def: Coordination game where joint cooperation pays most but is risky, so playing safe is the risk-dominant equilibrium. Models trust, liquidity provision and rescue consortiums.

concepts.name: Game of chicken
concepts.def: Two players head toward disaster; the one who swerves loses face, but if neither does both lose badly. Models debt-ceiling standoffs, price wars and brinkmanship.

concepts.name: Focal point
concepts.def: A solution people converge on without communicating because it seems natural or salient, such as a round number or precedent. Schelling (1960).

concepts.name: Credible commitment
concepts.def: A move that changes your own future incentives so a threat or promise becomes believable, such as burning bridges, public pledges or contracts with penalties. Schelling.

concepts.name: Credible threat
concepts.def: A threat the threatener would actually want to carry out when the time comes; rational opponents ignore threats that are not credible.

concepts.name: Cheap talk
concepts.def: Costless, non-binding, unverifiable communication; it conveys information only when sender and receiver interests are close enough. Crawford and Sobel (1982). Applies to guidance and management commentary.

concepts.name: Costly signaling
concepts.def: A signal is credible when it costs low-quality types more to send, as in Spence's (1973) education model; insider buying, buybacks and dividends can signal management confidence.

concepts.name: Separating equilibrium
concepts.def: In a signaling game, an equilibrium where different types send different signals so receivers can infer type; in a pooling equilibrium all types send the same signal and nothing is learned.

concepts.name: Screening
concepts.def: The uninformed side offers a menu of choices that leads informed parties to reveal their type, such as deductible choices or loan terms. Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976).

concepts.name: Bayesian persuasion
concepts.def: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011): a sender who commits in advance to how information will be revealed can shift a rational receiver's actions, the logic behind disclosure policy and forward guidance design.

concepts.name: Brinkmanship
concepts.def: Deliberately creating a risk of mutual disaster that neither side fully controls in order to force the other side to back down. Schelling.

concepts.name: War of attrition
concepts.def: A contest where players pay ongoing costs until one quits and the survivor takes the prize, as in price wars and standoffs; expected costs can eat most of the prize.

concepts.name: El Farol bar problem
concepts.def: Arthur's (1994) puzzle: people go to a bar only if they expect it not to be crowded, so any widely shared forecast defeats itself. A model of crowded trades and the minority game.

concepts.name: Price war
concepts.def: Competitors repeatedly cutting prices to win share, often destroying industry profits; commodity, airline and retail sectors are prone to them.

concepts.name: First-mover advantage
concepts.def: Gains from moving first, such as scale, customer lock-in or preempting capacity; can be offset by second-mover advantages like learning from the leader's mistakes.

concepts.name: Stackelberg competition
concepts.def: Leader-follower quantity competition in which the leader commits to output first and earns more than under simultaneous Cournot competition.

concepts.name: Cournot competition
concepts.def: Firms choose quantities at the same time; equilibrium price falls between monopoly and competitive levels and approaches marginal cost as the number of firms grows. Cournot (1838).

concepts.name: Bertrand competition
concepts.def: Firms choose prices at the same time; with identical products and costs, even two firms drive price to marginal cost, the Bertrand paradox. Differentiation and capacity limits soften it.

concepts.name: Entry deterrence
concepts.def: An incumbent's moves to make entry unprofitable, such as excess capacity, limit pricing or a reputation for fighting; credible only if the incumbent would follow through after entry.

concepts.name: Tacit collusion
concepts.def: Firms keeping prices high without an explicit agreement, through repeated interaction and threat of retaliation; easier with few players, transparent prices and stable demand.

concepts.name: Cartel cheating
concepts.def: Members of a cartel secretly producing above quota because each gains individually while the group loses, a prisoner's dilemma that makes cartels unstable without monitoring and punishment.

concepts.name: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.def: Shared resources get overused because each user captures the full benefit while costs are spread across all. Hardin (1968). Fits crowded trades and exits in a stampede.

concepts.name: Free rider problem
concepts.def: People enjoy a shared benefit without paying for it, so it is underprovided; dispersed shareholders free ride on monitoring, which is why blockholders and activists matter.

concepts.name: Public goods game
concepts.def: Experiment where players contribute to a pot that is multiplied and shared equally; contributions fall over rounds unless free riders can be punished.

concepts.name: Mechanism design
concepts.def: Designing the rules of a game so self-interested players produce a desired outcome, sometimes called reverse game theory. Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson shared the 2007 Nobel. The basis of auction and market design.
