concepts.name: Revelation principle
concepts.def: Any outcome achievable by some mechanism can also be achieved by one in which players truthfully report their private information, which simplifies mechanism design.

concepts.name: Incentive compatibility
concepts.def: A mechanism is incentive compatible when each participant does best by acting on its true preferences, as in a second-price auction.

concepts.name: Market for lemons
concepts.def: Akerlof (1970): when sellers know quality and buyers do not, buyers pay average prices, good sellers withdraw and the market can unravel. Applies to used cars, small private companies and new issues.

concepts.name: Common knowledge
concepts.def: Everyone knows a fact, knows that everyone knows it, and so on without end. A public announcement can change behavior even when everyone already knew privately.

concepts.name: Keynesian beauty contest
concepts.def: Keynes's analogy in which investors pick not what they think is best but what they think others will think is best, adding layers of expectation; formalized in guess-two-thirds-of-the-average games.
concepts.aliases: beauty contest,p beauty contest,guess two thirds

concepts.name: Level-k thinking
concepts.def: A model where a level-0 player acts naively and each level-k player best responds to level k-1; experiments show most people reason only one or two steps deep.

concepts.name: Dollar auction
concepts.def: Shubik's (1971) auction for a dollar in which the second-highest bidder also pays, so bidders escalate past the prize's value to avoid losing their bid. A model of escalation.

concepts.name: Holdout problem
concepts.def: When a deal needs every holder's consent, individuals can demand more by refusing, as in sovereign debt restructurings and land assembly; collective action clauses limit it.

concepts.name: Hold-up problem
concepts.def: After one party makes an investment specific to a relationship, the other can renegotiate to capture its value, so parties underinvest without protective contracts. Williamson; Klein, Crawford and Alchian.

concepts.name: Coase theorem
concepts.def: Coase (1960): if property rights are clear and bargaining costs are low, parties negotiate to the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; real transaction costs explain why allocation still matters.

concepts.name: Core of a cooperative game
concepts.def: The set of payoff splits no subgroup could beat by breaking off on its own; if it is empty, any deal is unstable because some coalition always wants to defect.

concepts.name: No-trade theorem
concepts.def: Milgrom and Stokey (1982): if all traders are rational with common priors and this is common knowledge, private information alone cannot generate trade, since any offer reveals information. Real trading needs noise, hedging or differing priors.

concepts.name: Agreeing to disagree
concepts.def: Aumann (1976): rational agents with a common prior whose posteriors are common knowledge cannot hold different posteriors. Persistent disagreement implies different priors or irrationality.

concepts.name: Grossman-Stiglitz paradox
concepts.def: Grossman and Stiglitz (1980): if prices fully reflected information, no one would pay to collect it, so markets must stay inefficient enough to reward the cost of research.

concepts.name: Tournament theory
concepts.def: Pay based on relative rank drives effort but also risk shifting: fund managers behind at midyear tend to raise risk to catch up. Lazear and Rosen (1981); Brown, Harlow and Starks (1996).

concepts.name: Gambling for resurrection
concepts.def: Distressed firms or traders with limited liability take big risks because owners keep the upside while creditors bear the downside. Seen in late-1980s US savings and loan failures.

concepts.name: Red Queen effect
concepts.def: Competition forcing constant improvement just to keep a relative position; trading edges decay as rivals copy them.

concepts.name: Predatory trading
concepts.def: Traders who know another investor must sell first sell ahead and then buy back cheaper, worsening the distressed party's losses. Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2005); seen around LTCM and Amaranth.

concepts.name: Diamond-Dybvig model
concepts.def: Diamond and Dybvig (1983): banks turn illiquid loans into demand deposits, creating two equilibria, one normal and one a self-fulfilling run; deposit insurance removes the run equilibrium.

concepts.name: Inequity aversion
concepts.def: Fehr and Schmidt (1999): people dislike unequal outcomes, especially being behind, which explains rejections in ultimatum games and punishment of free riders.

concepts.name: English auction
concepts.def: Open ascending auction where the price rises until one bidder remains; with private values, bidders stay in until the price reaches their value.

concepts.name: Dutch auction
concepts.def: Open descending auction where the price falls until a bidder accepts; strategically the same as a first-price sealed bid. Google used a Dutch-auction format for its 2004 IPO.

concepts.name: First-price sealed-bid auction
concepts.def: Each bidder submits one sealed bid; the highest wins and pays its own bid, so bidders shade below their values.

concepts.name: Vickrey auction
concepts.def: Sealed-bid second-price auction: the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, which makes bidding your true value a dominant strategy. Vickrey (1961).
concepts.aliases: second price auction,second price sealed bid

concepts.name: Revenue equivalence theorem
concepts.def: With independent private values, risk-neutral bidders and symmetric equilibrium, standard auction formats give the seller the same expected revenue. Myerson (1981); Riley and Samuelson (1981).

concepts.name: Reserve price
concepts.def: The minimum price a seller will accept in an auction; Myerson showed a well-set reserve raises expected revenue even though it risks no sale.

concepts.name: Bid shading
concepts.def: Bidding below your true value in a first-price auction to keep some profit if you win; the fewer the rivals, the more you shade.

concepts.name: All-pay auction
concepts.def: Every bidder pays its bid but only the highest wins; models lobbying, patent races and contests for talent.

concepts.name: Common value auction
concepts.def: An auction where the item is worth about the same to all bidders but that value is uncertain, such as an oil lease or a company; the winner tends to be whoever overestimated most.

concepts.name: Private value auction
concepts.def: Each bidder knows its own value, which differs across bidders and does not depend on what others know; no winner's curse arises.

concepts.name: Linkage principle
concepts.def: Milgrom and Weber (1982): when values are affiliated, revealing more information about the item raises expected revenue, which is why sellers publish data rooms and appraisals and why open ascending auctions beat sealed bids.

concepts.name: Uniform price auction
concepts.def: Multi-unit auction where all winning bidders pay the same market-clearing price; the US Treasury uses this format.

concepts.name: Discriminatory auction
concepts.def: Multi-unit auction where each winner pays its own bid; bidders shade more than in uniform price formats.
concepts.aliases: pay as bid auction,multiple price auction

concepts.name: Auction sniping
concepts.def: Placing a bid in the final seconds of a fixed-end online auction, as on eBay, to avoid bidding wars and to hide information from rivals; less useful against proxy bidding with true values.

concepts.name: Bid rigging
concepts.def: Bidders colluding to suppress competition, by rotating winners or submitting cover bids, so prices fall below competitive levels; illegal in most markets.

concepts.name: Bookbuilding
concepts.def: IPO process in which underwriters gather indications of interest from institutions to set the offer price and allocate shares; allocations reward investors who reveal demand, which helps explain underpricing.

concepts.name: Auctions versus negotiations
concepts.def: Bulow and Klemperer (1996): a simple auction with one extra serious bidder beats the best negotiation with fewer bidders, so for sellers competition is worth more than bargaining skill.

concepts.name: Gambler's ruin
concepts.def: A gambler with finite capital who keeps betting at fair or unfavorable odds against a far richer opponent will eventually go broke. At fair odds, the chance of ruin starting with a against b is b/(a+b).
concepts.formula: P(ruin) = b / (a + b) at fair odds

concepts.name: Martingale betting system
concepts.def: Doubling the stake after each loss so one win recovers everything plus one unit; fails because losing streaks, table limits and finite capital eventually cause ruin.

concepts.name: Anti-martingale
concepts.def: Raising size after wins and cutting after losses, as in pyramiding into winners, which caps damage during losing streaks.

concepts.name: House edge
concepts.def: The casino's expected profit as a share of each bet, such as about 5.26% on double-zero roulette; over many bets the law of large numbers makes it near certain.
concepts.formula: house edge = -EV per unit staked

concepts.name: Implied probability
concepts.def: The probability embedded in odds or prices: decimal odds d imply 1/d, and a binary contract priced at p cents implies about p%. Across all outcomes the total exceeds 100% by the bookmaker's margin.
concepts.formula: implied p = 1 / decimal odds

concepts.name: Vigorish
concepts.def: The bookmaker's margin built into odds so implied probabilities sum to more than 100%; standard minus 110 on both sides implies about 4.5% hold.
concepts.formula: overround = sum(1 / decimal odds) - 1

concepts.name: Closing line value
concepts.def: Comparing the odds a bet was placed at with the final pre-event line; consistently beating the close is the best evidence of betting skill because closing lines are efficient.

concepts.name: Sharp money
concepts.def: Bets from sophisticated, winning bettors whose action moves lines; books limit them and follow their flow, while recreational bettors are called squares.

concepts.name: Steam move
concepts.def: Sudden, broad line movement across books caused by coordinated sharp betting; chasing it late usually captures little value.

concepts.name: Line shopping
concepts.def: Comparing odds across books and placing each bet at the best available price; small price gains compound into large differences in long-run return.

concepts.name: Middling
concepts.def: Betting both sides of a game at different lines after the line moves, so a result landing between them wins both bets, while other results lose only the margin.

concepts.name: Betting arbitrage
concepts.def: Backing every outcome across books or platforms when combined implied probabilities sum below 100%, locking a profit if all bets settle as expected; risks include limits, voided bets and mismatched rules.
concepts.formula: arb exists if sum(1 / best decimal odds) < 1

concepts.name: Parlay
concepts.def: A bet combining several selections that pays only if all win; payouts multiply but so does the book's edge, making parlays some of the worst-value bets offered.

concepts.name: Pari-mutuel betting
concepts.def: Pool betting where all stakes on an event are pooled, the house takes a cut and winners share the rest, so odds are set by the crowd; used in horse racing.

concepts.name: Card counting
concepts.def: Tracking cards dealt in blackjack to know when the remaining deck favors the player, then betting more. Thorp's Beat the Dealer (1962) proved the edge and applied Kelly sizing.
concepts.aliases: beat the dealer,hi lo count,thorp blackjack

concepts.name: Poker win rate
concepts.def: Results measured in big blinds won per 100 hands; because hand outcomes are noisy, tens of thousands of hands are needed before a win rate is statistically meaningful.
concepts.formula: bb/100 = 100 x big blinds won / hands played

concepts.name: Semi-bluff
concepts.def: Betting a hand that is probably behind but has outs to improve, winning either through fold equity now or by hitting later.

concepts.name: Value bet
concepts.def: Betting a hand that is likely best so that worse hands call; a thin value bet targets hands only slightly worse.

concepts.name: Polarized range
concepts.def: A betting range made of very strong hands and bluffs with few medium hands; a linear or merged range bets from the strongest hands down to medium ones.

concepts.name: Balanced range
concepts.def: A range that mixes value hands and bluffs in proportions that leave opponents indifferent between calling and folding, so they cannot exploit it.

concepts.name: Overbet
concepts.def: A bet larger than the pot, used with a polarized range and nut advantage to apply maximum pressure on capped ranges.

concepts.name: Minimum defense frequency
concepts.def: The share of a range a player must continue with against a bet so that the bettor's bluffs do not profit automatically.
concepts.formula: MDF = pot / (pot + bet)

concepts.name: Bluff breakeven frequency
concepts.def: How often a bluff must succeed to break even, which depends only on bet size relative to the pot.
concepts.formula: alpha = bet / (bet + pot)

concepts.name: Blockers
concepts.def: Cards in your hand that remove combinations of strong hands from an opponent's range, which guides bluffing and calling choices.

concepts.name: Independent chip model
concepts.def: Tournament model converting chip stacks into shares of prize money; near pay jumps chips lost are worth more than chips won, so players must tighten.

concepts.name: Reverse implied odds
concepts.def: Expected future losses when you make a hand that is still second best, which reduce the true value of calling.

concepts.name: Stack-to-pot ratio
concepts.def: Effective stack divided by the pot on the flop; a low ratio favors committing with top pair, a high one favors drawing to nut hands.
concepts.formula: SPR = effective stack / pot

concepts.name: Pot commitment
concepts.def: When so much of a stack is already in the pot that folding is worse than calling; planning commitment in advance avoids getting stuck by accident.

concepts.name: Leveling
concepts.def: Poker term for thinking about what the opponent thinks you hold, and what they think you think; going one level beyond the opponent wins, going two can lose.

concepts.name: Equity realization
concepts.def: The share of a hand's raw equity it actually captures given position and playability; hands played out of position realize less.

concepts.name: Game selection
concepts.def: Choosing where to compete based on your edge over the opposition; for investors, picking markets with weak competition and forced or uninformed counterparties.

concepts.name: Rake
concepts.def: The house's fee on each pot or tournament; it makes poker negative sum, so a small edge can still lose money, much as fees do in active management.

concepts.name: Integrative negotiation
concepts.def: Bargaining that creates value by trading across issues the sides value differently, so both can gain; also called expanding the pie.

concepts.name: Distributive negotiation
concepts.def: Bargaining over a fixed amount where one side's gain is the other's loss, such as price alone; anchors, concessions and reservation prices dominate.

concepts.name: Interests versus positions
concepts.def: Positions are what parties demand; interests are why they demand it. Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes (1981) argues that probing interests uncovers trades positional bargaining misses.

concepts.name: Principled negotiation
concepts.def: Fisher and Ury's method: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests, invent options for mutual gain and insist on objective criteria, backed by a strong BATNA.

concepts.name: Objective criteria
concepts.def: Independent standards such as market comparables, appraisals or precedent used to justify terms, which makes concessions easier to accept and resists pressure tactics.

concepts.name: MESOs
concepts.def: Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers: presenting several packages of equal value to you to learn the other side's priorities and look flexible.

concepts.name: Aspiration point
concepts.def: The ambitious target a negotiator aims for; setting high, justifiable aspirations predicts better outcomes than focusing on the walk-away point.

concepts.name: Bracketing
concepts.def: Making offers so the midpoint between yours and theirs lands on your target, anticipating a split-the-difference close.

concepts.name: Splitting the difference
concepts.def: Settling at the midpoint of current offers; it feels fair but rewards whoever anchored more aggressively.

concepts.name: Conditional concession
concepts.def: Giving something only in exchange for something, phrased as if you do X, I can do Y, so concessions are traded rather than gifted.

concepts.name: Bidding against yourself
concepts.def: Making a second concession before the other side has answered the first, which signals weakness and moves the deal with no return.

concepts.name: Nibble
concepts.def: Asking for a small extra concession after the main deal is agreed, when the other side does not want to reopen talks; countered by asking for something back.

concepts.name: Limited authority
concepts.def: Claiming that a higher authority must approve terms, which slows concessions and lets a negotiator decline without confrontation.
concepts.aliases: higher authority,need to check with my boss

concepts.name: Hardball tactics
concepts.def: Aggressive moves such as extreme opening demands, threats, take-it-or-leave-it offers and fake deadlines; effective in one-off deals but costly to trust and reputation.

concepts.name: Exploding offer
concepts.def: An offer with a very short expiry meant to stop the other side from shopping alternatives; often met by asking for time or testing the deadline.

concepts.name: Boulwarism
concepts.def: Opening with a firm, final offer and refusing to concede, named for GE's Lemuel Boulware; can backfire because the other side sees it as unfair.

concepts.name: Tactical empathy
concepts.def: Voss's term for showing you understand the counterpart's emotions and perspective to build trust and draw out information, without conceding anything.

concepts.name: Mirroring
concepts.def: Repeating the last few words a counterpart said, as a question, to prompt them to keep talking and reveal more.

concepts.name: Labeling
concepts.def: Naming the counterpart's emotion or concern, as in it seems like you are worried about timing, to defuse it or confirm it.

concepts.name: Calibrated questions
concepts.def: Open how and what questions, such as how am I supposed to do that, that get the other side solving your problem and revealing its constraints.

concepts.name: Ackerman bargaining
concepts.def: Price model taught by Voss: open at 65% of your target, then move to 85%, 95% and 100% with shrinking steps, end on a precise number and add a non-monetary item.

concepts.name: Precise offer effect
concepts.def: Precise first offers such as 4,985 instead of 5,000 are seen as better researched and draw smaller counteroffers. Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames (2013).

concepts.name: Counteroffer
concepts.def: A reply that proposes new terms and implicitly rejects the original; a firm, reasoned counter re-anchors quickly so the first offer does not set the frame.

concepts.name: Strategic silence
concepts.def: Pausing after an offer or question so the other side fills the gap, often revealing information or improving their own offer.

concepts.name: Reciprocity norm
concepts.def: The tendency to return favors and concessions; it powers concession trading and the door-in-the-face tactic. One of Cialdini's influence principles.

concepts.name: Door in the face
concepts.def: Making a large request you expect to be refused, then a smaller one that looks like a concession and is more likely accepted.

concepts.name: Foot in the door
concepts.def: Getting agreement to a small request first, making a larger later request more likely to succeed through the wish to stay consistent.

concepts.name: Commitment and consistency
concepts.def: People act to stay consistent with what they have said or done, especially publicly; small written commitments make later agreement more likely. A Cialdini principle.

concepts.name: Scarcity principle
concepts.def: Options seem more valuable when limited or about to disappear; competing bids and deadlines exploit it. A Cialdini principle.

concepts.name: Contingent contract
concepts.def: Terms that depend on a future outcome, letting parties bet on their disagreement instead of deadlocking; earnouts and performance fees are examples.

concepts.name: Letter of intent
concepts.def: A mostly non-binding document setting price, structure and key deal terms, usually with binding exclusivity and confidentiality clauses; it frames the rest of the negotiation.

concepts.name: Escrow holdback
concepts.def: Part of the purchase price held back for a period to cover breaches of representations and indemnity claims, shifting risk from buyer to seller.

concepts.name: Representations and warranties
concepts.def: Seller's statements of fact about the business, such as financials, liabilities and compliance, backed by indemnities if they prove false; the scope is heavily negotiated.

concepts.name: Deal fatigue
concepts.def: Exhaustion late in a long negotiation that makes parties concede to get done, or walk away from a deal that still makes sense; time and sunk effort shift bargaining power.

concepts.name: Final offer arbitration
concepts.def: Each side submits a final offer and the arbitrator must pick one without compromise, which pushes both toward reasonable numbers; used in Major League Baseball salary disputes.

concepts.name: Mediation
concepts.def: A neutral third party helps the sides reach a voluntary agreement without imposing one; useful when emotions or information gaps block a deal.

concepts.name: Negotiator's dilemma
concepts.def: Lax and Sebenius: sharing information to create value leaves you exposed to value claiming, while claiming tactics block value creation, so negotiators must manage the tension.

concepts.name: Reactive devaluation
concepts.def: Discounting a proposal because the adversary made it; the same terms look worse coming from the other side. Ross and Stillinger.

concepts.name: Fixed-pie bias
concepts.def: Assuming the other side's interests directly oppose yours, which hides trades that would create value.

concepts.name: Post-settlement settlement
concepts.def: After reaching a deal, the parties look for improvements that leave both better off, keeping the signed deal as a fallback. Raiffa.

concepts.name: Agenda setting
concepts.def: Controlling which issues are discussed and in what order; settling easy issues first builds momentum, while the order of votes can decide outcomes.

concepts.name: Coalition building
concepts.def: Forming alliances with parties who share interests to gain bargaining power in multiparty settings such as creditor committees and proxy contests.

concepts.name: Two-level game
concepts.def: Putnam (1988): negotiators bargain with the other side and with their own constituents at once; a narrow set of terms acceptable at home can be a source of bargaining power.

concepts.name: 3-D negotiation
concepts.def: Lax and Sebenius's framework: beyond tactics at the table, shape deal design and set up the right parties, sequence and alternatives before talks begin.

concepts.name: Outside option principle
concepts.def: In bargaining models an outside option raises a player's share only if it is credible enough to be taken; otherwise the split is set by patience and the threat of delay. Binmore, Shaked and Sutton (1989).

concepts.name: Disagreement point
concepts.def: The payoffs each side gets if talks fail; in Nash bargaining, gains are split from this point, so improving yours raises your share.

concepts.name: Graham growth formula
concepts.def: Graham's rough value for a growth stock: earnings times 8.5 plus twice the expected growth rate, where 8.5 is his P/E for a no-growth firm; he later scaled it by 4.4 over the current AAA bond yield.
concepts.formula: V = EPS x (8.5 + 2g); revised V = EPS x (8.5 + 2g) x 4.4 / Y

concepts.name: Defensive investor
concepts.def: Graham's investor who wants safety and freedom from effort: a diversified portfolio of large, financially strong, consistent dividend payers at moderate multiples, with a stock-bond mix between 25% and 75%. The enterprising investor does more work for more return.

concepts.name: Investment versus speculation
concepts.def: Graham's test: an investment operation, after thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return; anything else is speculation. Price paid relative to value decides which it is.

concepts.name: Cigar butt investing
concepts.def: Buying very cheap, mediocre businesses for one last free puff of value; Buffett's early Graham style, later replaced by buying great businesses at fair prices.

concepts.name: Wonderful business at a fair price
concepts.def: Buffett's shift, under Munger's influence, from fair businesses at wonderful prices to great, high-return businesses at fair prices, since time is the friend of the wonderful business and the enemy of the mediocre one.
concepts.aliases: quality at a fair price,see's candies

concepts.name: Too-hard pile
concepts.def: Munger's bin for decisions too difficult to judge well, which are simply passed over; good results need only a few sound decisions, not an opinion on everything.

concepts.name: Punch card investing
concepts.def: Buffett's thought experiment of a lifetime card with 20 investment slots, forcing extreme selectivity and conviction-weighted concentration.

concepts.name: Fat pitch
concepts.def: Buffett's baseball analogy: investing has no called strikes, so an investor can wait as long as needed for an obvious bargain inside their competence and then swing hard.
concepts.aliases: no called strikes,waiting for the fat pitch

concepts.name: Look-through earnings
concepts.def: Buffett's measure that adds a holder's share of investees' retained earnings, less the tax due if distributed, to its reported earnings, since dividends understate the economics of minority stakes.

concepts.name: Retained earnings test
concepts.def: Buffett's one-dollar test: every dollar of earnings a company retains should, over time, create at least one dollar of market value; otherwise it should be paid out.

concepts.name: Institutional imperative
concepts.def: Buffett's term for the pressure that makes companies resist change, absorb all available cash, feed leaders' pet projects and copy peers, regardless of shareholder value.

concepts.name: Berkshire model
concepts.def: Buffett's structure: permanent ownership of whole businesses, decentralized operations, central allocation of all spare cash, insurance float as cheap funding and a stated aim of compounding per-share value.

concepts.name: Latticework of mental models
concepts.def: Munger's call to learn the big ideas of the main disciplines, such as math, psychology, economics, physics and biology, and use them together instead of relying on one narrow specialty.

concepts.name: Inversion
concepts.def: Solving a problem backward by asking what would guarantee failure and then avoiding it. Munger borrowed Jacobi's advice to invert, always invert.

concepts.name: Lollapalooza effect
concepts.def: Munger's term for extreme outcomes when several psychological tendencies act in the same direction at once, as in auctions, cults and manias.

concepts.name: Psychology of human misjudgment
concepts.def: Munger's 1995 talk listing about two dozen standard causes of misjudgment, such as incentives, social proof, consistency, envy and denial, meant as a checklist against error.

concepts.name: Incentive-caused bias
concepts.def: Judgment bends toward what pays the judge, often unconsciously; Munger's never ask a barber whether you need a haircut. Check how advisers, managers and sell-side analysts are paid.

concepts.name: Man with a hammer
concepts.def: Munger's warning that to a man with a hammer every problem looks like a nail; investors with one model force it on situations it does not fit.

concepts.name: Sit on your hands
concepts.def: Munger's view that the money is made in the waiting, not in the trading: buy great businesses and refrain from activity. Livermore said much the same about sitting tight.

concepts.name: Soros boom-bust model
concepts.def: Soros's sequence in which a prevailing bias and an underlying trend reinforce each other, accelerate past reality, survive tests, reach a moment of truth and then reverse into a self-reinforcing bust.

concepts.name: Fallibility
concepts.def: Soros's premise that participants' views are always incomplete or distorted, so markets are always somewhat wrong and those errors shape the fundamentals they are meant to reflect.

concepts.name: Invest first, investigate later
concepts.def: Soros's practice of taking a small position on a hypothesis to focus attention, then adding or exiting quickly as evidence comes in.

concepts.name: Four-quadrant regimes
concepts.def: Dalio's framework that sorts environments by whether growth and inflation are rising or falling relative to expectations; each asset class does best in particular quadrants, so balance across them.

concepts.name: Long-term debt cycle
concepts.def: Dalio's cycle, lasting roughly 50 to 75 years, of debt rising faster than income until rates can fall no further, ending in deleveraging; the short-term debt cycle is the 5 to 10 year business cycle.
concepts.aliases: big debt cycle,economic machine,short term debt cycle

concepts.name: Beautiful deleveraging
concepts.def: Dalio's term for a deleveraging that balances austerity, debt restructuring, wealth transfers and money printing so nominal growth stays above nominal interest rates and debt burdens fall without depression.

concepts.name: Holy grail of investing
concepts.def: Dalio's observation that combining about 15 good, uncorrelated return streams can cut portfolio risk by roughly 80% without lowering expected return.

concepts.name: Believability weighting
concepts.def: Bridgewater practice of weighting opinions by each person's track record and ability to explain their reasoning, not by seniority or a simple vote.

concepts.name: Radical transparency
concepts.def: Bridgewater principle of recording meetings and making blunt feedback normal so ideas are judged on merit rather than politics.

concepts.name: Pain plus reflection equals progress
concepts.def: Dalio's principle that losses and mistakes are the best teachers if examined honestly, so each failure should produce a written rule for next time.

concepts.name: Second-level thinking
concepts.def: Marks's term for going past the obvious first-level conclusion to ask what the consensus expects, what is priced in and why your view differs; a good company is not the same as a good investment.

concepts.name: Pendulum of investor psychology
concepts.def: Marks's image of sentiment swinging between greed and fear, credulity and skepticism, rarely resting at the reasonable midpoint.

concepts.name: Permanent loss of capital
concepts.def: Marks and Buffett define risk as the chance of losing money for good, not price volatility; volatility only becomes loss for those forced to sell.

concepts.name: Taking the market's temperature
concepts.def: Marks's approach: you cannot predict, but you can prepare by judging where the cycle stands from valuations, credit terms and investor behavior, then adjusting aggressiveness.
concepts.aliases: where are we in the cycle,you cant predict you can prepare

concepts.name: Defensive investing
concepts.def: Marks's emphasis on winning by avoiding big losers: limiting downside capture matters more than chasing upside, and risk control is the mark of a great investor.

concepts.name: Druckenmiller approach
concepts.def: Concentrate when conviction is high, watch liquidity and central bank policy above earnings, look about 18 months ahead, and cut quickly when wrong; preserve capital first, then go for big wins.

concepts.name: Medallion approach
concepts.def: Renaissance's style: many weak, short-horizon signals combined statistically, high turnover, leverage on low-volatility returns and strict adherence to models. Edge comes from breadth and the law of large numbers.

concepts.name: Many small edges
concepts.def: Simons and Thorp style of making money from thousands of small, nearly independent bets each slightly better than even, so results depend on breadth and costs, not on any single call.

concepts.name: Ten-bagger
concepts.def: Lynch's term for a stock that rises tenfold; he argued a few big winners drive a portfolio's results, so selling winners too early is costly.

concepts.name: Lynch stock categories
concepts.def: Lynch's six types: slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds and asset plays, each with different expectations, valuation yardsticks and sell rules.

concepts.name: Invest in what you know
concepts.def: Lynch's advice that everyday observation of products and stores can spot winners early, as a starting point for research rather than a replacement for it.

concepts.name: Diworsification
concepts.def: Lynch's word for acquisitions outside a company's core that destroy value; also used for spreading a portfolio across too many mediocre ideas.

concepts.name: Two-minute drill
concepts.def: Lynch's test: explain in about two minutes why you own a stock, what has to happen for it to work and what could go wrong.

concepts.name: Cocktail party theory
concepts.def: Lynch's sentiment gauge: when people at a party avoid talking stocks, the market is near a low; when they give you tips, it is near a high.

concepts.name: Point of maximum pessimism
concepts.def: Templeton's rule to buy when pessimism is greatest and sell when optimism peaks; at the outbreak of war in 1939 he bought a basket of cheap US stocks, many near bankruptcy.

concepts.name: Global bargain hunting
concepts.def: Templeton's practice of searching every country for the cheapest stocks against long-run earnings power, an early form of global value investing.

concepts.name: Cost matters hypothesis
concepts.def: Bogle's argument that investors as a group earn the market return minus costs, so the lowest-cost funds must, on average, deliver the best net returns.

concepts.name: Arithmetic of active management
concepts.def: Sharpe (1991): before costs the average actively managed dollar must earn the passive market return, so after costs it must earn less.

concepts.name: Fisher's fifteen points
concepts.def: Philip Fisher's checklist for growth stocks from Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits (1958), covering sales growth potential, R&D, margins, management depth and integrity.
concepts.aliases: philip fisher,common stocks and uncommon profits

concepts.name: Pyramiding
concepts.def: Adding to a winning position only after the market confirms the trade, usually in smaller increments, and never adding to losers. Associated with Livermore.

concepts.name: Line of least resistance
concepts.def: Livermore's idea that prices trend in the direction of least resistance, so a trader should wait for price action to confirm it and then trade with it.

concepts.name: Defense-first trading
concepts.def: Paul Tudor Jones's emphasis on what could go wrong: use stops, cut losers, and seek trades with about five-to-one reward to risk; he also used the 200-day moving average as an exit rule.

concepts.name: Long best, short worst
concepts.def: Julian Robertson's Tiger approach: own the best companies and short the worst, often in the same industry, based on fundamental research.

concepts.name: Dhandho
concepts.def: Pabrai's framework: invest in simple, distressed businesses with durable moats, place few bets with favorable odds, and seek setups where heads I win, tails I don't lose much.
concepts.aliases: mohnish pabrai,heads i win tails i dont lose much

concepts.name: Cloning
concepts.def: Copying high-conviction ideas of investors with strong records, often found in 13F filings, then doing your own work; Pabrai advocates it openly.

concepts.name: Three-legged stool
concepts.def: Chuck Akre's test for a compounder: an extraordinary business with high returns on capital, talented and honest management, and ample room to reinvest at high returns.

concepts.name: Schloss approach
concepts.def: Walter Schloss's simple value method: buy statistically cheap stocks, often near lows, diversify widely, avoid debt-laden firms and hold patiently, with little contact with management.

concepts.name: Neff total return ratio
concepts.def: John Neff's low P/E screen comparing earnings growth plus dividend yield with the P/E; ratios well above one flagged neglected value.
concepts.formula: (EPS growth % + dividend yield %) / P/E

concepts.name: Darvas box
concepts.def: Nicolas Darvas's method of buying stocks that break above a trading range of new highs on rising volume, with stops just below the box.

concepts.name: Grantham's two-sigma bubble
concepts.def: Jeremy Grantham's definition of a bubble as a two standard deviation departure from an asset's long-run price trend; he found nearly all such episodes eventually reverted.

concepts.name: Terry Smith approach
concepts.def: Fundsmith's three steps: buy good companies, do not overpay, do nothing; focus on high return, cash-generative businesses held for long periods.
concepts.aliases: fundsmith,buy good companies dont overpay do nothing

concepts.name: Klarman approach
concepts.def: Seth Klarman's value investing as risk aversion: demand a margin of safety, hold cash when bargains are scarce, favor catalysts and complexity others avoid, and judge results on an absolute basis.

concepts.name: Stocks for the long run
concepts.def: Jeremy Siegel's case that over long periods US equities have beaten bonds and cash in real terms, with lower real risk over very long horizons than commonly assumed. Critics stress survivorship of the US market.

concepts.name: Cash as an option
concepts.def: Treating cash as a call option on future bargains rather than a drag; its value rises with volatility and the chance of dislocations. Buffett and Klarman hold it when opportunities are scarce.

concepts.name: Buy and hold
concepts.def: Owning assets for long periods regardless of short-term moves, which cuts costs, taxes and timing errors but requires tolerating deep drawdowns.

concepts.name: Dollar-cost averaging
concepts.def: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, buying more units when prices are low. Lump sum investing usually wins on expected return since markets tend to rise, but DCA reduces regret and timing risk.

concepts.name: Market timing
concepts.def: Moving in and out of markets based on forecasts. Because a few large up days drive long-run returns and often follow sharp drops, missing them hurts badly; few investors time markets profitably after costs.
concepts.aliases: timing the market,time in the market

concepts.name: Keynes investment approach
concepts.def: Keynes moved from macro-driven timing, which failed for him, to concentrated holdings of a few businesses he understood well, held through volatility; he managed King's College's endowment this way.

concepts.name: Tulip mania (1637)
concepts.def: Dutch speculation in rare tulip bulbs, traded largely through informal forward contracts, that peaked and collapsed in early 1637. Historians debate its economic scale, but it remains the archetype of a speculative mania.

concepts.name: Dutch East India Company (1602)
concepts.def: The VOC, founded in 1602, issued transferable shares that traded in Amsterdam, creating an early permanent joint-stock company and one of the first active secondary stock markets.
concepts.aliases: voc,dutch east india company,first stock market

concepts.name: Mississippi bubble (1720)
concepts.def: John Law merged a note-issuing royal bank with the Mississippi Company in France, used new paper money to inflate its shares, and saw both collapse in 1720, discrediting paper money in France for decades.

concepts.name: South Sea bubble (1720)
concepts.def: South Sea Company shares soared in 1720 on a plan to swap UK government debt for its stock, then crashed; many other bubble companies floated alongside. Newton reportedly lost heavily.

concepts.name: Credit crisis of 1772
concepts.def: Panic that began in London when banker Alexander Fordyce fled after speculative losses, bringing down Scottish banks such as Ayr Bank and spreading to Amsterdam and the American colonies through credit chains.

concepts.name: Panic of 1792
concepts.def: First US financial panic, set off by William Duer's failed leveraged speculation in government debt and bank stock; Treasury Secretary Hamilton bought securities and supported lending to calm markets.

concepts.name: Panic of 1825
concepts.def: British banking panic after a boom in Latin American bonds and mining shares, including a fictitious country, Poyais; dozens of banks failed before the Bank of England lent freely.

concepts.name: Panic of 1837
concepts.def: US panic and long depression after land speculation, the Specie Circular requiring hard money for land and tighter British credit; many banks suspended specie payments.

concepts.name: Railway mania
concepts.def: British railway share boom of the 1840s that peaked around 1845 and 1846, then collapsed; many lines were built and investors lost heavily, a template for technology capex booms.

concepts.name: Panic of 1857
concepts.def: Triggered by the failure of the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company amid falling grain and railroad values; spread through telegraph-linked markets to Europe, an early global crisis.

concepts.name: Overend, Gurney crisis (1866)
concepts.def: Collapse of London discount house Overend, Gurney and Company in May 1866 set off a panic; Bank of England lending during it shaped Bagehot's Lombard Street.

concepts.name: Black Friday gold corner (1869)
concepts.def: Jay Gould and Jim Fisk tried to corner the New York gold market; gold collapsed on September 24, 1869 when the Treasury sold gold, ruining many speculators.

concepts.name: Panic of 1873
concepts.def: Jay Cooke and Company failed in September 1873 over railroad financing; the NYSE closed for ten days and a long depression followed in the US and Europe.

concepts.name: Baring crisis (1890)
concepts.def: Barings nearly failed after losses on Argentine securities; the Bank of England organized a guarantee fund with other banks to prevent a wider panic.

concepts.name: Lifeboat rescue
concepts.def: A central bank, treasury or leading banker organizes private institutions to jointly guarantee or recapitalize a failing firm to prevent contagion, as the Bank of England did for Barings in 1890, J.P. Morgan did in 1907 and the New York Fed did for LTCM in 1998.

concepts.name: Panic of 1893
concepts.def: Railroad failures and bank runs amid doubts about US gold reserves led to a severe depression; J.P. Morgan helped the Treasury restore gold reserves in 1895.

concepts.name: Northern Pacific corner (1901)
concepts.def: A control fight between Harriman and the Hill-Morgan group cornered Northern Pacific stock in May 1901, squeezing short sellers and briefly crashing the wider market.

concepts.name: Panic of 1907
concepts.def: A failed copper corner triggered runs on trust companies such as Knickerbocker Trust; J.P. Morgan organized private rescues. Its lessons led to the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.

concepts.name: NYSE closure (1914)
concepts.def: The NYSE closed from July 31, 1914 until December 1914 at the start of World War I to stop European selling of US securities from draining gold.

concepts.name: Classical gold standard
concepts.def: International system from about the 1870s to 1914 in which major currencies were convertible into gold at fixed rates; it gave price stability over decades but transmitted deflation and limited crisis lending.

concepts.name: Weimar hyperinflation (1923)
concepts.def: German hyperinflation that peaked in 1923 as money-financed deficits and reparations pressure destroyed the mark; holders of real assets and foreign currency survived while savers and bondholders were wiped out.

concepts.name: Florida land boom
concepts.def: Mid-1920s Florida real estate frenzy driven by trading of purchase binders and easy credit, which collapsed by 1926 and foreshadowed 1929.

concepts.name: Ponzi scheme
concepts.def: Fraud that pays earlier investors with money from new ones rather than from profits, named for Charles Ponzi's 1920 postal coupon scheme; it collapses when new money slows.

concepts.name: Great Depression
concepts.def: Worldwide depression from 1929 through the 1930s in which US output and prices fell sharply, thousands of banks failed and unemployment soared. Friedman and Schwartz blamed monetary contraction; Bernanke stressed credit disruption.

concepts.name: Bank of United States failure (1930)
concepts.def: Failure of the large New York Bank of United States in December 1930 after merger talks collapsed; one of the biggest bank failures of the early Depression and a blow to confidence.

concepts.name: Smoot-Hawley tariff (1930)
concepts.def: US tariff act of June 1930 that raised duties on many imports; trading partners retaliated and world trade shrank, though economists debate its share in the Depression.

concepts.name: Sterling leaves gold (1931)
concepts.def: Britain suspended gold convertibility in September 1931 after reserve losses; Eichengreen showed countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner from the Depression.

concepts.name: Kreuger crash (1932)
concepts.def: Ivar Kreuger's match empire collapsed after his death in March 1932, revealing large-scale fraud and fake assets; it fed demands for US securities disclosure laws.

concepts.name: Bank holiday (1933)
concepts.def: Roosevelt closed all US banks in March 1933 and reopened those judged sound with federal backing, ending the run wave; deposits flowed back.

concepts.name: Glass-Steagall (1933)
concepts.def: The Banking Act of 1933 separated commercial from investment banking and created federal deposit insurance through the FDIC; the separation was largely repealed in 1999.

concepts.name: Gold confiscation (1933)
concepts.def: Executive Order 6102 in April 1933 required Americans to sell most gold to the government; the Gold Reserve Act of 1934 then raised the official price to 35 dollars an ounce, devaluing the dollar.

concepts.name: Recession of 1937-1938
concepts.def: A sharp relapse within the Depression after fiscal tightening and higher bank reserve requirements; the standard warning about withdrawing support too early.

concepts.name: Treasury-Fed Accord (1951)
concepts.def: March 1951 agreement ending the Fed's wartime commitment to cap Treasury yields, restoring independent monetary policy after a period of rising inflation.

concepts.name: Onion Futures Act (1958)
concepts.def: After traders cornered onion futures in the mid-1950s, Congress banned onion futures trading in 1958; the ban still stands.

concepts.name: Kennedy slide (1962)
concepts.def: Sharp US stock decline in the first half of 1962, worst in late May, that ended an overvalued growth stock boom.

concepts.name: Salad oil scandal (1963)
concepts.def: Tino De Angelis borrowed against warehouse receipts for vegetable oil that largely did not exist; the 1963 collapse hit American Express and brokerages. Lesson: verify collateral yourself.

concepts.name: Go-go era
concepts.def: Late-1960s boom in concept stocks, conglomerates and aggressive performance funds, which ended in the 1969 to 1970 bear market.

concepts.name: Conglomerate boom
concepts.def: 1960s wave of unrelated acquisitions, often by high-P/E acquirers buying low-P/E firms with stock to manufacture EPS growth; it reversed when acquirer multiples fell.

concepts.name: Paperwork crisis
concepts.def: Late-1960s back-office breakdown when Wall Street volume overwhelmed manual settlement, forcing shortened trading days and broker failures; it led to SIPC in 1970 and central securities depositories.

concepts.name: Penn Central collapse (1970)
concepts.def: The Penn Central railroad's June 1970 bankruptcy left it in default on commercial paper and froze that market; the Fed opened the discount window so banks could replace issuers' funding.

concepts.name: Nixon shock (1971)
concepts.def: On August 15, 1971 Nixon suspended dollar convertibility into gold and imposed wage and price controls and an import surcharge, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system.

concepts.name: Nifty Fifty
concepts.def: Early-1970s large growth stocks treated as one-decision buys at very high P/Es; they fell hard in 1973 and 1974, though some later earned their prices. Lesson: quality at any price fails.

concepts.name: Bear market of 1973-1974
concepts.def: Severe US bear market in which the S&P 500 fell by nearly half amid the oil shock, rising inflation, Watergate and tight policy; real losses were among the worst since the 1930s.

concepts.name: Herstatt failure (1974)
concepts.def: German regulators closed Bankhaus Herstatt in June 1974 after it had received Deutsche marks but before it paid dollars to counterparties, giving FX settlement risk its name and prompting the Basel Committee.

concepts.name: Franklin National failure (1974)
concepts.def: Franklin National Bank of New York failed in October 1974 after FX losses and fraud, then the largest US bank failure; the Fed lent heavily to manage the wind-down.

concepts.name: May Day (1975)
concepts.def: On May 1, 1975 the SEC ended fixed brokerage commissions, cutting trading costs and opening the way for discount brokers.

concepts.name: Hunt silver collapse (1980)
concepts.def: The Hunt brothers built huge leveraged silver positions; exchange margin rule changes and Fed pressure forced liquidation, and silver crashed on Silver Thursday, March 27, 1980.

concepts.name: Latin American debt crisis
concepts.def: Mexico said in August 1982 it could not service its foreign debt, setting off a decade of defaults and restructurings across Latin America, resolved largely through Brady bonds from 1989.

concepts.name: Penn Square failure (1982)
concepts.def: Oklahoma's Penn Square Bank failed in July 1982 after reckless energy lending, much of which it had sold to larger banks such as Continental Illinois.

concepts.name: Continental Illinois rescue (1984)
concepts.def: A wholesale funding run on Continental Illinois in May 1984 led regulators to protect all depositors and creditors, giving rise to the phrase too big to fail.
concepts.aliases: continental illinois,too big to fail origin

concepts.name: Big Bang (1986)
concepts.def: Deregulation of the London Stock Exchange on October 27, 1986, ending fixed commissions and allowing outside ownership of member firms, which moved trading onto screens.

concepts.name: Savings and loan crisis
concepts.def: Failure of hundreds of US thrifts in the 1980s and early 1990s after rate mismatches, deregulation and risky lending, with deposit insurance encouraging gambling for resurrection; the Resolution Trust Corporation sold off assets.

concepts.name: RJR Nabisco buyout (1988)
concepts.def: KKR won a 1988 bidding war for RJR Nabisco, the largest LBO of its era, epitomizing the 1980s leverage boom and the winner's curse risk in auctions; chronicled in Barbarians at the Gate.

concepts.name: Friday the 13th mini-crash (1989)
concepts.def: US stock drop on Friday, October 13, 1989 after financing for a UAL buyout fell through, marking the end of the junk-financed LBO wave.

concepts.name: Drexel Burnham collapse (1990)
concepts.def: Drexel Burnham Lambert, the dominant junk bond underwriter under Michael Milken, filed for bankruptcy in February 1990 after legal penalties and losses in a weakening junk market.

concepts.name: Japanese asset bubble (1989)
concepts.def: Japanese stock and land bubble fed by easy money after the Plaza Accord; the Nikkei peaked at the end of 1989 and did not regain that level for over three decades, followed by years of deflation.

concepts.name: Nordic banking crisis
concepts.def: Early-1990s banking crises in Sweden, Finland and Norway after credit and property booms; Sweden's blanket guarantees, recapitalizations and bad banks became a model response.

concepts.name: BCCI closure (1991)
concepts.def: Regulators in several countries shut the Bank of Credit and Commerce International in July 1991 after uncovering massive fraud, money laundering and hidden losses across its global network.

concepts.name: ERM crisis (1992)
concepts.def: On Black Wednesday, September 16, 1992, the UK left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism after failing to defend sterling; Soros's Quantum Fund profited heavily from shorting the pound.

concepts.name: Orange County bankruptcy (1994)
concepts.def: Orange County, California filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after its treasurer's leveraged bet on falling rates through reverse repos and inverse floaters failed as the Fed raised rates.

concepts.name: Tequila crisis (1994)
concepts.def: Mexico devalued the peso in December 1994 amid a run on dollar-linked short-term debt; a US-led rescue followed. It showed the danger of short-term foreign currency borrowing.

concepts.name: Barings collapse (1995)
concepts.def: Barings Bank failed in February 1995 after trader Nick Leeson hid huge losses on Nikkei futures and options in Singapore; he controlled both trading and settlement.

concepts.name: Sumitomo copper affair (1996)
concepts.def: Sumitomo trader Yasuo Hamanaka's years-long manipulation of copper prices and hidden losses came to light in 1996, costing the firm billions.

concepts.name: Bre-X fraud (1997)
concepts.def: Canadian miner Bre-X's claimed giant Indonesian gold deposit was exposed in 1997 as salted core samples, wiping out investors. Lesson: verify primary data independently.

concepts.name: Russian default (1998)
concepts.def: In August 1998 Russia devalued the ruble, defaulted on domestic debt and froze some foreign payments, causing a global flight to quality that helped sink LTCM.

concepts.name: Hong Kong market intervention (1998)
concepts.def: In August 1998 the Hong Kong government bought large amounts of local stocks to defeat speculators who were shorting equities while attacking the currency peg.

concepts.name: Palm and 3Com mispricing (2000)
concepts.def: After 3Com sold part of Palm in a March 2000 IPO, Palm's market value implied 3Com's remaining businesses had large negative value, yet shorting Palm was hard. Lamont and Thaler's limits-to-arbitrage case.

concepts.name: Telecom bust
concepts.def: Collapse in 2000 to 2002 of telecom carriers and equipment makers after debt and vendor-financed overbuilding of fiber networks; much capacity sat unused for years.

concepts.name: September 11 market closure (2001)
concepts.def: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, US stock markets stayed closed until September 17; the Fed supplied heavy liquidity and stocks fell sharply in the week after reopening.

concepts.name: Enron collapse (2001)
concepts.def: Enron used off-balance-sheet partnerships and mark-to-market accounting to hide debt and inflate earnings; it filed for bankruptcy in December 2001 and its auditor Arthur Andersen collapsed.

concepts.name: Argentine default (2001)
concepts.def: Argentina defaulted at the end of 2001 as its one-to-one dollar peg collapsed; litigation by holdout creditors dragged on until 2016.

concepts.name: WorldCom fraud (2002)
concepts.def: WorldCom booked ordinary line costs as capital expenditure to inflate profits, then filed for bankruptcy in July 2002, the largest US filing to that date.

concepts.name: Parmalat collapse (2003)
concepts.def: Italian dairy group Parmalat collapsed in December 2003 when a bank account supposedly holding billions in cash turned out not to exist. Lesson: confirm cash balances directly.

concepts.name: US housing bubble
concepts.def: Mid-2000s US home price boom fed by loose lending, securitization and the belief that national prices never fall; its bust set off the 2008 crisis.

concepts.name: Paulson subprime trade
concepts.def: John Paulson's 2006 and 2007 bet against subprime mortgages through credit default swaps, one of the most profitable trades on record; cheap, asymmetric protection on fragile credit.

concepts.name: BNP Paribas fund freeze (2007)
concepts.def: On August 9, 2007 BNP Paribas froze three funds holding US subprime assets, saying they could not be valued; often marked as the start of the global financial crisis.

concepts.name: Northern Rock run (2007)
concepts.def: UK lender reliant on wholesale funding suffered the first British bank run in over a century in September 2007 after it sought Bank of England support; it was nationalized in 2008.

concepts.name: Societe Generale trading loss (2008)
concepts.def: Societe Generale disclosed in January 2008 that trader Jerome Kerviel had built huge unauthorized futures positions; unwinding them cost billions of euros.

concepts.name: Bear Stearns rescue (2008)
concepts.def: In March 2008 Bear Stearns lost its repo funding within days and was sold to JPMorgan with Fed support, showing how fast a wholesale-funded dealer can fail.

concepts.name: Lehman bankruptcy (2008)
concepts.def: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 without a rescue, freezing funding markets worldwide and turning a crisis into a panic.

concepts.name: Reserve Primary Fund breaks the buck (2008)
concepts.def: The Reserve Primary Fund fell below one dollar per share in September 2008 because of Lehman paper, sparking a run on money funds that the Treasury stopped with a guarantee.

concepts.name: AIG rescue (2008)
concepts.def: AIG had sold vast CDS protection on mortgage securities; collateral calls it could not meet led to a government rescue in September 2008 that also protected its counterparties.

concepts.name: TARP (2008)
concepts.def: The Troubled Asset Relief Program, enacted in October 2008, was used mainly to inject capital into banks and later automakers, a fiscal backstop for the financial system.

concepts.name: Short-sale ban (2008)
concepts.def: In September 2008 the SEC temporarily banned short selling in hundreds of financial stocks; studies found it widened spreads and hurt liquidity without stopping the declines.

concepts.name: Volkswagen squeeze (2008)
concepts.def: In October 2008 Porsche revealed it controlled most of Volkswagen's shares through stock and options, leaving little free float; shorts scrambled to cover and VW briefly became the world's most valuable company.

concepts.name: Madoff fraud (2008)
concepts.def: Bernard Madoff's decades-long Ponzi scheme was exposed in December 2008 as redemptions surged; red flags included unusually smooth returns, a tiny auditor and self-custody.

concepts.name: Icelandic banking collapse (2008)
concepts.def: Iceland's three main banks, grown to many times GDP on foreign funding, collapsed in October 2008, leading to capital controls and an IMF program.

concepts.name: MF Global collapse (2011)
concepts.def: Futures broker MF Global filed for bankruptcy in October 2011 after a large leveraged bet on European sovereign bonds; customer funds that should have been segregated were found missing.

concepts.name: US downgrade (2011)
concepts.def: S&P cut the US credit rating below AAA in August 2011 after a debt ceiling standoff; stocks fell but Treasuries rallied as a safe haven anyway.

concepts.name: Whatever it takes (2012)
concepts.def: ECB President Mario Draghi's July 2012 pledge to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro, backed by the OMT program, compressed periphery bond spreads without OMT ever being used.

concepts.name: Cyprus bail-in (2013)
concepts.def: The March 2013 Cyprus rescue imposed losses on uninsured depositors and capital controls, a template for bail-ins.

concepts.name: Treasury flash rally (2014)
concepts.def: On October 15, 2014 the 10-year Treasury yield swung sharply within minutes without major news, exposing fragile liquidity in a market dominated by automated trading.

concepts.name: China stock crash (2015)
concepts.def: Chinese stocks surged on margin financing, then crashed from June 2015 despite state buying; a surprise yuan devaluation in August spread turmoil to global markets.

concepts.name: Brexit vote (2016)
concepts.def: The UK's June 23, 2016 vote to leave the EU sent sterling sharply lower and caused a brief risk-off move; global equities recovered within weeks.

concepts.name: Blockchain name effect (2017)
concepts.def: In late 2017 small firms that added blockchain to their names, such as Long Island Iced Tea becoming Long Blockchain, saw sharp share jumps, a replay of the dot-com name effect.

concepts.name: Woodford fund suspension (2019)
concepts.def: Neil Woodford's flagship UK fund suspended redemptions in June 2019 after illiquid and unlisted holdings collided with outflows, then was wound up.

concepts.name: Powell pivot (2019)
concepts.def: After a sharp late-2018 selloff, the Fed signaled patience in January 2019 and paused rate hikes, reinforcing beliefs that the Fed would respond to market stress.

concepts.name: Hertz bankruptcy rally (2020)
concepts.def: Shares of bankrupt Hertz surged on retail buying in June 2020 and the company tried to sell new stock into the rally until the SEC objected; equity in bankruptcy is usually wiped out.

concepts.name: Wirecard collapse (2020)
concepts.def: German payments firm Wirecard admitted in June 2020 that a large share of its reported cash likely did not exist and filed for insolvency; short sellers and journalists had flagged it for years.

concepts.name: China property crisis
concepts.def: From 2021 Evergrande and other Chinese developers defaulted after regulators capped leverage with the three red lines, exposing a model funded by presales and rising prices.

concepts.name: Credit Suisse rescue (2023)
concepts.def: In March 2023 Credit Suisse was pushed into a takeover by UBS; its AT1 bonds were written to zero while shareholders received something, upending expectations about the creditor hierarchy.

concepts.name: DeepSeek selloff (2025)
concepts.def: In late January 2025 Chinese lab DeepSeek's low-cost reasoning model raised doubts about AI compute demand; Nvidia suffered one of the largest single-day market value losses on record and AI infrastructure stocks sold off.

concepts.name: Williams %R
concepts.def: Momentum oscillator by Larry Williams that places the close within the recent high-low range on a scale from 0 to -100; readings near 0 are overbought and near -100 oversold.
concepts.formula: %R = (highest high - close) / (highest high - lowest low) x -100

concepts.name: Commodity Channel Index
concepts.def: Oscillator by Donald Lambert measuring how far the typical price sits from its moving average in units of mean absolute deviation; moves beyond plus or minus 100 flag unusual strength or weakness.
concepts.formula: CCI = (typical price - SMA of typical price) / (0.015 x mean deviation)

concepts.name: Typical price
concepts.def: The average of a bar's high, low and close, used as the input price in CCI, money flow index, pivot points and some VWAP calculations.
concepts.formula: typical price = (high + low + close) / 3

concepts.name: Rate of change
concepts.def: Momentum indicator giving the percentage change in price over a fixed lookback; crossing zero marks a shift from falling to rising momentum over that window.
concepts.formula: ROC = (close / close n periods ago - 1) x 100

concepts.name: Chaikin money flow
concepts.def: Volume-weighted measure by Marc Chaikin of where closes fall within each bar's range, summed over a window; positive values suggest accumulation, negative values distribution.
concepts.formula: CMF = sum(money flow multiplier x volume, n) / sum(volume, n)

concepts.name: Money flow multiplier
concepts.def: Ratio from -1 to +1 locating the close within the bar's high-low range; +1 means a close at the high. It is the building block of Chaikin's volume indicators.
concepts.formula: MFM = ((close - low) - (high - close)) / (high - low)

concepts.name: Accumulation/distribution line
concepts.def: Cumulative running total of money flow volume developed by Marc Chaikin; divergence between the line and price is read as hidden buying or selling.
concepts.formula: ADL = prior ADL + money flow multiplier x volume

concepts.name: Technical indicator
concepts.def: A mathematical transformation of price, volume or open interest plotted with or below a chart to summarize trend, momentum, volatility or participation.

concepts.name: Oscillator
concepts.def: Indicator that fluctuates within a band or around a centre line, used to judge momentum and stretched conditions; most useful in ranges and prone to staying extreme in strong trends.

concepts.name: Keltner channels
concepts.def: Volatility envelope around an exponential moving average set at a multiple of average true range; closes outside the channel signal strong momentum, and Bollinger bands inside Keltner signal a squeeze.
concepts.formula: bands = EMA(n) plus or minus k x ATR(n)

concepts.name: Donchian channels
concepts.def: Bands drawn at the highest high and lowest low of the last n periods, from Richard Donchian; a new channel high or low is the classic breakout entry used by trend followers.
concepts.formula: upper = max(high, n); lower = min(low, n)

concepts.name: Price channel
concepts.def: Pair of lines bounding price action, either parallel trendlines, highest-high and lowest-low bands, or volatility envelopes, used to define trend and breakout levels.

concepts.name: Aroon indicator
concepts.def: Tushar Chande's indicator measuring how many periods have passed since the latest n-period high and low; Aroon up near 100 with Aroon down near 0 marks a strong uptrend.
concepts.formula: Aroon up = (n - periods since n-period high) / n x 100

concepts.name: Directional movement system
concepts.def: Welles Wilder's system of +DI and -DI lines comparing upward and downward range expansion to true range; their crossovers give direction and ADX gives trend strength.
concepts.formula: +DI = 100 x smoothed +DM / ATR; -DI = 100 x smoothed -DM / ATR

concepts.name: Force index
concepts.def: Alexander Elder's indicator combining price change and volume to measure the force behind a move; usually smoothed with a short EMA.
concepts.formula: force index = (close - prior close) x volume

concepts.name: Coppock curve
concepts.def: Long-term momentum indicator by Edwin Coppock: a weighted moving average of the sum of two long rates of change on monthly index data, traditionally used to spot major bear market bottoms.
concepts.formula: Coppock = WMA10(ROC14 + ROC11) on monthly data

concepts.name: Choppiness index
concepts.def: Indicator by E.W. Dreiss comparing the sum of true ranges with the overall high-low range over n bars; high values mean sideways chop, low values mean directional trending.
concepts.formula: CHOP = 100 x log10(sum TR(n) / (max high - min low)) / log10(n)

concepts.name: Weighted moving average
concepts.def: Moving average that gives linearly larger weights to more recent prices, reacting faster than a simple average of the same length.
concepts.formula: WMA = sum(w_i x P_i) / sum(w_i), with w = 1..n

concepts.name: Kaufman adaptive moving average
concepts.def: Moving average whose smoothing constant rises in trending markets and falls in noisy ones, set by the efficiency ratio, so it follows trends and flattens in chop.
concepts.formula: SC = (ER x (fast - slow) + slow)^2; KAMA_t = KAMA_t-1 + SC x (P - KAMA_t-1)

concepts.name: Linear regression channel
concepts.def: Least squares trendline fitted to price over a window with parallel lines at a multiple of the residual standard deviation, framing trend and dispersion around it.

concepts.name: Pivot points
concepts.def: Floor-trader levels computed from the prior period's high, low and close that mark likely intraday support and resistance; widely watched, which partly explains why they matter.

concepts.name: Anchored VWAP
concepts.def: Volume-weighted average price computed from a chosen event, such as an earnings gap or a major low, showing the average cost of everyone who traded since then.
concepts.formula: AVWAP = sum(P x V since anchor) / sum(V since anchor)

concepts.name: Volume profile
concepts.def: Histogram of traded volume at each price level over a period, plotted sideways, showing where the market accepted value and where it moved through quickly.

concepts.name: Point of control
concepts.def: The price level with the most traded volume or time in a profile; it acts as a magnet and as a reference for fair value during the session.

concepts.name: Value area
concepts.def: The price range around the point of control that contains a set share of volume or time, conventionally about 70 percent; trading outside it suggests initiative activity.

concepts.name: Market Profile
concepts.def: J. Peter Steidlmayer's chart format, developed at the CBOT, that stacks time-price opportunities by half-hour to show the distribution of activity across prices within a session.

concepts.name: Auction market theory
concepts.def: View that markets move to facilitate trade, auctioning up until buyers stop and down until sellers stop, alternating between balance around value and imbalance toward new value.

concepts.name: Bollinger bandwidth and %B
concepts.def: Bandwidth measures the width of Bollinger bands relative to the middle band and flags volatility contractions; %B locates price within the bands, with 1 at the upper band.
concepts.formula: BW = (upper - lower) / middle; %B = (price - lower) / (upper - lower)

concepts.name: Volatility squeeze
concepts.def: Setup where volatility contracts so far that Bollinger bands move inside Keltner channels, on the idea that compressed volatility tends to be followed by expansion and a directional move.

concepts.name: Chandelier exit
concepts.def: Trailing stop placed a multiple of ATR below the highest high since entry for longs, or above the lowest low for shorts, letting stops adapt to volatility.
concepts.formula: long stop = highest high(n) - k x ATR(n)

concepts.name: Heikin-Ashi
concepts.def: Candlestick variant built from averaged prices that smooths noise so trends show as runs of same-coloured candles; its plotted prices are not actual traded prices.
concepts.formula: HA close = (O + H + L + C) / 4; HA open = (prior HA open + prior HA close) / 2

concepts.name: OHLC bar chart
concepts.def: Chart that shows each period's open, high, low and close as a vertical range with left and right ticks; the Western equivalent of a candlestick.
concepts.aliases: bar chart,open high low close,hlc bar

concepts.name: Candlestick chart
concepts.def: Japanese charting form, popularized in the West by Steve Nison, that shows each period's open-to-close range as a body and its extremes as shadows, making buyer-seller balance easy to see.

concepts.name: Renko chart
concepts.def: Chart made of fixed-size bricks added only when price moves by the box size, ignoring time and small fluctuations to isolate trend.

concepts.name: Point and figure chart
concepts.def: Time-independent chart of X columns for rising prices and O columns for falling prices, with a new column only after a reversal of a set number of boxes.

concepts.name: Logarithmic price scale
concepts.def: Chart axis where equal distances represent equal percentage changes; essential for long histories, and trendlines drawn on it can differ from arithmetic ones.

concepts.name: Zigzag indicator
concepts.def: Line joining swing highs and lows that exceed a set percentage move, filtering minor noise; its last leg repaints, so it describes the past rather than signalling.

concepts.name: Moving average crossover
concepts.def: Signal generated when a faster moving average crosses a slower one, or price crosses an average; simple and robust in trends, costly in sideways markets through whipsaws.

concepts.name: MACD histogram
concepts.def: Bars showing MACD minus its signal line; shrinking bars show momentum slowing before the lines actually cross.
concepts.formula: histogram = MACD - signal line

concepts.name: Hidden divergence
concepts.def: Pattern where price makes a higher low while an oscillator makes a lower low (or the mirror for downtrends), read as a sign the trend will continue rather than reverse.

concepts.name: Repainting
concepts.def: When an indicator's past values change after new data arrives, as with zigzag or centred averages; backtests on repainted values show signals no trader could have acted on.

concepts.name: Whipsaw
concepts.def: A signal that reverses soon after it is taken, producing a small loss; frequent in range-bound markets and the main cost of trend-following systems.

concepts.name: False breakout
concepts.def: Move through support or resistance that quickly reverses back inside the range, trapping breakout traders; the trapped positions can fuel a sharp move the other way.

concepts.name: Breakout retest
concepts.def: Return of price to a broken level after a breakout, where former resistance should act as support (or vice versa); a hold confirms the breakout.

concepts.name: Role reversal (polarity)
concepts.def: Principle that broken support tends to become resistance and broken resistance becomes support, because traders who missed or lost on the level act around it.

concepts.name: Pullback
concepts.def: A temporary counter-trend move within an established trend, often toward a moving average or prior breakout level, used as a lower-risk entry point.

concepts.name: Trendline
concepts.def: Straight line joining successive higher lows in an uptrend or lower highs in a downtrend; more touches and a gentler slope make it more significant.

concepts.name: Swing highs and lows
concepts.def: Local price peaks and troughs that stand above or below neighbouring bars; their sequence defines trend structure and common stop placement.

concepts.name: Market structure (price)
concepts.def: Sequence of swing points: higher highs and higher lows define an uptrend, lower highs and lower lows a downtrend; a break of the last swing is a change of structure.
concepts.aliases: higher highs higher lows,hh hl,break of structure

concepts.name: Trend reversal
concepts.def: A change in the direction of the prevailing trend, signalled by broken structure, reversal patterns or divergence; distinct from a pullback, which resumes the trend.

concepts.name: Price action trading
concepts.def: Trading from raw price bars, swings and levels with few or no indicators, on the view that indicators only repackage price.

concepts.name: Multiple time frame analysis
concepts.def: Reading the same market on several chart periods so that trades follow the higher time frame trend and use the lower time frame for timing.

concepts.name: Regime filter
concepts.def: Rule that switches a strategy on or off based on a market condition, such as price above its 200-day average or volatility below a threshold, to avoid trading in hostile regimes.

concepts.name: Volatility breakout
concepts.def: Entry when price moves more than a multiple of recent volatility from a reference, such as the open or prior close; aims to catch range expansion early.

concepts.name: Chart pattern
concepts.def: Recurring geometric shape in price, classed as reversal or continuation, from which traders infer the likely next move and a measured target; evidence of reliability is mixed.

concepts.name: Head and shoulders
concepts.def: Reversal pattern of three peaks with the middle highest; a close below the neckline joining the troughs completes the top, with a target equal to head-to-neckline height.
concepts.formula: target = neckline - (head - neckline)

concepts.name: Inverse head and shoulders
concepts.def: Bottoming version of head and shoulders with three troughs, the middle lowest; a break above the neckline, ideally on rising volume, completes the reversal.
concepts.formula: target = neckline + (neckline - head)

concepts.name: Neckline
concepts.def: Line joining the reaction lows (or highs) of a head and shoulders or double top or bottom; its break is the trigger that completes the pattern.

concepts.name: Double top and double bottom
concepts.def: Reversal patterns where price fails twice near the same high (an M) or holds twice near the same low (a W); confirmed only when the intervening trough or peak breaks.

concepts.name: Cup with handle
concepts.def: Bullish continuation base popularized by William O'Neil: a U-shaped cup followed by a small, shallow pullback (the handle) near the old high, with entry on a breakout above the handle.

concepts.name: Triangles
concepts.def: Converging patterns where swings narrow between two trendlines: ascending (flat top, rising lows), descending (flat bottom, falling highs) and symmetrical; usually continuation, with breakouts in either direction possible.

concepts.name: Rising and falling wedges
concepts.def: Converging pattern where both trendlines slope the same way; a rising wedge is usually bearish and a falling wedge bullish, because momentum fades within the move.

concepts.name: Flag
concepts.def: Short, rectangular counter-trend consolidation after a sharp move (the pole), on declining volume; a breakout in the trend direction projects a move similar to the pole.
concepts.formula: target = breakout point + pole length

concepts.name: Pennant
concepts.def: Small symmetrical triangle forming after a sharp move, read the same way as a flag: brief pause, then continuation by roughly the length of the prior move.

concepts.name: Rectangle (trading range)
concepts.def: Sideways range bounded by horizontal support and resistance; a close outside it signals the direction of the next move, often by about the range height.

concepts.name: Measured move
concepts.def: Price target method assuming the next leg will roughly equal a prior leg or pattern height, used with flags, ranges and head and shoulders.

concepts.name: V-shaped reversal
concepts.def: Abrupt trend reversal with no base or topping process, hard to anticipate because no pattern forms first; common after capitulation.

concepts.name: Capitulation
concepts.def: Final stage of a decline when remaining holders sell in panic regardless of price, often on extreme volume and breadth; frequently marks or precedes a low.

concepts.name: Price gap
concepts.def: Range on a chart with no trading because a bar opened beyond the prior bar's high or low, usually after news; classed as common, breakaway, runaway or exhaustion.

concepts.name: Breakaway gap
concepts.def: Gap that launches price out of a base or range on heavy volume, marking the start of a new trend; it often stays unfilled.

concepts.name: Runaway gap
concepts.def: Gap in the middle of a strong trend, signalling continued urgency; it is said to occur near the halfway point of the move.

concepts.name: Exhaustion gap
concepts.def: Late-trend gap on climactic volume that is soon reversed and filled, marking the final burst of buying or selling.

concepts.name: Island reversal
concepts.def: Cluster of bars isolated by a gap on each side, an exhaustion gap then a breakaway gap in the opposite direction; a sharp reversal signal.

concepts.name: Earnings gap
